steps.why: Quiet inspiration is active: muscles do the work, and they contract only when their nerves fire.

steps.label: Thorax enlarges
steps.text: The diaphragm contracts, flattens and moves down, and the external intercostals lift the ribs up and out: the thoracic cavity gets longer and wider.
steps.why: Both muscles contract together when their nerves fire. The diaphragm does most of the work of a quiet breath in; the ribs rising like a bucket handle widen the chest from side to side and from front to back.

steps.label: Intrapleural pressure falls
steps.text: The chest wall moves outward and pulls harder on the pleural fluid film: intrapleural pressure falls from about −4 to about −6 mm Hg.
steps.why: The fluid film holds the lung to the chest wall, so an outward pull on the wall stretches the film and lowers its pressure.

steps.label: Lungs expand
steps.text: Transpulmonary pressure rises from 4 to about 6 mm Hg, and the lungs and alveoli expand.
steps.why: Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus intrapleural pressure; a larger difference stretches the lungs to a larger size.

steps.label: Alveolar pressure falls
steps.text: By Boyle’s law, the larger alveolar volume lowers alveolar pressure to about −1 mm Hg.
steps.why: The same number of gas molecules in a larger space strike the walls less often, so the pressure falls.

steps.label: Air flows in
steps.text: Air flows down the pressure gradient from the atmosphere into the alveoli.
steps.why: Air, like any fluid, flows from higher to lower pressure, and the alveoli are now below atmospheric.

steps.label: Gradient gone: flow stops
steps.text: Alveolar pressure climbs back to 0, and when it equals atmospheric pressure, flow stops.
steps.why: Incoming air adds molecules to the alveoli, raising their pressure until no gradient is left.

distractors.text: The lungs pull air in by contracting their own smooth muscle.
distractors.why: The lungs have no muscle that sucks air in. They expand passively because the chest wall pulls on them through the pleural film.

distractors.text: Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure.
distractors.why: A pressure above atmospheric would push air out. For air to flow in, alveolar pressure must fall below it.

distractors.text: Intrapleural pressure rises to atmospheric pressure.
distractors.why: That is what happens in a pneumothorax, and it collapses the lung. In a normal breath in, intrapleural pressure falls.

error.text: The chest wall moves outward, and intrapleural pressure rises from about −4 to about −2 mm Hg.
error.why: An outward pull on the pleural film lowers its pressure further below atmospheric, to about −6 mm Hg. That larger negative pressure is what raises transpulmonary pressure and expands the lungs.

pathways.summary: Nerve signal, muscles contract, thorax enlarges, intrapleural pressure falls, the lungs expand, alveolar pressure falls by Boyle’s law, and air flows in until the gradient is gone. Quiet expiration is the same chain run backward by elastic recoil, with no muscle needed.

pathways.title: Oxygen from air to a tissue cell
pathways.intro: Follow one oxygen molecule from a breath of air to the mitochondria of a muscle cell in your leg.

steps.label: Breathed in
steps.text: Air is breathed in, warmed and moistened, and reaches the alveoli, where its PO2 is about 100 mm Hg.
steps.why: Mixing with the air already in the alveoli lowers the PO2 from about 150 in the airways to about 100 mm Hg.

steps.label: Crosses membrane
steps.text: Oxygen diffuses across the respiratory membrane and dissolves in the plasma of a pulmonary capillary.
steps.why: Blood arriving from the tissues has a PO2 of about 40, so oxygen moves down a 60 mm Hg gradient.

steps.label: Binds hemoglobin
steps.text: Oxygen diffuses into a red blood cell and binds heme iron, forming oxyhemoglobin; blood leaves the lungs about 97 to 98% saturated.
steps.why: Oxygen must dissolve in plasma before it can reach hemoglobin. At a PO2 near 100 mm Hg hemoglobin sits on the flat top of its curve and loads almost fully.

steps.label: Left heart
steps.text: The pulmonary veins carry the blood to the left atrium, and the left ventricle pumps it into the aorta.
steps.why: Oxygenated blood returns to the left side of the heart, which pumps it through the systemic circuit.

steps.label: Systemic arteries
steps.text: Systemic arteries carry the blood to a capillary bed in the working muscle.
steps.why: The arteries branch down to arterioles that feed each capillary bed.

steps.label: Hemoglobin unloads
steps.text: Low PO2, high PCO2, acid and warmth in the muscle make hemoglobin release oxygen, which dissolves in the plasma.
steps.why: At the low PO2 of the tissue, hemoglobin is on the steep part of its curve, and the right shift from carbon dioxide, acid and heat releases even more.

steps.label: Into the cell
steps.text: Oxygen diffuses from the plasma through the interstitial fluid into the cell.
steps.why: The cell keeps using oxygen, so its PO2 stays below that of the blood and oxygen keeps moving in.

steps.label: Mitochondria
steps.text: In the mitochondria, the electron transport chain uses the oxygen.
steps.why: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of aerobic respiration, and using it up is what keeps the gradient running from the air to the cell.

distractors.text: Oxygen stays dissolved in the plasma instead of entering red blood cells, because plasma carries almost all of the oxygen that blood delivers to the tissues.
distractors.why: Plasma dissolves only 0.3 mL of oxygen per 100 mL at a PO2 of 100 mm Hg. About 98.5% of the oxygen in blood rides on hemoglobin.

distractors.text: Oxygen binds the globin chains of hemoglobin rather than its iron.
distractors.why: Oxygen binds the iron at the center of each heme group, one oxygen molecule per iron, so one hemoglobin carries four.

distractors.text: Oxygen is pumped into red blood cells by active transport.
distractors.why: Nothing pumps oxygen. It crosses every membrane by simple diffusion, down its partial pressure gradient.

error.text: High PO2 and low PCO2 in the muscle make hemoglobin hold on to its oxygen more tightly.
error.why: Working muscle has a low PO2 and a high PCO2, with acid and heat. Those conditions put hemoglobin on the steep part of its curve and shift the curve right, so it releases oxygen.

pathways.summary: Every step runs downhill in PO2: air 150, alveoli 100, arterial blood about 95, tissue 40 or less, mitochondria lowest. Hemoglobin carries almost all of it between the lungs and the tissues, loading on the flat top of its curve and unloading on the steep middle.

pathways.title: Carbon dioxide from a tissue cell to air
pathways.intro: Follow one carbon dioxide molecule, made in a muscle cell, to the air you breathe out. Most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate, so follow that route.

steps.label: Made in mitochondria
steps.text: A cell makes carbon dioxide in its mitochondria during cellular respiration.
steps.why: Carbon dioxide is a waste product of aerobic respiration, so the trip starts where it is made.

steps.label: Into a capillary
steps.text: Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the cell, through the interstitial fluid and into a systemic capillary.
steps.why: PCO2 is highest in the cell and lower in the arriving blood, so it moves down its gradient: internal respiration.

steps.label: Into a red blood cell
steps.text: Most of it diffuses on into a red blood cell.
steps.why: The red blood cell holds the enzyme that turns carbon dioxide into bicarbonate quickly; the plasma has almost none.

steps.label: Carbonic anhydrase
steps.text: Carbonic anhydrase converts it to carbonic acid, which splits into a hydrogen ion and a bicarbonate ion.
steps.why: At high PCO2 the reaction runs to the right, and the enzyme lets it finish within the second the blood spends in the capillary.

steps.label: H+ bound; chloride shift
steps.text: The hydrogen ion binds deoxyhemoglobin, and the bicarbonate leaves the cell through band 3 in exchange for chloride.
steps.why: Removing both products keeps the reaction running: hemoglobin buffers the H+, and the chloride shift moves bicarbonate out into the plasma.

steps.label: Veins → right heart
steps.text: The bicarbonate travels in the plasma through the veins and the right side of the heart to a pulmonary capillary.
steps.why: Venous blood returns to the right side of the heart, which pumps it to the lungs.

steps.label: Bicarbonate re-enters
steps.text: Alveolar PCO2 is lower, and bicarbonate re-enters the red blood cell in exchange for chloride.
steps.why: In the lungs the whole sequence reverses, starting with the chloride shift in reverse.

steps.label: CO2 re-formed
steps.text: Oxygen binds hemoglobin, which releases its hydrogen ions; they combine with bicarbonate, and carbonic anhydrase turns the carbonic acid into carbon dioxide and water.
steps.why: Oxyhemoglobin holds H+ less tightly (the Haldane effect), and at low PCO2 the reaction runs to the left.

steps.label: Into the alveolus
steps.text: Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the red blood cell, across the respiratory membrane and into the alveoli.
steps.why: Blood PCO2 of about 46 exceeds the alveolar 40 mm Hg, so it diffuses out: external respiration.

steps.label: Breathed out
steps.text: You breathe it out.
steps.why: Expiration carries the alveolar air, and the carbon dioxide in it, back up the airway to the outside.

distractors.text: The bicarbonate stays inside the red blood cell, bound to hemoglobin, and is carried there all the way through the veins to the lungs.
distractors.why: Bicarbonate does not bind hemoglobin, and building up inside the cell would slow the reaction. Most of it leaves through band 3 and travels in the plasma.

distractors.text: The hydrogen ion stays free in the plasma, and venous blood becomes strongly acidic.
distractors.why: Almost all the hydrogen ions bind hemoglobin, which buffers them. Venous pH is only about 7.36, against 7.40 in arterial blood.

distractors.text: An ATP-driven pump swaps bicarbonate out for sodium in.
distractors.why: Band 3 swaps bicarbonate for chloride, one negative ion for another, by facilitated diffusion. No ATP is used.

error.text: Carbonic anhydrase in the plasma converts it to carbonic acid, which splits into a hydrogen ion and a bicarbonate ion.
error.why: Plasma has almost none of the enzyme, so little bicarbonate forms there. The fast conversion happens inside red blood cells.

pathways.summary: Made in the cell, diffused into the blood, turned into bicarbonate inside red blood cells, carried in the plasma, turned back into carbon dioxide in the lungs, and breathed out. The same reactions run in both places; only the direction differs, set by PCO2.

pathways.title: Inside a red blood cell: bicarbonate and the chloride shift
pathways.intro: A red blood cell enters a capillary in a working muscle. Trace what carbon dioxide does inside it, step by step.

steps.label: CO2 diffuses in
steps.text: Carbon dioxide diffuses from the plasma into the red blood cell.
steps.why: The muscle makes carbon dioxide, so PCO2 around the cell is higher than inside it.

steps.label: Carbonic anhydrase acts
steps.text: Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO2 + H2O → H2CO3.
steps.why: This first step is slow on its own. The enzyme speeds it thousands of times, so it finishes while the cell is still in the capillary.

steps.label: Split; H+ bound
steps.text: Carbonic acid splits into H+ and HCO3−, and the H+ binds deoxyhemoglobin.
steps.why: The split is almost instant. Hemoglobin is giving up oxygen at this moment, and deoxyhemoglobin binds H+ more readily, so it mops up the acid as it forms.

steps.label: Band 3: HCO3− out, Cl− in
steps.text: Bicarbonate leaves through band 3, and one chloride ion comes in for each.
steps.why: Bicarbonate is building up inside, so it moves out down its concentration gradient. A one-for-one swap keeps the charge across the membrane unchanged.

steps.label: Cell swells slightly
steps.text: The cell has gained ions, so water follows and it swells a little.
steps.why: Bicarbonate made inside and chloride brought in add dissolved particles, and water follows solute by osmosis. Venous hematocrit is a few percent higher for this reason.

distractors.text: Bicarbonate leaves through band 3, and one sodium ion leaves alongside each one.
distractors.why: Band 3 is an exchanger for negative ions: one bicarbonate out, one chloride in.

distractors.text: The sodium–potassium pump drives bicarbonate out of the cell.
distractors.why: The chloride shift uses no ATP. It is facilitated diffusion through band 3, each ion moving down its own gradient.

distractors.text: Bicarbonate binds the heme iron in place of oxygen.
distractors.why: Heme iron binds oxygen and carbon monoxide. Bicarbonate is carried in the plasma, not on hemoglobin.

error.text: Carbonic acid splits into H+ and HCO3−, and the H+ binds oxyhemoglobin, which holds H+ more tightly than deoxyhemoglobin.
error.why: It is the other way round: deoxyhemoglobin binds H+ more readily. That is why hemoglobin becomes a better buffer as it gives up oxygen in the tissues.

pathways.summary: In, convert, split, buffer, swap: carbonic anhydrase makes bicarbonate fast, hemoglobin soaks up the H+, and band 3 trades bicarbonate for chloride so more carbon dioxide can follow. In the lungs every step runs backward.

pathways.title: Carbon dioxide drives breathing through the brain
pathways.intro: Your arterial PCO2 creeps up from 40 to 45 mm Hg. Trace how that change reaches the neurons that set your breathing, and how breathing brings it back.

steps.label: Arterial PCO2 rises
steps.text: Arterial PCO2 rises.
steps.why: The loop starts with the regulated variable moving away from its set point.

steps.label: CO2 crosses the barrier
steps.text: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood–brain barrier into the brain’s interstitial fluid.
steps.why: Carbon dioxide is small and dissolves in lipids, so it crosses easily. Hydrogen ions and bicarbonate cross poorly.

steps.label: H+ forms in brain fluid
steps.text: In the brain’s fluid, carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions.
steps.why: The same reaction as in blood runs to the right when PCO2 rises.

steps.label: Brain fluid pH falls
steps.text: The fluid holds little protein and buffers poorly, so its pH falls more than blood pH would.
steps.why: Fewer buffers means more of the new hydrogen ions stay free.

steps.label: Central chemoreceptors fire
steps.text: Central chemoreceptors near the front surface of the medulla oblongata sense the rise in hydrogen ions.
steps.why: These neurons respond to H+ in the fluid around them, not to oxygen.

steps.label: Centers drive harder
steps.text: They stimulate the respiratory centers, which send stronger, more frequent bursts down the phrenic and intercostal nerves.
steps.why: Short connections within the brainstem carry the signal to the control center, which sets depth and rate.

steps.label: Ventilation rises
steps.text: Breathing gets deeper and faster, and alveolar ventilation rises.
steps.why: The diaphragm and intercostals contract harder and more often.

steps.label: PCO2 falls back
steps.text: More carbon dioxide is breathed out, and arterial PCO2 falls back toward 40 mm Hg.
steps.why: At steady production, PCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation: negative feedback removes the stimulus.

distractors.text: Hydrogen ions from the blood cross the blood–brain barrier freely into the brain’s interstitial fluid.
distractors.why: Hydrogen ions cross the barrier poorly. That is why acid added to the blood by other causes reaches the central chemoreceptors only slowly.

distractors.text: The carotid bodies send the signal to the cerebral cortex.
distractors.why: The carotid bodies report to the medulla oblongata through the glossopharyngeal nerves. This chain is the central route, which accounts for most of the response to carbon dioxide.

distractors.text: Low oxygen crosses into the brain and stimulates the central chemoreceptors.
distractors.why: Central chemoreceptors do not sense oxygen. Only the peripheral chemoreceptors respond to a low PO2.

error.text: Central chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies sense the fall in oxygen.
error.why: Central chemoreceptors lie in the medulla oblongata and sense hydrogen ions made from carbon dioxide. The carotid bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors, and oxygen has not changed in this chain.

pathways.summary: Carbon dioxide slips across the blood–brain barrier, becomes acid in poorly buffered brain fluid, and the central chemoreceptors drive breathing up until the extra carbon dioxide is blown off. Over a day or two they adapt to a lasting change, as bicarbonate in the cerebrospinal fluid is adjusted.

pathways.title: How smoking causes emphysema
pathways.intro: A man smokes a pack a day for decades. Trace how the smoke turns healthy alveoli into air trapping and breathlessness.

steps.label: Chronic inflammation
steps.text: Smoke irritates the lungs, draws in neutrophils and activates alveolar macrophages.
steps.why: The chain begins with the body’s defensive response to a constant irritant.

steps.label: Enzymes unchecked
steps.text: These cells release protein-digesting enzymes that break down elastic fibers in the alveolar walls, while smoke inactivates alpha-1 antitrypsin, the protein that normally blocks them.
steps.why: Normally protective proteins keep the enzymes in check. Smoke adds enzymes and disables the protection at the same time, so the balance tips toward digestion.

steps.label: Walls destroyed
steps.text: Alveolar walls and their capillaries are destroyed faster than they are repaired, and small alveoli merge into large spaces.
steps.why: Unopposed enzymes digest the walls, and each lost wall takes its capillaries with it.

steps.label: Recoil and support lost
steps.text: Elastic recoil weakens, and the small airways lose the outward pull that held them open.
steps.why: Elastic fibers both push air out and act like guy ropes on the outside of the small airways, which have no cartilage.

steps.label: Airways collapse
steps.text: During each breath out, the pressure around the small airways squeezes them shut.
steps.why: Without the outward pull, nothing resists the rising pressure around the airways as the lungs shrink.

steps.label: Air trapped
steps.text: Air is trapped behind the closed airways: residual volume rises and the chest becomes barrel-shaped.
steps.why: Air that cannot get out stays in the lungs, which become overinflated and flatten the diaphragm.

distractors.text: Goblet cells multiply and mucus plugs the bronchi.
distractors.why: That is the mechanism of chronic bronchitis. Emphysema is a disease of the alveolar walls, and people with it cough up little mucus.

distractors.text: Scar tissue builds up in the alveolar walls, thickening them and making the whole lung stiffer.
distractors.why: Scarring is fibrosis, which lowers compliance. Emphysema destroys walls and raises compliance.

distractors.text: Airway smooth muscle contracts in response to histamine.
distractors.why: Bronchoconstriction driven by mast cells is the mechanism of asthma, which largely reverses. The damage in emphysema does not.

error.text: The lungs become stiffer, and elastic recoil strengthens.
error.why: Losing elastic fibers makes the lungs floppier: compliance rises and recoil weakens. That is why breathing out, not in, becomes the hard part.

pathways.summary: Inflammation, unchecked enzymes, lost walls: less surface for diffusion, and less elastic support for the airways, which collapse and trap air on every breath out. Pursed-lip breathing keeps the airway pressure up and holds them open a little longer.

pathways.title: Regrowth of a cut axon in a nerve
pathways.intro: A carpenter cuts a nerve at the base of his thumb, and a surgeon sews the ends together. Trace what happens to one of its axons, from the cut to working again.

steps.label: Axon cut
steps.text: The axon is cut, separating the far part from its soma.
steps.why: Everything that follows starts from the far part losing its connection to the soma, where nearly all of the axon’s proteins are made.

steps.label: Far part breaks down
steps.text: Within days the far part of the axon fragments and its myelin falls apart (Wallerian degeneration).
steps.why: Cut off from axonal transport, the far part gets no new proteins, so it cannot maintain itself and breaks down first.

steps.label: Debris cleared
steps.text: Schwann cells break down their own myelin and call in macrophages from the blood, and together they clear the debris over a few weeks.
steps.why: The wreckage has to go before a path can form, and it is there to clear only once the far part has broken down.

steps.label: Schwann cells form a tube
steps.text: Schwann cells multiply and line up inside the old connective tissue sheath, forming a regeneration tube coated with growth-promoting molecules.
steps.why: Once the sheath is cleared, the Schwann cells can fill it and build the guide the new axon will need.

steps.label: Sprout grows ~1 mm/day
steps.text: Sprouts grow from the cut end, and one that finds the tube is guided along it at about 1 millimeter a day.
steps.why: The sprout needs the tube to follow; without it, sprouts wander into scar tissue. Meanwhile the soma has swollen, dispersed its Nissl bodies and switched to making growth proteins, which slow axonal transport delivers at about the rate the tip advances.

steps.label: Reconnects and remyelinated
steps.text: The axon reaches a target, Schwann cells wrap it in new, shorter myelin segments, and it can carry signals again.
steps.why: Myelination and function return last, only after the axon has made the whole journey to its target.

distractors.text: Oligodendrocytes move out of the spinal cord into the nerve, multiply and line up inside the old connective tissue sheath, forming a tube that guides the regrowing axon.
distractors.why: Oligodendrocytes are CNS glia and do not form a guiding tube; that is one reason CNS axons rarely regrow. In a nerve, Schwann cells build the tube.

distractors.text: Astrocytes wall off the cut with a dense glial scar that the axon grows through.
distractors.why: Astrocytes are CNS glia, and a glial scar blocks regrowing axons rather than guiding them.

distractors.text: The two cut ends of the axon fuse back together within a day.
distractors.why: Cut axons do not rejoin. The far part dies, and a new axon has to grow the whole distance from the stump.

error.text: Sprouts grow from the cut end, and one that finds the tube is guided along it at about 1 centimeter a day.
error.why: Regrowth is about 1 millimeter a day, the speed of slow axonal transport. That is why a nerve cut 20 cm from a fingertip takes six months or more to bring back feeling.

pathways.summary: The part beyond the cut dies back and is cleared while the soma retools for growth; Schwann cells build a tube; the axon regrows along it at about a millimeter a day and is remyelinated once it reaches its target.

pathways.title: How a Schwann cell builds myelin
pathways.intro: A Schwann cell settles against one segment of a peripheral axon. Trace how it turns part of itself into the myelin sheath.

steps.label: Settles on one segment
steps.text: The Schwann cell settles against one segment of a single axon.
steps.why: A Schwann cell devotes itself to one segment of one axon, so wrapping starts only once it has found its segment.

steps.label: Flattens into a sheet
steps.text: It flattens part of itself into a thin sheet and lays the edge against the axon.
steps.why: A thin sheet of membrane is what gets wound around the axon, so it must form before any wrapping can happen.

steps.label: Spirals round the axon
steps.text: The sheet spirals around the axon many times, sometimes a hundred, like a bandage wound around a finger.
steps.why: Each turn adds two more layers of membrane. The more turns, the better the insulation.

steps.label: Cytoplasm squeezed out
steps.text: As it winds, the cytoplasm is squeezed out of the layers, leaving tightly packed membranes that are mostly lipid.
steps.why: Packing only happens once the layers are wound. The lipid-rich, tightly packed membrane is what makes myelin a good insulator.

steps.label: Nucleus left outside
steps.text: The Schwann cell’s nucleus and remaining cytoplasm end up in a thin outer layer, the neurilemma, and a node of Ranvier is left bare on each side.
steps.why: Whatever cytoplasm is squeezed out collects on the outside, so the living outer layer is the last part to take shape. It is what later lets Schwann cells help repair a cut axon.

distractors.text: The sheet wraps segments of dozens of different axons at once.
distractors.why: That is what an oligodendrocyte does in the CNS, with a separate arm for each axon. A Schwann cell wraps one segment of one axon.

distractors.text: The cell secretes a fatty coat onto the axon, the way a gland releases its product.
distractors.why: Myelin is not secreted. It is the glial cell’s own plasma membrane, wound around the axon in layers.

error.text: As it winds, cytoplasm fills the space between the layers, so myelin is mostly water and protein.
error.why: The cytoplasm is squeezed out, not packed in. That leaves layer on layer of membrane, so myelin is mostly lipid, about 70 to 80% of its dry weight.

pathways.summary: A Schwann cell flattens part of itself into a sheet, winds it around one axon segment many times, squeezes the cytoplasm out of the layers, and ends with its nucleus in a thin outer layer, the neurilemma.

pathways.title: Action potential steps in detail: gates and refractory periods
pathways.intro: You met the short version of the action potential in Foundations. Now trace one spike at the trigger zone of an axon with the sodium channel’s two gates and the refractory periods, from rest back to rest.

steps.label: Rest: Na+ channels ready
steps.text: At rest, about −70 mV, each sodium channel’s activation gate is shut and its inactivation gate hangs open: closed and ready.
steps.why: The cycle starts and ends here. Only a channel in this ready state can be opened by depolarization.

steps.label: Graded potential spreads
steps.text: A graded depolarization spreads to the trigger zone, the initial segment just beyond the axon hillock.
steps.why: The initial segment has the densest sodium channels, so it is where a graded potential can first bring the membrane to threshold.

steps.label: Threshold, about −55 mV
steps.text: At about −55 mV, enough activation gates open that sodium entering outruns potassium leaving.
steps.why: That crossover is what threshold means; below it, potassium leaving wins and the depolarization fades.

steps.label: Positive feedback to +30
steps.text: Sodium entry depolarizes the membrane, which opens more activation gates: the rising phase reaches about +30 mV in half a millisecond.
steps.why: Each bit of depolarization opens more channels, which let in more sodium, so once past threshold the rise feeds itself.

steps.label: Inactivation gates plug
steps.text: About a millisecond after opening, the inactivation gates swing into the pores and sodium entry stops. With every channel open or inactivated, the axon is absolutely refractory.
steps.why: The inactivation gate is slower than the activation gate, so it closes only after the rise. With every channel open or inactivated, no stimulus can start a second spike.

steps.label: Delayed K+ out: falling
steps.text: The delayed potassium channels, opened by the same depolarization, are now open; potassium flows out and the membrane repolarizes.
steps.why: The potassium channels respond about as slowly as inactivation, so their outflow arrives just as sodium inflow ends, and the voltage falls.

steps.label: Na+ channels reset
steps.text: As the membrane repolarizes, sodium channels begin resetting to closed and ready. A stronger-than-normal stimulus could now fire the axon: the relative refractory period.
steps.why: Resetting needs repolarization, so it can only start during the falling phase. With some channels ready but potassium channels still open, a spike is possible but harder.

steps.label: Dip to about −80 mV
steps.text: The potassium channels close slowly, so extra potassium leaves and the membrane dips to about −80 mV, the afterhyperpolarization.
steps.why: Potassium keeps leaving until its slow channels shut, pulling the voltage past rest toward potassium’s equilibrium potential of about −90 mV.

steps.label: Back to rest
steps.text: The potassium channels close, the leak channels restore −70 mV, and every sodium channel is ready again.
steps.why: Once the extra potassium channels shut, the leak channels alone set the voltage, and the axon can fire normally again.

distractors.text: The sodium–potassium pump restores the ion gradients that the spike used up, and until it has finished, no new action potential can start at the trigger zone, however strong the stimulus that arrives.
distractors.why: One spike moves only a tiny fraction of the ions, and the pump works slowly in the background. The refractory period comes from inactivated sodium channels, not from the pump.

distractors.text: The activation gates close at the peak, and they can reopen at once if another stimulus arrives.
distractors.why: The rise is ended by the inactivation gate plugging the pore while the activation gate is still open. An inactivated channel cannot reopen until repolarization resets it.

distractors.text: Potassium rushes into the axon and cancels the sodium, stopping the rise.
distractors.why: Potassium is concentrated inside, so it flows out, not in. The rise stops because sodium channels inactivate as the delayed potassium channels open.

error.text: As the membrane repolarizes, sodium channels begin resetting to closed and ready. No stimulus of any strength can fire the axon until every channel has reset.
error.why: That describes the absolute refractory period, which ends when some channels have reset. During the relative refractory period a spike is possible, but only with a stronger-than-normal stimulus.

pathways.summary: Threshold starts positive feedback through the activation gates; the slower inactivation gates end the rise and make the axon absolutely refractory; delayed potassium channels repolarize it and carry it below rest; channels reset only as the membrane repolarizes, so the relative refractory period follows.

pathways.title: Saltatory conduction along a myelinated axon
pathways.intro: Touch information leaves your fingertip on a myelinated axon. Trace how the signal gets from one node of Ranvier to the next.

steps.label: Node fires
steps.text: An action potential fires at one node of Ranvier, and sodium rushes in through its densely packed channels.
steps.why: Nodes are the only places with many voltage-gated sodium channels, so they are where the membrane can fire.

steps.label: Current flows inside
steps.text: The entering positive charge spreads as current along the inside of the axon, under the myelin.
steps.why: Charge that enters at the node has to go somewhere; it spreads along the axoplasm toward the neighboring stretches.

steps.label: Myelin limits leak
steps.text: The myelin insulates the wall, so very little of the current leaks out through the internode.
steps.why: Layer on layer of lipid-rich membrane conducts poorly, so most of the current stays inside and keeps going.

steps.label: Next node to threshold
steps.text: The current reaches the next node, about a millimeter away, still strong enough to bring it to threshold.
steps.why: Only because little was lost on the way does enough current arrive to depolarize the next node to threshold.

steps.label: Next node fires
steps.text: That node fires a full action potential of its own.
steps.why: Each node regenerates the spike at full size, so the signal does not fade however long the axon is.

steps.label: Only forward
steps.text: The node behind is in its absolute refractory period, so the signal moves only forward, node to node.
steps.why: The node that just fired has inactivated sodium channels, so the current spreading back toward it cannot fire it again.

distractors.text: The action potential jumps across the myelin through the air outside the axon.
distractors.why: Nothing literally jumps. Current flows the whole way along the inside of the axon; only the slow firing step is skipped under the myelin.

distractors.text: Every patch of membrane under the myelin fires in turn.
distractors.why: That is continuous conduction in an unmyelinated axon. Under myelin there are very few sodium channels, so those stretches do not fire.

error.text: The current reaches the next node, about a millimeter away, having grown stronger as it traveled.
error.why: Current spreading passively along an axon always weakens with distance. Myelin keeps the loss small, which is why the current is still strong enough to reach threshold at the next node.

pathways.summary: A node fires, current flows along the inside under the insulating myelin, arrives at the next node strong enough to reach threshold, and that node fires; the refractory node behind keeps the signal moving forward.

pathways.title: Chemical synaptic transmission
pathways.intro: A neuron in your spinal cord passes a signal to the next neuron. Trace it across a chemical synapse, from the arriving action potential to the synapse being ready again.

steps.label: AP reaches the terminal
steps.text: An action potential reaches the axon terminal of the presynaptic neuron and depolarizes it.
steps.why: Everything at the synapse is triggered by the arriving depolarization.

steps.label: Ca2+ channels open
steps.text: Voltage-gated calcium channels in the terminal open, and calcium rushes in down its electrochemical gradient.
steps.why: These channels open only when the terminal depolarizes. Calcium is about 10,000 times more concentrated outside, and the inside is negative, so it rushes in.

steps.label: Vesicles fuse
steps.text: Calcium binds sensor proteins on docked synaptic vesicles, which fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.
steps.why: Calcium is the trigger for release; without it, vesicles stay docked even though the action potential arrived.

steps.label: Diffuses across cleft
steps.text: The neurotransmitter diffuses across the 20 nm synaptic cleft.
steps.why: It can only cross once released, and diffusion over so short a distance takes well under a millisecond.

steps.label: Binds receptor proteins
steps.text: It binds receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, specifically and reversibly.
steps.why: Binding can happen only after the neurotransmitter reaches the far side of the cleft.

steps.label: Channels open or close
steps.text: Ion channels open or close, directly for ionotropic receptor proteins or through a G protein for metabotropic ones.
steps.why: Binding changes the receptor protein’s shape, and that shape change is what gates the ions.

steps.label: EPSP or IPSP
steps.text: Ions flow and the postsynaptic membrane depolarizes (an EPSP) or is pulled away from threshold (an IPSP).
steps.why: The postsynaptic potential is the result of the ion flow through the channels that just opened or closed.

steps.label: Summed at trigger zone
steps.text: EPSPs and IPSPs spread to the trigger zone and add up; if the sum reaches threshold, the postsynaptic neuron fires.
steps.why: Postsynaptic potentials are small graded potentials, so they count only once they are added together at the trigger zone.

steps.label: Transmitter removed
steps.text: Diffusion, enzymes and reuptake transporters clear the neurotransmitter, the channels close, and the synapse is ready for the next signal.
steps.why: The signal must end before the next action potential, or one signal could not be told from the next. Removal ends it.

distractors.text: The action potential jumps across the synaptic cleft to the postsynaptic neuron.
distractors.why: The cleft is about 20 nm wide, far too wide for current to jump. The signal crosses as a chemical, and release needs calcium entry first.

distractors.text: Sodium channels in the terminal open, and the sodium that rushes in binds the docked vesicles and makes them fuse with the membrane.
distractors.why: Sodium carries the action potential into the terminal, but calcium, entering through voltage-gated calcium channels, is what triggers vesicle fusion.

distractors.text: Calcium leaves the terminal, which lets the vesicles fuse.
distractors.why: Calcium flows in, not out: it is far more concentrated outside the cell, and the inside is negative.

error.text: Ions flow and the postsynaptic neuron fires a full action potential every time a single synapse releases neurotransmitter.
error.why: At neuron-to-neuron synapses a single EPSP is tiny, often under 1 mV. The neuron fires only when many PSPs add up to threshold at the trigger zone.

pathways.summary: The action potential opens calcium channels, calcium triggers exocytosis, the neurotransmitter diffuses and binds receptor proteins, channels change the postsynaptic potential, the potentials are summed at the trigger zone, and removal ends the signal.

pathways.title: From neural plate to five brain vesicles
pathways.intro: Every region of your brain grew from one hollow tube. Trace how it formed, from the third week of development to the fifth.

steps.label: Neural plate
steps.text: A strip of cells along the back of the embryo thickens into the neural plate.
steps.why: The plate is the starting tissue; nothing can fold until it has formed.

steps.label: Folds and groove
steps.text: Its edges rise as two neural folds with a neural groove between them.
steps.why: The flat plate has to lift at its edges before it can close into a tube.

steps.label: Neural tube closes
steps.text: The folds meet and fuse over the groove, closing it into the neural tube, by the end of the fourth week.
steps.why: The rising folds meet in the middle; fusing them turns the groove into a hollow tube, and its hollow becomes the fluid-filled spaces of the brain.

steps.label: Three primary vesicles
steps.text: The front end of the tube swells into three primary vesicles: prosencephalon, mesencephalon and rhombencephalon.
steps.why: Only a closed tube can swell into vesicles, and it does so at its front end, which becomes the brain.

steps.label: Five secondary vesicles
steps.text: By the fifth week the forebrain and hindbrain each divide in two, giving five secondary vesicles.
steps.why: The secondary vesicles come from splitting two of the primary ones, so they must come after them.

steps.label: Telencephalon balloons
steps.text: The telencephalon grows much faster than the rest and balloons over the diencephalon and midbrain, becoming the cerebrum.
steps.why: This overgrowth happens after the vesicles form, and it is why the adult cerebrum covers most of the other regions.

distractors.text: The middle vesicle divides into two, giving the pons and the medulla oblongata, while the forebrain stays whole.
distractors.why: The mesencephalon does not split; it becomes the midbrain. The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) splits into the metencephalon and myelencephalon.

distractors.text: The neural tube opens again to form the fluid-filled spaces inside the brain.
distractors.why: The tube stays closed. Its hollow center simply persists as the fluid-filled spaces inside the brain and the thin canal inside the spinal cord.

error.text: The back end of the tube swells into three primary vesicles: prosencephalon, mesencephalon and rhombencephalon.
error.why: The front end of the neural tube becomes the brain; the rest of the tube becomes the spinal cord.

pathways.summary: The neural plate folds, closes into the neural tube, swells at its front end into three primary vesicles, splits into five secondary vesicles, and the telencephalon overgrows the rest to form the cerebrum.

pathways.title: How the cerebellum corrects a movement
pathways.intro: You reach out to pick up a cup. Trace how the cerebellum keeps your hand on target.

steps.label: Cortex sends command
steps.text: The motor areas of the frontal lobe send the command to move the hand.
steps.why: Movement starts in the cerebral cortex, not in the cerebellum, so the command comes first.

steps.label: Copy via the pons
steps.text: A copy of the command reaches the cerebellum through the pons.
steps.why: The cerebellum can judge a movement only if it knows what was intended, and the copy is sent with the command itself.

steps.label: Sensory input arrives
steps.text: As the hand moves, signals from its muscles and joints and from the balance organs in the ear reach the cerebellum.
steps.why: These signals report what the body is actually doing, which exists only once the movement has begun.

steps.label: Intended vs actual
steps.text: The cerebellum compares the intended movement with the actual one and detects any error.
steps.why: A comparison needs both inputs, the copy and the sensory report, so it comes after both arrive.

steps.label: Corrections via thalamus
steps.text: It sends corrections through the thalamus to the motor areas of the cortex.
steps.why: The cerebellum does not drive muscles itself. It acts by adjusting the cortex’s command, relayed through the thalamus.

steps.label: Hand stops on target
steps.text: The cortex adjusts the force, timing and direction while the movement is under way, and the hand stops on the cup.
steps.why: The adjusted command is the last link: only now does the correction reach the muscles.

distractors.text: The cerebellum starts a new movement of its own to replace the first.
distractors.why: The cerebellum does not start movements. It compares and corrects the one the cortex started.

distractors.text: The cerebellum sends the command straight to the hand muscles through the spinal cord.
distractors.why: Its corrections go through the thalamus to the motor cortex and through the brainstem; the command to the muscles still comes from the cortex.

error.text: A copy of the command reaches the cerebellum through the corpus callosum.
error.why: The corpus callosum joins the two cerebral hemispheres. The copy of a motor command reaches the cerebellum through the pons, the bridge between the cortex and the cerebellum.

pathways.summary: The cortex sends a command and a copy goes to the cerebellum through the pons; the cerebellum compares it with sensory reports of the actual movement and sends corrections through the thalamus, so the cortex adjusts the movement while it happens.

pathways.title: Cerebrospinal fluid circulation
pathways.intro: You make about 500 mL of cerebrospinal fluid a day. Trace one drop from where it is made to where it leaves.

steps.label: Choroid plexus secretes
steps.text: The choroid plexus in a lateral ventricle secretes CSF.
steps.why: Most CSF is made here, and the largest choroid plexuses are in the lateral ventricles, the start of the route.

steps.label: Interventricular foramen
steps.text: It flows through the interventricular foramen.
steps.why: This small hole is the only way out of each lateral ventricle.

steps.label: Third ventricle
steps.text: It enters the third ventricle, in the midline of the diencephalon, where more CSF is added.
steps.why: The foramina from both lateral ventricles open into this single midline ventricle.

steps.label: Cerebral aqueduct
steps.text: It flows down the cerebral aqueduct, through the midbrain.
steps.why: The aqueduct is the narrow canal that links the third ventricle to the fourth.

steps.label: Fourth ventricle
steps.text: It enters the fourth ventricle, between the pons and medulla and the cerebellum.
steps.why: The aqueduct opens into the fourth ventricle, the last ventricle on the route.

steps.label: Median and lateral apertures
steps.text: It leaves through the median and lateral apertures.
steps.why: These three holes are the only exits from the ventricles into the subarachnoid space.

steps.label: Subarachnoid space
steps.text: It flows through the subarachnoid space around the brain and spinal cord.
steps.why: The apertures open into the subarachnoid space, which surrounds the whole CNS.

steps.label: Arachnoid granulations
steps.text: It crosses the arachnoid granulations into the venous channels of the dura and rejoins the blood.
steps.why: CSF pressure is a little higher than the pressure of the venous blood there, so fluid flows across one way, balancing what the choroid plexus makes.

distractors.text: It flows down the central canal of the spinal cord to the fourth ventricle.
distractors.why: The central canal lies below the fourth ventricle, not between the third and fourth. The cerebral aqueduct connects those two.

distractors.text: It flows straight out into the subarachnoid space through the roof of the third ventricle.
distractors.why: The only exits from the ventricles are the median and lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle. That is why blocking the aqueduct swells the lateral and third ventricles.

error.text: It crosses the choroid plexus back into the capillaries and rejoins the blood.
error.why: The choroid plexus makes CSF; it does not take it back. CSF returns to the blood mainly through the arachnoid granulations into the venous channels of the dura, with some also draining along nerve sheaths.

pathways.summary: Lateral ventricle choroid plexus → interventricular foramen → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → median and lateral apertures → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → venous blood.

pathways.title: The needle’s path in a lumbar puncture
pathways.intro: A needle is placed between the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae to sample CSF. Trace the layers it passes through, from outside in.

steps.label: Skin
steps.text: The needle passes through the skin of the lower back.
steps.why: The skin is the outermost layer, so it is crossed first.

steps.label: Ligaments
steps.text: It passes through the ligaments between the vertebrae.
steps.why: The needle slips between two vertebrae, where ligaments, not bone, bridge the gap.

steps.label: Epidural space
steps.text: It crosses the epidural space, a real space filled with fat and veins.
steps.why: Around the spinal cord the dura is not attached to the vertebrae, so a real space lies between the bone and the dura.

steps.label: Dura mater
steps.text: It pierces the dura mater, the tough outer meninx.
steps.why: The dura is the outermost of the three meninges.

steps.label: Arachnoid mater
steps.text: It passes through the arachnoid mater, pressed against the inside of the dura.
steps.why: The arachnoid lies directly under the dura, with only a potential space between them.

steps.label: Subarachnoid space
steps.text: It enters the subarachnoid space, full of CSF and floating nerve roots.
steps.why: CSF lies between the arachnoid and the pia. Below the end of the cord, this space holds only nerve roots floating in the fluid, which slide away from the needle.

distractors.text: It passes through the pia mater, the thin layer that lines the inside of the dura around the cord.
distractors.why: The pia clings to the surface of the cord itself, not to the dura. The layer just inside the dura is the arachnoid.

distractors.text: It passes through the spinal cord before reaching the fluid.
distractors.why: In an adult the cord ends at about L1–L2. At L4–L5 the needle enters the fluid below the cord’s end.

error.text: It crosses the subdural space, a real space filled with fat and veins.
error.why: The space outside the dura, between it and the bone, is the epidural space; around the spinal cord it is real and holds fat and veins. The subdural space, between dura and arachnoid, is only a potential space.

pathways.summary: Skin, ligaments, epidural space, dura, arachnoid, subarachnoid space: a needle below L2 reaches the CSF without touching the cord.

pathways.title: A signal through the spinal cord: tack to foot lift
pathways.intro: You step on a tack and lift your foot. Trace the signal in and back out of your spinal cord.

steps.label: Sensory neuron fires
steps.text: A sensory neuron’s ending in the sole of the foot fires.
steps.why: The signal begins where the stimulus is detected.

steps.label: Past the DRG
steps.text: The signal travels up its peripheral process, past its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion.
steps.why: This neuron is pseudounipolar: the signal runs past the cell body, which sits to one side in the ganglion outside the cord.

steps.label: Enters via dorsal root
steps.text: Its central process runs in through the dorsal root into the back of the cord.
steps.why: Sensory axons enter the cord only through the dorsal root; sensation comes in at the back.

steps.label: Dorsal horn
steps.text: It ends in the dorsal horn, exciting interneurons and neurons that send the signal up to the brain.
steps.why: The dorsal horn is the sensory part of the gray matter, where incoming pain axons end.

steps.label: Ventral horn
steps.text: Interneurons excite motor neurons in the ventral horn.
steps.why: Interneurons connect the sensory side of the gray matter to the motor side.

steps.label: Out via ventral root
steps.text: The motor axons leave through the ventral root and the joined nerve.
steps.why: Commands leave the cord only at the front, through the ventral root.

steps.label: Leg muscles contract
steps.text: The leg muscles contract and lift the foot.
steps.why: The skeletal muscle is the effector, the last link in the chain.

distractors.text: Its central process runs in through the ventral root into the front of the cord.
distractors.why: The ventral root carries motor axons out. Sensory axons enter through the dorsal root.

distractors.text: It synapses in the dorsal root ganglion on a second neuron that carries the signal on.
distractors.why: The dorsal root ganglion holds cell bodies, not synapses between neurons on this route. The same axon runs on past the ganglion into the cord.

error.text: Interneurons excite motor neurons in the lateral horn.
error.why: The lateral horn holds sympathetic motor neurons and is present only from T1 to L2. Motor neurons to skeletal muscle sit in the ventral horn.

pathways.summary: Sensory ending → past the dorsal root ganglion → dorsal root → dorsal horn → interneurons → ventral horn motor neurons → ventral root → leg muscles. In at the back, out at the front.

pathways.title: Repeating a word you hear
pathways.intro: Someone says a word and you repeat it. Trace the route through the language areas, in the classic model.

steps.label: Relayed via thalamus
steps.text: Signals from your ears relay through the thalamus.
steps.why: Hearing, like every sense except smell, passes through the thalamus before it reaches the cortex.

steps.label: Primary auditory cortex
steps.text: The primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe receives the sound.
steps.why: A primary sensory area always receives the raw signal first.

steps.label: Wernicke’s area
steps.text: Wernicke’s area, beside it, recognizes the word and its meaning.
steps.why: Interpretation needs the raw sound pattern, so the association area works on it after the primary area.

steps.label: Arcuate fasciculus
steps.text: A curved band of white matter, the arcuate fasciculus, carries the word forward.
steps.why: White matter carries signals between regions; this band links Wernicke’s area to Broca’s area.

steps.label: Broca’s area
steps.text: Broca’s area in the frontal lobe builds a speech plan.
steps.why: Only a recognized word can be turned into a plan for saying it.

steps.label: Motor cortex face area
steps.text: The face area of the primary motor cortex, next to Broca’s area, drives the lips, tongue and throat, and you say the word.
steps.why: Planning areas hand their plan to a primary motor area, which sends the commands out.

distractors.text: Broca’s area recognizes the word and its meaning.
distractors.why: Broca’s area produces speech. Recognizing words and their meaning is the job of Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe.

distractors.text: The primary visual cortex, at the back of the occipital lobe, recognizes the word.
distractors.why: The word was heard, not seen, and the primary visual cortex handles vision.

error.text: The corpus callosum carries the word forward to Broca’s area.
error.why: The corpus callosum joins the two hemispheres. Both language areas lie in the same (usually left) hemisphere, linked by the arcuate fasciculus.

pathways.summary: Ear → thalamus → primary auditory cortex → Wernicke’s area (recognize) → arcuate fasciculus → Broca’s area (plan) → primary motor cortex face area → speech.

pathways.title: Consolidating a declarative memory
pathways.intro: You meet someone new at a party. Trace how the memory of it goes from fragile to lasting.

steps.label: Cortical groups fire
steps.text: During the experience, groups of cortical neurons fire for its sights, sounds and meanings, each in its own area.
steps.why: The raw material of the memory is activity in the separate areas that handle each part of the experience.

steps.label: Hippocampus links them
steps.text: The hippocampus links these scattered groups into one memory.
steps.why: It can bind them only while they are active, so linking follows the experience directly.

steps.label: Replay in sleep
steps.text: Over the following days, especially during slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus replays the pattern to the cortex.
steps.why: Replay needs a pattern the hippocampus has already linked, and it happens later, mostly in deep sleep.

steps.label: Cortex links directly
steps.text: Each replay strengthens the direct connections between the cortical groups.
steps.why: Replay drives the cortical groups together again, so their own connections strengthen.

steps.label: Stored in the cortex
steps.text: In the end the cortex can recall the memory without the hippocampus.
steps.why: Once the direct cortical connections are strong enough, the hippocampus is no longer needed; this is why old memories survive loss of the hippocampus.

distractors.text: The cerebellum links the scattered groups into one memory.
distractors.why: The cerebellum helps form procedural memories of skills. The hippocampus links the parts of a declarative memory of an event.

distractors.text: The memory is copied into the hippocampus, where it is stored for good.
distractors.why: The hippocampus forms and consolidates declarative memories, but long-term memories end up stored in the cerebral cortex.

error.text: Over the following days, especially during REM sleep, the hippocampus erases the pattern so the cortex can start fresh.
error.why: During slow-wave sleep the hippocampus replays the day’s patterns to the cortex, strengthening them. People who sleep after learning remember more.

pathways.summary: Cortical areas fire for each part of an experience; the hippocampus links them; synapses strengthen; replay in slow-wave sleep builds direct cortical links; finally the cortex holds the memory on its own.

pathways.title: An ascending sensory pathway: vibration from the big toe
pathways.intro: A clinician holds a buzzing tuning fork on your right big toe, and a moment later you feel the buzz. Trace the signal from the toe to the cortex through the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway.

steps.label: Lamellated corpuscles fire
steps.text: The vibration deforms lamellated corpuscles in the skin of the toe, and their sensory neurons fire.
steps.why: Every pathway starts at a sensory receptor. Lamellated corpuscles are phasic, so a vibration, which keeps changing, fires them over and over.

steps.label: Dorsal root
steps.text: The first-order axon passes its cell body in a dorsal root ganglion and enters the cord through a dorsal root.
steps.why: The first-order neuron is the sensory neuron itself, and all somatic sensory axons enter the cord through the dorsal roots.

steps.label: Right dorsal column
steps.text: Without synapsing, it turns upward in the right dorsal column, in the fasciculus gracilis.
steps.why: The dorsal column axon climbs on the side it entered. Axons from below about T6 run in the fasciculus gracilis, near the midline.

steps.label: Nucleus gracilis
steps.text: It synapses on a second-order neuron in the nucleus gracilis of the lower medulla oblongata.
steps.why: The first synapse of this pathway comes only in the medulla, a meter or more from the toe.

steps.label: Crosses in the medulla
steps.text: The second-order axon crosses the midline in the medulla.
steps.why: Crossing (decussation) always happens on the second-order axon, so the left side of the brain feels the right side of the body.

steps.label: Left medial lemniscus
steps.text: It climbs through the brainstem in the left medial lemniscus to the thalamus.
steps.why: After crossing, the axons gather into the flat ribbon of the medial lemniscus on the opposite side.

steps.label: Relay in the thalamus
steps.text: In the thalamus it synapses on a third-order neuron.
steps.why: Every pathway to conscious touch relays in the thalamus before the cortex.

steps.label: Left somatosensory cortex
steps.text: The third-order axon runs through the internal capsule to the foot area of the left primary somatosensory cortex, and you feel the buzz.
steps.why: The foot is mapped near the top of the postcentral gyrus, in the longitudinal fissure. Arrival there produces the perception.

distractors.text: The second-order axon crosses the midline in the spinal cord, within a segment or two of entry.
distractors.why: That is the plan of the spinothalamic tract. The dorsal column pathway crosses only in the medulla.

distractors.text: The second-order axon stays on the right and climbs to the right thalamus.
distractors.why: The second-order axon always crosses; if it did not, the right hemisphere would feel the right foot.

distractors.text: The axon joins a spinocerebellar tract and ends in the cerebellum.
distractors.why: The spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious position signals to the cerebellum and never reach awareness. Conscious vibration goes to the cortex.

error.text: Without synapsing, it crosses and climbs in the left dorsal column.
error.why: The first-order axon climbs the dorsal column on the side it entered, the right. Crossing waits until after the synapse in the medulla.

pathways.summary: Three neurons in a row: the first climbs uncrossed to the medulla, the second crosses there and rises in the medial lemniscus to the thalamus, and the third reaches the somatosensory cortex. Because it crosses so high, damage to one side of the cord removes vibration and position on the same side.

pathways.title: Pain from a pinprick on the right hand
pathways.intro: You prick your right index finger on a thorn. Trace the signal through the spinothalamic tract until you feel it.

steps.label: Nociceptors fire
steps.text: The thorn damages the skin, and free nerve endings that act as nociceptors fire.
steps.why: Nociceptors detect harm to tissue, not pain itself; pain is what the brain later makes of their signal.

steps.label: Dorsal root
steps.text: The first-order axon passes its cell body in a dorsal root ganglion and enters the cervical cord through a dorsal root.
steps.why: Sensory axons from the index finger enter at about C6–C7, the segments whose dermatomes cover it.

steps.label: Synapse in the dorsal horn
steps.text: It synapses almost at once on a second-order neuron in the dorsal horn.
steps.why: Unlike the dorsal column axon, the pain axon ends within a segment or two of where it entered.

steps.label: Crosses in the cord
steps.text: The second-order axon crosses the midline in front of the central canal.
steps.why: The crossing happens in the cord, close to the level of entry, which is why a cord lesion removes pain from the opposite side.

steps.label: Left spinothalamic tract
steps.text: It climbs in the left spinothalamic tract, through the brainstem, sending branches to the reticular formation.
steps.why: The crossed axons run in the lateral and anterior columns. Branches to the reticular formation help make pain arousing.

steps.label: Relay in the thalamus
steps.text: It synapses on a third-order neuron in the thalamus.
steps.why: Like other conscious senses of the body, pain relays in the thalamus.

steps.label: Cortex, insula, limbic areas
steps.text: Third-order neurons carry it to the hand area of the left primary somatosensory cortex and to the insula and limbic areas, and you feel a sharp, unpleasant prick.
steps.why: The somatosensory cortex tells you where it hurts; the insula and limbic areas add how unpleasant it is.

distractors.text: It climbs without synapsing in the right dorsal column to the medulla.
distractors.why: That is the dorsal column route for fine touch and vibration. Pain axons synapse in the dorsal horn.

distractors.text: It synapses directly on motor neurons in the ventral horn.
distractors.why: Nociceptor signals reach motor neurons only through interneurons, and that is not the route to awareness. The pain pathway runs through the dorsal horn.

error.text: It climbs in the right spinothalamic tract, on the same side as the finger.
error.why: The second-order axon has already crossed in the cord, so it climbs in the left spinothalamic tract, opposite the finger.

pathways.summary: Pain and temperature use three neurons: the first ends in the dorsal horn, the second crosses at once and climbs the opposite spinothalamic tract to the thalamus, and the third reaches the cortex, insula and limbic areas.

pathways.title: The corticospinal pathway: point your right index finger
pathways.intro: You decide to point your right index finger. Trace the command from the cortex to the finger muscles.

steps.label: Upper motor neurons fire
steps.text: Upper motor neurons in the finger area of the left precentral gyrus fire.
steps.why: Voluntary commands start in the motor cortex, laid out as a map: the hand area sits partway down the precentral gyrus.

steps.label: Internal capsule
steps.text: Their axons funnel down through the internal capsule.
steps.why: Leaving the cortex, the axons pack tightly into the internal capsule beside sensory axons, which is why a small injury here weakens a whole side.

steps.label: Cerebral peduncle
steps.text: They run in the cerebral peduncle on the front of the midbrain.
steps.why: The midbrain is the first level of the brainstem they pass.

steps.label: Through the pons
steps.text: They pass in small bundles among the nuclei of the pons.
steps.why: Below the midbrain comes the pons, where the tract splits into bundles.

steps.label: Pyramid of the medulla
steps.text: They regroup as the pyramid on the front of the medulla oblongata.
steps.why: The bundles gather again on the front of the medulla, forming the ridge that gives the pyramidal tract its name.

steps.label: Pyramidal decussation
steps.text: At the junction of the medulla and the spinal cord, most of them cross the midline at the pyramidal decussation.
steps.why: About 85 to 90% of the axons cross here, so the left cortex commands the right side of the body.

steps.label: Right lateral tract
steps.text: They descend in the right lateral corticospinal tract to the cervical enlargement.
steps.why: The crossed axons run in the lateral white column and end where the limb’s motor neurons are, in the enlargement.

steps.label: Synapse in the ventral horn
steps.text: They synapse on lower motor neurons in the right ventral horn, some of them directly.
steps.why: Direct synapses onto the finger motor neurons give the fine, individual finger control this tract is known for.

steps.label: Out to the forearm
steps.text: The lower motor neurons’ axons leave through the ventral roots and travel through the brachial plexus to the forearm.
steps.why: The lower motor neuron is the final common path: only its axon leaves the CNS for skeletal muscle.

steps.label: The finger points
steps.text: Acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junctions makes the finger’s extensor muscles contract, and the finger points.
steps.why: The last step is the muscle itself contracting.

distractors.text: They cross the midline in the internal capsule, before they leave the cerebral hemisphere.
distractors.why: The internal capsule lies within one hemisphere. The corticospinal tract crosses at the bottom of the medulla.

distractors.text: They stay on the left side and descend, uncrossed, in the left lateral corticospinal tract to the left cervical enlargement.
distractors.why: Then the left cortex would move the left hand. Most axons cross at the pyramidal decussation before descending.

distractors.text: They synapse in the thalamus, which relays them to the spinal cord.
distractors.why: The thalamus relays signals up to the cortex. Corticospinal axons run all the way from the cortex to the cord without a relay.

error.text: They synapse on lower motor neurons in the right dorsal horn.
error.why: Lower motor neurons sit in the ventral horn. The dorsal horn receives sensory input.

pathways.summary: Two neurons carry every voluntary command: an upper motor neuron from the cortex, crossing at the pyramidal decussation, and a lower motor neuron from the ventral horn to the muscle. Damage above the crossing weakens the opposite side; damage in the cord weakens the same side.

pathways.title: The reflex arc: the knee jerk
pathways.intro: A clinician taps just below your kneecap, and your lower leg kicks about 20 milliseconds later. Trace the signal through the five parts of the reflex arc.

steps.label: Tap stretches quadriceps
steps.text: The tap pushes in the patellar ligament, which pulls on the quadriceps femoris and stretches it for a split second.
steps.why: Every reflex starts with a stimulus. Here it is a brief stretch of the muscle.

steps.label: Muscle spindles fire
steps.text: Stretch opens mechanically gated channels in the endings wrapped around the muscle spindles, and their sensory neurons fire.
steps.why: The muscle spindle is the sensory receptor, the first part of the arc. It lies parallel to the muscle fibers, so it stretches with them.

steps.label: In through the dorsal root
steps.text: The action potentials travel past the cell body in a dorsal root ganglion and into the cord through the dorsal roots of about L2 to L4.
steps.why: The sensory neuron, the second part of the arc, carries the signal into the CNS.

steps.label: One synapse, ventral horn
steps.text: In the ventral horn, the sensory axons release glutamate directly onto the lower motor neurons of the quadriceps.
steps.why: The integration center, the third part, is a single synapse: the stretch reflex is monosynaptic.

steps.label: Out through the ventral root
steps.text: The lower motor neurons fire, and their action potentials leave through the ventral roots and the femoral nerve.
steps.why: The motor neuron, the fourth part, carries the command out to the muscle.

steps.label: Acetylcholine at the junction
steps.text: At the neuromuscular junctions, acetylcholine triggers action potentials in the quadriceps muscle fibers.
steps.why: The signal must cross from nerve to muscle before the effector can respond.

steps.label: Quadriceps contracts: kick
steps.text: The quadriceps femoris, the effector, contracts, and the knee straightens.
steps.why: The effector’s response completes the arc. Most of the 20 ms delay was spent in the axons.

distractors.text: The signal climbs to the primary motor cortex, which decides to straighten the knee.
distractors.why: The knee jerk needs no brain: its circuit lies in the spinal cord, which is why the kick comes before you notice the tap.

distractors.text: The sensory axons excite inhibitory interneurons that silence the quadriceps motor neurons.
distractors.why: Inhibitory interneurons in this reflex act on the antagonist, the hamstrings (reciprocal inhibition), not on the stretched muscle.

distractors.text: Golgi tendon organs in the patellar ligament report the tap to the dorsal horn.
distractors.why: The sensor of every deep tendon reflex is the muscle spindle. Tendon organs report tension and inhibit the same muscle.

error.text: The lower motor neurons fire, and their action potentials leave through the dorsal roots.
error.why: Motor axons leave through the ventral roots. The dorsal roots carry only sensory axons into the cord.

pathways.summary: Sensory receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector: every reflex runs on these five parts. In the knee jerk the integration center is one synapse, so a missing knee jerk can mean a break anywhere along a short, testable arc.

pathways.title: The corneal reflex: a touch on the eye makes both eyes blink
pathways.intro: A clinician touches a wisp of cotton to the clear front surface of a patient’s right eye, and both eyes blink. Trace the arc through the brainstem.

steps.label: Cotton touches the eye
steps.text: The cotton touches the clear front surface of the right eye.
steps.why: The stimulus is a light touch on a surface packed with sensitive nerve endings.

steps.label: Ophthalmic branch of V fires
steps.text: Nerve endings of the ophthalmic division of the right trigeminal nerve fire.
steps.why: Touch from the surface of the eye is carried by V1, the sensory division for the forehead and eye.

steps.label: Into the pons
steps.text: The signal travels to the trigeminal nuclei in the brainstem at the level of the pons.
steps.why: The trigeminal nerve joins the brainstem at the pons, where its sensory axons end.

steps.label: Signal sent to both sides
steps.text: Interneurons carry the signal to the facial nuclei on both sides of the brainstem.
steps.why: Because the signal is shared with both sides, touching one eye makes both blink.

steps.label: Both facial nerves fire
steps.text: Motor neurons of both facial nuclei fire, and their axons run out in the facial nerves.
steps.why: The facial nerve (VII) supplies the muscles of facial expression, including the ones that close the eyes.

steps.label: Both eyes blink
steps.text: The orbicularis oculi on each side contracts, and both eyes blink.
steps.why: The ring of muscle around each eye closes the lids.

distractors.text: The optic nerve carries the touch signal to the brainstem.
distractors.why: The optic nerve carries vision only. Touch on the eye travels in the trigeminal nerve.

distractors.text: The facial nerve carries the touch signal into the pons.
distractors.why: The facial nerve carries the blink out, not the touch in. V feels, VII moves.

error.text: Motor neurons of the oculomotor nuclei fire, and their axons run out in the oculomotor nerves.
error.why: The oculomotor nerve raises the upper lid. Closing the eyes is done by the orbicularis oculi, supplied by the facial nerve.

pathways.summary: The corneal reflex tests two cranial nerves and a stretch of brainstem at once: V1 carries the touch in, the pons shares it with both sides, and both facial nerves carry the blink out. In a deeply unresponsive patient, an absent corneal reflex points to failure of the brainstem around the pons.

pathways.title: From an odorant to a smell
pathways.intro: Coffee is brewing in the next room. Trace one odorant molecule from the air in your nose to a signal in your olfactory cortex.

steps.label: Odorant dissolves in mucus
steps.text: The odorant reaches the olfactory epithelium at the top of the nose and dissolves in its mucus.
steps.why: An odorant must dissolve in the watery film before it can reach the cilia of the sensory neurons.

steps.label: Binds a receptor protein
steps.text: It binds an odorant receptor protein on a cilium of an olfactory sensory neuron.
steps.why: Each neuron makes one of about 400 kinds of odorant receptor protein, and each odorant binds several kinds.

steps.label: G protein activated
steps.text: The receptor protein activates a G protein, which switches on an enzyme that makes cAMP.
steps.why: Odorant receptor proteins are G protein–coupled, so a second messenger carries the signal inside.

steps.label: Cation channels open
steps.text: cAMP opens ligand-gated cation channels in the cilium, and Na+ and Ca2+ flow in.
steps.why: The second messenger is the ligand that opens these channels.

steps.label: Chloride flows out
steps.text: The Ca2+ opens chloride channels, and Cl− flows out, depolarizing the cell further.
steps.why: These neurons keep unusually high chloride inside, so opening chloride channels adds a second, larger depolarizing current.

steps.label: Action potentials fire
steps.text: The depolarization spreads to the axon, and if it reaches threshold, action potentials fire.
steps.why: The depolarization is graded; firing begins only at threshold.

steps.label: Through the cribriform plate
steps.text: The unmyelinated axon carries them up through a hole in the cribriform plate, in the olfactory nerve.
steps.why: The axons of all the olfactory sensory neurons together form the olfactory nerve (I).

steps.label: Olfactory bulb
steps.text: In the olfactory bulb, all axons from neurons with the same receptor protein converge on the same few clusters of synapses.
steps.why: The bulb sorts the signals by receptor protein type and pools weak signals before passing them on.

steps.label: Olfactory cortex, no thalamus
steps.text: The olfactory tract carries the signal straight to the olfactory cortex of the temporal lobe and to limbic areas.
steps.why: Smell is the one sense that reaches the cortex without first relaying in the thalamus.

distractors.text: The Ca2+ opens potassium channels, and K+ flows out, hyperpolarizing the cell.
distractors.why: Hyperpolarization would silence the neuron. In olfactory neurons the Ca2+ opens chloride channels, and chloride leaving depolarizes them.

distractors.text: The cell releases neurotransmitter onto a separate sensory neuron in the epithelium.
distractors.why: That is how taste cells work. Olfactory sensory neurons are neurons themselves and fire their own action potentials.

error.text: The olfactory tract carries the signal to the thalamus, which relays it to the olfactory cortex.
error.why: Smell reaches the olfactory cortex directly. Only later do some signals pass through the thalamus to the frontal lobe.

pathways.summary: An odorant binds a G protein–coupled receptor protein, cAMP opens cation channels, and chloride leaving boosts the depolarization. Axons pass through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, and the olfactory tract reaches the cortex and limbic system without a stop in the thalamus.

pathways.title: Light through the eye to the cortex
pathways.intro: Light from a friend waving on your right enters your eye. Follow it through the eye, and then follow the signal it starts to your visual cortex.

steps.label: Cornea
steps.text: Light passes through the cornea, which does about two thirds of the bending.
steps.why: The cornea is the first clear surface, and the jump from air into it bends light the most.

steps.label: Aqueous humor
steps.text: It crosses the aqueous humor in the anterior chamber.
steps.why: Behind the cornea lies the watery fluid that fills the front of the eye.

steps.label: Pupil
steps.text: It passes through the pupil, the opening in the iris.
steps.why: The iris sits in front of the lens, and its opening sets how much light goes on.

steps.label: Lens
steps.text: The lens adds the remaining bending, adjusted for distance.
steps.why: The lens lies just behind the iris and is the only part whose bending can change.

steps.label: Vitreous humor
steps.text: Light crosses the clear gel of the vitreous humor.
steps.why: The gel fills the large cavity behind the lens.

steps.label: Through the retina’s layers
steps.text: It passes through the nearly transparent ganglion cell and bipolar cell layers of the retina.
steps.why: The light-sensitive cells lie at the back of the retina, so light crosses the other layers first.

steps.label: Rods and cones respond
steps.text: Rods and cones absorb it, hyperpolarize and change their glutamate release.
steps.why: Photoreceptors turn light into an electrical change and pass it on at a synapse.

steps.label: Bipolar cells
steps.text: Bipolar cells respond with graded potentials.
steps.why: Bipolar cells carry the signal toward the front of the retina.

steps.label: Ganglion cells fire
steps.text: Retinal ganglion cells fire action potentials.
steps.why: Ganglion cells are the first cells in the pathway to fire action potentials.

steps.label: Optic nerve
steps.text: Their axons leave at the optic disc in the optic nerve.
steps.why: All ganglion cell axons exit together at the optic disc, the blind spot.

steps.label: Optic chiasm
steps.text: At the optic chiasm, axons from the nasal half of each retina cross.
steps.why: Crossing the nasal fibers sends each half of the visual field to one side of the brain.

steps.label: Left optic tract
steps.text: The left optic tract carries everything from your right visual field.
steps.why: Behind the chiasm, each tract holds the temporal fibers of the same eye and the nasal fibers of the other.

steps.label: Lateral geniculate nucleus
steps.text: The axons synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the left thalamus.
steps.why: Like other senses except smell, vision relays in the thalamus.

steps.label: Left primary visual cortex
steps.text: The optic radiation carries the signal to the primary visual cortex of the left occipital lobe.
steps.why: The primary visual cortex maps the opposite visual field point by point.

distractors.text: At the optic chiasm, axons from the temporal half of each retina cross.
distractors.why: Temporal fibers stay on their own side. It is the nasal fibers that cross.

distractors.text: At the optic chiasm, every axon from each eye crosses to the other side.
distractors.why: Only the nasal fibers cross. If all crossed, each eye would report to only one hemisphere, and a chiasm tumor would blind both eyes completely.

error.text: The lens does about two thirds of the bending, at a fixed power.
error.why: The cornea does about two thirds of the bending at a fixed power. The lens does the remaining third, and it is the part that can change.

pathways.summary: Light is bent by the cornea and the lens, crosses the fluids and the inner retina, and is caught by rods and cones at the back. The signal passes through bipolar and ganglion cells, the optic nerve, chiasm and tract, and the lateral geniculate nucleus to the occipital cortex opposite the half of the field it came from.

pathways.title: Tear flow
pathways.intro: A speck of dust makes your eye water, and a moment later your nose runs. Follow the tears from where they are made to where they drain.

steps.label: Lacrimal gland
steps.text: The lacrimal gland, in the upper outer corner of the orbit, makes tears.
steps.why: Tears start in the gland, driven by parasympathetic fibers carried by the facial nerve.

steps.label: Lacrimal ducts
steps.text: Several small lacrimal ducts carry them onto the upper outer part of the eye.
steps.why: The ducts open under the upper lid, so tears land on the top outer corner of the eye.

steps.label: Blinks sweep them inward
steps.text: Each blink sweeps the tears across the eye toward the inner corner.
steps.why: The lids spread the film across the eye and push it toward the nose.

steps.label: Lacrimal puncta
steps.text: They drain into the lacrimal puncta, one tiny opening on the edge of each lid at the inner corner.
steps.why: The drainage openings sit at the inner corner, where the blinks deliver the tears.

steps.label: Lacrimal canaliculi
steps.text: Short lacrimal canaliculi carry them to the lacrimal sac.
