pathways.summary: Find, bind, engulf, fuse with lysosomes, kill with the oxidative burst. In chronic granulomatous disease the burst enzyme is faulty, so phagocytes engulf bacteria but cannot kill many of them.

pathways.title: Making a T cell in the thymus
pathways.intro: A lymphoid stem cell in the red bone marrow gives rise to a cell that will become a T cell. Put the steps that turn it into a mature, naïve T cell in order.

steps.label: Thymocyte leaves marrow
steps.text: An immature T cell, a thymocyte, leaves the bone marrow and travels in the blood to the thymus.
steps.why: T cells are made in the marrow but mature only in the thymus.

steps.label: Random receptor built
steps.text: In the thymus cortex it cuts and joins gene pieces at random to build its own unique T cell receptor protein.
steps.why: The thymocyte needs a finished antigen receptor protein before it can be tested.

steps.label: Positive selection
steps.text: Cortical epithelial cells show it self peptides on self MHC; if its receptor protein binds self MHC at least weakly, it gets a survival signal.
steps.why: A receptor protein that cannot bind your MHC would be useless, so the first test keeps only cells that can use self MHC.

steps.label: Negative selection
steps.text: In the medulla, dendritic and epithelial cells show self peptides from all over the body; a thymocyte that binds them too strongly is killed.
steps.why: Only cells that passed the first test are worth checking for danger; this second test removes self-reactive cells (clonal deletion).

steps.label: Naïve T cell released
steps.text: The survivors, about 2 percent, leave the thymus as mature, naïve T cells.
steps.why: Release comes last, after both tests; the survivors can see foreign peptides on self MHC without reacting strongly to self.

distractors.text: In the medulla, each thymocyte meets foreign antigens from microbes and keeps whichever it binds best.
distractors.why: Thymocytes are tested against self, not against microbes; they meet foreign antigen only later, in the lymph nodes.

distractors.text: In the medulla, thymocytes that bind self peptides strongly are kept, because they bind most firmly.
distractors.why: Strong binding to self means the cell could attack your own tissues. Those cells are deleted, not kept.

error.text: Cortical epithelial cells show it self peptides on self MHC; if its receptor protein cannot bind self MHC at all, it gets a survival signal.
error.why: It is the reverse. A thymocyte whose receptor protein binds self MHC at least weakly survives; one that cannot bind it at all dies of neglect.

pathways.summary: Marrow, thymus cortex (receptor built, positive selection), thymus medulla (negative selection), release. About 98 percent of thymocytes fail and die by apoptosis. The survivors are restricted to self MHC and tolerant of self.

pathways.title: Antigen presentation to T cell activation
pathways.intro: A virus infects the lining of your nose. A week later your blood holds a large clone of T cells that recognize it. Trace the steps from the dendritic cell that meets the virus to the effector and memory T cells.

steps.label: Dendritic cell captures
steps.text: A dendritic cell under the lining engulfs virus and is switched on by its pattern recognition receptor proteins.
steps.why: Detecting danger is what makes the dendritic cell stop sampling and move; without it, no response starts.

steps.label: Antigen processing
steps.text: It cuts viral proteins into peptides and loads them into its MHC proteins.
steps.why: A T cell can see only a short peptide held in an MHC protein, so the antigen has to be processed first.

steps.label: Travels to lymph node
steps.text: It travels through afferent lymphatic vessels to the paracortex of the nearest lymph node.
steps.why: Naïve T cells circulate between the blood and lymph nodes, never into the tissue, so the antigen must be carried to them.

steps.label: Signal 1: recognition
steps.text: A rare naïve T cell whose receptor protein fits one displayed peptide binds it, with CD4 or CD8 clamping onto the MHC.
steps.why: Recognition can happen only once the loaded dendritic cell is in the node, where thousands of T cells pass through each hour.

steps.label: Signal 2: costimulation
steps.text: CD28 on the T cell binds B7 on the dendritic cell, confirming that the antigen came with danger.
steps.why: Signal 1 alone leads to anergy. The confirming signal must come with recognition for the T cell to switch on.

steps.label: Signal 3: cytokines
steps.text: Cytokines from the dendritic cell and nearby cells steer what kind of effector cell the T cell will become.
steps.why: Once the T cell is committed to responding, the cytokines around it decide its direction, such as Th1 or Th2.

steps.label: IL-2 made
steps.text: The activated T cell makes IL-2 and the receptor protein for it, stimulating itself.
steps.why: Activation switches on the IL-2 genes; this autocrine loop drives the divisions that follow.

steps.label: Clonal expansion
steps.text: It divides every 6 to 8 hours, building a clone of tens of thousands to millions of identical cells over about a week.
steps.why: Division follows the IL-2 signal, and it is the reason a first response takes about a week.

steps.label: Effector and memory cells
steps.text: Most of the clone become short-lived effector T cells that leave the node; a smaller number become memory T cells.
steps.why: Differentiation comes after expansion, and the effector cells then do the work in the tissues.

distractors.text: Naïve T cells leave the blood and search the lining of the nose for the dendritic cell.
distractors.why: Naïve T cells circulate between the blood and the lymph nodes and never wander into a small patch of infected tissue. The dendritic cell carries the antigen to them.

distractors.text: It releases its loaded MHC proteins into the blood, where passing T cells can find them.
distractors.why: MHC proteins stay in the presenting cell’s membrane. The whole dendritic cell travels through afferent lymph to the node.

distractors.text: It stays in the lining and waits for T cells to pass through the infected tissue.
distractors.why: The dendritic cell stops sampling and migrates. By the time it reaches the paracortex, a day or so later, it is covered in loaded MHC proteins.

error.text: CD28 on the T cell binds B7 on the dendritic cell, which a resting dendritic cell from healthy tissue makes in plenty.
error.why: A dendritic cell makes plenty of B7 only after its pattern recognition receptor proteins have sensed a microbe. A resting one gives signal 1 without signal 2, and a T cell that meets it becomes anergic, which protects healthy tissue.

pathways.summary: Capture, processing, migration to the lymph node, recognition, costimulation, cytokines, IL-2, clonal expansion, effector and memory cells. The two-signal rule means a T cell expands only when its antigen appears together with signs of infection.

pathways.title: A cytotoxic T cell kills an infected cell
pathways.intro: An effector cytotoxic T cell arrives in virus-infected tissue in your airway lining. Put the steps by which it kills one infected cell in order.

steps.label: Recognition
steps.text: Its T cell receptor protein and CD8 bind a viral peptide held in MHC class I on an infected cell.
steps.why: Killing is aimed; the T cell must first find a cell showing its peptide.

steps.label: Aim
steps.text: It grips that cell tightly and turns its store of granules toward the contact point.
steps.why: Pointing the granules at the contact point means the weapons hit only the infected cell.

steps.label: Perforin
steps.text: The granules release perforin, which inserts into the target’s plasma membrane and forms pores.
steps.why: Pores come first, to open a route into the target.

steps.label: Granzymes
steps.text: Granzymes enter through the pores and activate the target’s own caspases.
steps.why: Granzymes need the pores perforin made to get inside the target.

steps.label: Apoptosis
steps.text: The target dies by apoptosis within minutes, breaking into tidy fragments, with the virus inside it destroyed.
steps.why: Caspases carry out apoptosis once they are switched on.

steps.label: Moves on
steps.text: The cytotoxic T cell lets go and moves on to kill the next infected cell.
steps.why: The killer is not used up; one cell can kill many targets in a row.

distractors.text: The granules release antibody, which coats the target so the T cell can engulf it.
distractors.why: T cells do not make antibody, and a cytotoxic T cell does not engulf its target. Its granules release perforin.

distractors.text: The granules release histamine, which makes the target cell swell and burst.
distractors.why: Histamine is a mast cell messenger. The target is killed by apoptosis, from inside, not by bursting.

error.text: The target swells and bursts open, spilling its contents, including new virus, into the tissue.
error.why: The target dies by apoptosis, breaking into tidy, membrane-wrapped fragments that macrophages engulf. Virus still being assembled is destroyed with it, and there is little inflammation.

pathways.summary: Recognize, aim, perforin, granzymes, caspases and apoptosis, detach and repeat. Fas ligand binding Fas on the target is a second route to the same caspases.

pathways.title: B cell activation to antibody
pathways.intro: Tetanus toxoid from a first vaccine dose reaches a lymph node. Trace the steps from a naïve B cell that fits it to the antibody that neutralizes tetanus toxin.

steps.label: Antigen binds BCR
steps.text: The toxoid binds the B cell receptor proteins of a naïve B cell that fits it, and the B cell takes it inside.
steps.why: A B cell receptor protein binds the antigen in its natural, folded shape; no MHC is needed for this first step.

steps.label: Presents on MHC II
steps.text: The B cell cuts the protein into peptides and displays them in MHC class II.
steps.why: This turns the B cell into an antigen-presenting cell, so a helper T cell can recognize it.

steps.label: Helper T cell help
steps.text: A helper T cell already activated against the same antigen binds the peptide, engages CD40 with CD40 ligand and releases cytokines onto the B cell.
steps.why: Most protein antigens are T cell-dependent: without this help the B cell cannot respond fully.

steps.label: Clonal expansion
steps.text: The activated B cell divides into a clone.
steps.why: Help switches on division, building the numbers the response needs.

steps.label: Germinal center
steps.text: In a germinal center, clone members switch class from IgM to IgG and are selected for better-fitting antibody.
steps.why: Class switching and affinity maturation happen after expansion, and they also need helper T cell contact.

steps.label: Plasma and memory cells
steps.text: Daughter cells become plasma cells and memory B cells.
steps.why: Differentiation comes last in the B cell’s own story; memory B cells will drive the secondary response.

steps.label: Antibody released
steps.text: Each plasma cell releases about 2,000 antibody molecules per second into the blood and tissue fluid.
steps.why: Plasma cells are packed with rough ER for exactly this export.

steps.label: Neutralization
steps.text: The antibody binds tetanus toxin and covers the part that attaches to nerve endings.
steps.why: Antibody can act only after it has been released and reaches the toxin.

distractors.text: A cytotoxic T cell recognizes the peptide and kills the B cell, which releases its stored antibody.
distractors.why: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. A B cell is switched on by a helper T cell’s contact and cytokines.

distractors.text: A dendritic cell binds the B cell directly and releases antibody onto it to switch it on.
distractors.why: Dendritic cells activate helper T cells; the helper T cell is the one that helps the B cell.

error.text: In a germinal center, clone members switch class from IgG to IgM and are selected for better-fitting antibody.
error.why: Every B cell starts out making IgM (with IgD). Class switching goes from IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE, keeping the same variable region, and it cannot be reversed because the DNA is cut out.

pathways.summary: Bind and take in antigen, present on MHC class II, get helper T cell help, expand, switch class and improve fit, become plasma and memory cells, release antibody, neutralize. T cell-independent antigens such as repeating capsule sugars skip the help, giving mostly IgM and few memory cells.

pathways.title: Type I hypersensitivity: from sensitization to symptoms
pathways.intro: A child prone to allergy breathes in grass pollen one spring with no symptoms. The next spring, the same pollen sets off sneezing within minutes. Put the steps in order.

steps.label: Th2 cells release IL-4
steps.text: On the first exposure, Th2 helper T cells that recognize the pollen release IL-4.
steps.why: Sensitization starts with helper T cells; IL-4 is the cytokine that steers B cells toward IgE.

steps.label: Class switch to IgE
steps.text: B cells that recognize the pollen switch class to IgE, and plasma cells release it.
steps.why: The B cells need the IL-4 signal before they switch.

steps.label: IgE arms mast cells
steps.text: IgE binds by its Fc region to receptor proteins on mast cells in the lining of the nose.
steps.why: The IgE must be made before it can sit on mast cells; the child is now sensitized but has no symptoms.

steps.label: Re-exposure cross-links IgE
steps.text: The next spring, pollen binds two neighboring IgE molecules on a mast cell and cross-links them.
steps.why: A reaction needs this later exposure; the first contact only primed the system.

steps.label: Degranulation
steps.text: Within seconds the mast cell releases histamine and tryptase, then makes leukotrienes and prostaglandins.
steps.why: Cross-linking is the trigger for the mast cell to release its granules.

steps.label: Symptoms
steps.text: Histamine widens and opens small vessels, stimulates itch nerves and increases mucus: sneezing and a running nose.
steps.why: The mediators have to be released before they can act on nearby vessels, glands and nerves.

distractors.text: IgE circulates free in the blood, waiting to meet the pollen in the plasma.
distractors.why: Almost all IgE sits bound to mast cells and basophils by its Fc region. That is where the pollen meets it.

distractors.text: The pollen itself binds straight to histamine stores inside the mast cells.
distractors.why: Pollen does not enter mast cells. It acts from outside by cross-linking IgE bound to their surface.

error.text: On the first exposure, Th1 helper T cells that recognize the pollen release interferon gamma.
error.why: Allergy is a Th2 response. IL-4 from Th2 cells drives the switch to IgE; interferon gamma from Th1 cells blocks Th2 development and steers B cells toward the IgG types that coat microbes.

pathways.summary: Th2 cells and IL-4, class switch to IgE, IgE arms mast cells, re-exposure cross-links IgE, degranulation, symptoms. Where the mast cells sit decides the symptoms; when an allergen reaches the blood and mast cells degranulate everywhere at once, the result is anaphylaxis.

pathways.title: Food through the GI tract
pathways.intro: Follow a bite of a cheese sandwich from the moment it enters your mouth to what is left when it leaves your body. Put the parts of the alimentary canal in order.

steps.label: Mouth
steps.text: The mouth: teeth chew the bite and saliva wets it.
steps.why: Ingestion happens here, so the mouth is the start of the tube.

steps.label: Pharynx
steps.text: The pharynx: a swallow pushes the chewed food into the throat.
steps.why: The pharynx is shared with the airway and links the mouth to the esophagus.

steps.label: Esophagus
steps.text: The esophagus: peristalsis carries the food down through the chest.
steps.why: The esophagus runs from the bottom of the pharynx through the diaphragm to the stomach.

steps.label: Stomach
steps.text: The stomach: the food is held for a few hours and churned into a thin paste.
steps.why: The stomach sits just below the diaphragm, where the esophagus ends.

steps.label: Small intestine
steps.text: The small intestine: most chemical digestion and nearly all absorption happen along its few meters.
steps.why: It receives the stomach’s contents a little at a time, and the accessory organs’ ducts open into its first part.

steps.label: Large intestine
steps.text: The large intestine: water is absorbed and what is left becomes feces.
steps.why: It frames the small intestine and receives whatever the small intestine did not absorb.

steps.label: Anus
steps.text: The anus: feces leave the body by defecation.
steps.why: The tube ends here, so defecation is the last of the six digestive processes.

distractors.text: The larynx: the food passes through the voice box on its way down.
distractors.why: The larynx is the entrance to the airway. During a swallow it is sealed off so food does not enter it.

distractors.text: The liver: the food is broken down by bile before it reaches the stomach.
distractors.why: The liver is an accessory organ. Food never passes through it; its bile reaches the small intestine through a duct.

error.text: The pancreas: food passes through it and is digested by its enzymes.
error.why: The pancreas is an accessory organ outside the tube. Its enzymes travel to the small intestine through a duct, and food never enters it.

pathways.summary: Mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus: one continuous tube. The accessory organs (teeth, tongue, glands that make saliva, liver, gallbladder, pancreas) help from outside it, and food never passes through them.

pathways.title: The three phases of swallowing
pathways.intro: You decide to swallow a bite of chewed food. In about a second, more than 25 pairs of muscles act in a fixed order. Trace the swallow from the tongue to the stomach.

steps.label: Tongue pushes bolus back
steps.text: Voluntary phase: the tongue presses the bolus up against the hard palate and back into the oropharynx.
steps.why: This is the only step you control. It starts everything that follows.

steps.label: Swallowing center triggered
steps.text: Touch-sensitive sensory receptors in the oropharynx signal the swallowing center in the brainstem through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.
steps.why: The reflex needs the bolus to touch the back of the mouth first; from here on, you cannot stop it.

steps.label: Nose and airway sealed
steps.text: Pharyngeal phase: the soft palate lifts to seal the nasopharynx, and the vocal folds close to seal the airway from inside.
steps.why: The swallowing center protects the nose and airway first, before the bolus is squeezed through the pharynx.

steps.label: Larynx rises, epiglottis tips
steps.text: Muscles on the hyoid bone pull the larynx up and forward, and the epiglottis tips down over its opening; breathing pauses.
steps.why: The vocal folds close at or before the start of this rise, which adds a second cover over the already closed airway.

steps.label: Constrictors squeeze
steps.text: The pharyngeal constrictors contract from top to bottom while the upper esophageal sphincter relaxes and is pulled open.
steps.why: Only once the airway is covered is the bolus squeezed down; the rising larynx is what pulls the sphincter open.

steps.label: Peristalsis down esophagus
steps.text: Esophageal phase: the upper esophageal sphincter closes behind the bolus, and a peristaltic wave carries it down in about 5 to 10 seconds.
steps.why: The bolus must be inside the esophagus before the sphincter can close behind it and the wave can start.

steps.label: Bolus enters stomach
steps.text: The bolus reaches the lower esophageal sphincter, relaxed by nitric oxide since the swallow began, and passes into the stomach.
steps.why: This is the end of the tube’s journey through the chest; the sphincter then closes again behind the bolus.

distractors.text: The epiglottis lifts up and the larynx drops, opening the airway wide so you can keep breathing in and out during the swallow.
distractors.why: Breathing pauses during a swallow. The larynx rises and the epiglottis tips down to cover the airway.

distractors.text: The upper esophageal sphincter contracts hard to stop the bolus entering too fast.
distractors.why: The upper sphincter is closed between swallows and relaxes during one; it closes again only after the bolus has passed.

distractors.text: Gravity carries the bolus down the pharynx without any muscle action.
distractors.why: The bolus is squeezed down by the constrictors. You can swallow upside down.

error.text: Pharyngeal phase: the soft palate drops to close off the mouth, and the vocal folds open wide so air can escape.
error.why: The soft palate lifts to seal the nasopharynx, and the vocal folds close, so food cannot go up into the nose or down into the airway.

pathways.summary: Voluntary push by the tongue; then a brainstem reflex that seals the nose and airway, lifts the larynx, tips the epiglottis and squeezes the bolus into the esophagus; then peristalsis carries it to a lower esophageal sphincter that has been relaxed since the swallow began.

pathways.title: Phases of gastric secretion
pathways.intro: You smell dinner cooking, eat a plate of chicken, and an hour later the first chyme leaves your stomach. Trace how acid secretion is switched on, peaks and is braked.

steps.label: Smell and sight of food
steps.text: The sight, smell, taste or thought of food acts on the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata.
steps.why: The cephalic phase starts in the head, before any food reaches the stomach.

steps.label: Vagus releases ACh
steps.text: Vagal signals release acetylcholine onto parietal and chief cells and stimulate the G cells, so acid secretion begins.
steps.why: The brain’s signal reaches the stomach through the vagus nerves. This phase supplies roughly a third of the acid.

steps.label: Food stretches stomach
steps.text: Food arrives and stretches the stomach wall; short reflexes and vagovagal reflexes add acetylcholine.
steps.why: The gastric phase begins only when food is in the stomach.

steps.label: Protein releases gastrin
steps.text: Protein fragments stimulate the G cells, and gastrin, mostly through histamine from ECL cells, drives the largest share of the meal’s acid.
steps.why: Food first buffers the acid and raises the pH, lifting the brake on gastrin, so the gastric phase secretes the most.

steps.label: Low pH brakes gastrin
steps.text: As acid accumulates, the pH in the antrum falls below about 3, and somatostatin from D cells slows gastrin release.
steps.why: This brake follows the acid it responds to: the product switches off its own stimulus.

steps.label: Chyme enters intestine
steps.text: Chyme passes the pylorus into the first part of the small intestine.
steps.why: The intestinal phase is named for this: the stimulus is now in the small intestine.

steps.label: Intestine slows stomach
steps.text: Acid, fat and stretch there trigger the enterogastric reflex and release secretin and CCK, which slow acid secretion and emptying.
steps.why: The intestinal phase is mostly a brake: the intestine holds the stomach back until it has dealt with what it received.

distractors.text: As acid accumulates, the low pH in the antrum makes the G cells release even more gastrin, which drives acid secretion higher still.
distractors.why: Low pH shuts gastrin off, through somatostatin. The loop is negative feedback, not positive.

distractors.text: Pepsin digests the G cells, so gastrin release stops.
distractors.why: The mucosal barrier protects the lining from pepsin. Gastrin falls because low pH releases somatostatin.

error.text: Acid, fat and stretch there trigger the enterogastric reflex, which speeds up the stomach so it empties faster.
error.why: The enterogastric reflex slows the stomach: it weakens the antrum’s waves and tightens the pyloric sphincter so the intestine is not overloaded.

pathways.summary: Cephalic phase (head, vagus): about a third of the acid. Gastric phase (stretch, protein, gastrin): about half or more, braked by low pH through somatostatin. Intestinal phase (acid, fat, stretch in the small intestine): mostly a brake, through the enterogastric reflex, secretin and CCK.

pathways.title: How a parietal cell makes hydrochloric acid
pathways.intro: Within minutes of the first bite, the fluid in your gastric glands reaches a pH near 1. Trace how a parietal cell builds that million-fold gradient.

steps.label: Signals stimulate the cell
steps.text: Acetylcholine, histamine and gastrin act on the parietal cell’s receptor proteins.
steps.why: The cell makes acid on command; together these three signals drive far more secretion than any one alone.

steps.label: Carbonic anhydrase
steps.text: Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase combines CO2 and water, and the carbonic acid splits into H+ and HCO3−.
steps.why: The H+ to be secreted has to be made first. The HCO3− left behind is traded for Cl− and enters the blood: the alkaline tide.

steps.label: Proton pump pushes H+ out
steps.text: The H+/K+ proton pump spends ATP to push H+ into the gland lumen and bring K+ in.
steps.why: Moving H+ against a million-fold gradient needs primary active transport, and it can only pump H+ that the cell has made.

steps.label: Cl− follows: HCl
steps.text: Cl− leaves through channels in the same membrane, and H+ and Cl− together make hydrochloric acid in the lumen.
steps.why: The acid forms in the lumen, not in the cell, once both ions have been moved there.

steps.label: Stomach pH falls
steps.text: The pH of the stomach contents falls toward 1 to 2.
steps.why: Acid added to the lumen faster than food buffers it lowers the pH.

steps.label: Pepsin switched on
steps.text: In the acid, pepsinogen from the chief cells cuts itself into active pepsin.
steps.why: Pepsinogen activates only below about pH 5, so it has to wait for the acid.

distractors.text: H+ diffuses out of the cell through open channels into the gland lumen, moving down its concentration gradient without any ATP.
distractors.why: The lumen holds over a million times more H+ than the cell. H+ must be pumped uphill, using ATP.

distractors.text: Vesicles of ready-made hydrochloric acid are released by exocytosis.
distractors.why: Parietal cells make acid by pumping ions, not by storing and releasing acid.

distractors.text: Sodium–potassium pumps push H+ out in exchange for sodium.
distractors.why: The pump that secretes H+ is the H+/K+ ATPase, which trades H+ for K+.

error.text: Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase splits hydrochloric acid into H+ and Cl−.
error.why: Carbonic anhydrase combines CO2 with water; the H+ comes from carbonic acid. Hydrochloric acid only forms in the lumen.

pathways.summary: Signals on; carbonic anhydrase makes H+ and HCO3− from CO2 and water; the proton pump spends ATP pushing H+ out; Cl− follows to make HCl in the lumen; the pH falls; pepsinogen becomes pepsin. The bicarbonate goes to the blood as the alkaline tide.

pathways.title: Bile from liver to duodenum
pathways.intro: A hepatocyte secretes bile between meals. Follow it until, after your next fatty meal, it reaches the duodenum.

steps.label: Bile canaliculi
steps.text: Hepatocytes secrete bile into bile canaliculi, tiny grooves between neighboring cells.
steps.why: Bile starts in the hepatocytes, the cells that make it.

steps.label: Bile ducts in portal triads
steps.text: The canaliculi carry bile outward, away from the central vein, to the bile ducts in the portal triads.
steps.why: Bile flows outward in the lobule, the opposite direction to blood.

steps.label: Right and left hepatic ducts
steps.text: Bile ducts merge into the right and left hepatic ducts, which drain the two halves of the liver.
steps.why: Small ducts join into larger ones as they leave the liver.

steps.label: Common hepatic duct
steps.text: The two hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct.
steps.why: The two halves’ ducts must join before the cystic duct can meet them.

steps.label: Cystic duct to gallbladder
steps.text: With the hepatopancreatic sphincter closed, bile backs up the cystic duct into the gallbladder, which concentrates it.
steps.why: Between meals the exit is closed, so bile collects in the gallbladder until a meal.

steps.label: Gallbladder contracts
steps.text: After a fatty meal, CCK contracts the gallbladder, and bile flows down the cystic duct into the common bile duct.
steps.why: The cystic duct carries bile both ways: in to be stored, out after a meal.

steps.label: Hepatopancreatic ampulla
steps.text: The common bile duct runs behind the duodenum and through the pancreas to meet the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
steps.why: In most people the bile and pancreatic routes share one chamber before the duodenum.

steps.label: Into the duodenum
steps.text: CCK relaxes the hepatopancreatic sphincter, and bile enters the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.
steps.why: The sphincter is the last gate; it opens only when CCK signals that fat has arrived.

distractors.text: The hepatic ducts empty into the hepatic veins.
distractors.why: The hepatic veins carry blood to the inferior vena cava. Bile and blood never mix.

distractors.text: The hepatic ducts drain straight into the gallbladder, which makes more bile.
distractors.why: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; it does not make any. Bile reaches it by the cystic duct.

error.text: The common bile duct joins the hepatic portal vein, which carries the bile to the duodenum.
error.why: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the gut to the liver. Bile travels only in ducts, joining the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

pathways.summary: Hepatocytes, bile canaliculi, bile ducts in the portal triads, right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct; between meals up the cystic duct into the gallbladder; after a meal back down into the common bile duct, the hepatopancreatic ampulla and, through the relaxed sphincter, the duodenum.

pathways.title: The enterohepatic circulation of bile salts
pathways.intro: Your body holds only 2 to 4 g of bile salts, yet one fatty meal needs more than that. Follow a bile salt around the loop that lets it be used again and again.

steps.label: Hepatocytes secrete
steps.text: Hepatocytes secrete bile salts into bile.
steps.why: The liver is where bile salts are made from cholesterol and where recycled ones are sent out again.

steps.label: Stored in gallbladder
steps.text: Between meals, bile is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder.
steps.why: Bile made between meals waits here until CCK releases it.

steps.label: Emulsify fat in intestine
steps.text: After a meal, bile salts enter the duodenum and emulsify fat along the small intestine.
steps.why: They do their job in the lumen before anything can reclaim them.

steps.label: Absorbed in terminal ileum
steps.text: Carriers in the last part of the ileum absorb about 95% of them.
steps.why: Only the terminal ileum has these carriers, so bile salts are reclaimed at the end of the small intestine, after the fat has been absorbed.

steps.label: Hepatic portal vein
steps.text: They travel in the hepatic portal vein back to the liver.
steps.why: Blood from the intestine drains to the liver first.

steps.label: Taken up from sinusoids
steps.text: Hepatocytes take them up from the sinusoids, ready to secrete them again.
steps.why: The loop closes: the same bile salts are secreted again, several times a day.

distractors.text: The colon absorbs almost all of them along with the water.
distractors.why: Most bile salts are reclaimed before the colon, by carriers in the terminal ileum. Only a small amount reaches the colon.

distractors.text: They are broken down, and the liver makes a completely new supply for every meal.
distractors.why: The pool is too small for that. About 95% are reabsorbed; only the few percent lost in the feces are replaced from cholesterol.

error.text: They enter the lacteals and travel in the lymph through the thoracic duct back to the liver.
error.why: Bile salts are absorbed into the blood capillaries and travel in the hepatic portal vein. The lacteal route is for packaged fat droplets.

pathways.summary: Liver, bile, gallbladder, duodenum and small intestine, terminal ileum, hepatic portal vein, liver again. About 95% is reclaimed each pass; the small loss in the feces is replaced from cholesterol. Remove the terminal ileum and the pool drains away.

pathways.title: Switching on the pancreas’s protein-digesting enzymes
pathways.intro: The pancreas makes enzymes strong enough to digest it, yet in health it is never digested. Trace how those enzymes stay switched off until they reach the gut.

steps.label: Zymogens made in acini
steps.text: Acinar cells make trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen and proelastase as inactive zymogens, along with a trypsin inhibitor.
steps.why: Making them inactive is what protects the acinar cells that make them.

steps.label: Down the pancreatic duct
steps.text: The zymogens are released by exocytosis and flow down the pancreatic duct into the duodenum.
steps.why: They must leave the gland before anything can switch them on.

steps.label: Enteropeptidase cuts
steps.text: Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border cuts a short piece off trypsinogen, making active trypsin.
steps.why: Enteropeptidase exists only in the intestine, so this first cut happens only there.

steps.label: Trypsin activates trypsin
steps.text: Trypsin cuts more trypsinogen into trypsin, so activation speeds up.
steps.why: Trypsin can only activate its own precursor once the first trypsin exists.

steps.label: Trypsin activates the rest
steps.text: Trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen into chymotrypsin, proelastase into elastase, and the other protein-digesting precursors.
steps.why: One enzyme, trypsin, is the master switch for all the others.

steps.label: Proteins cut into peptides
steps.text: The active enzymes cut proteins and polypeptides into shorter peptides.
steps.why: Only active enzymes can digest; this is the payoff of the cascade.

distractors.text: Stomach acid entering the duodenum lowers the pH, and the acid itself cuts trypsinogen into active trypsin.
distractors.why: Acid switches on pepsinogen, not trypsinogen, and bicarbonate neutralizes the acid in the duodenum anyway. Enteropeptidase makes the first trypsin.

distractors.text: Bile salts cut trypsinogen into trypsin.
distractors.why: Bile has no enzymes; bile salts emulsify fat. Enteropeptidase is the switch.

error.text: Acinar cells make active trypsin and store it in their vesicles, ready to release.
error.why: Active trypsin inside the gland would digest it; that is what happens in acute pancreatitis. The cells make inactive trypsinogen.

pathways.summary: Zymogens made and shipped out, enteropeptidase in the duodenum makes the first trypsin, trypsin makes more of itself and switches on chymotrypsin and elastase, and only then does protein digestion begin. A trypsin inhibitor and the constant flow down the ducts add more safety.

pathways.title: Carbohydrate digestion and absorption
pathways.intro: You eat a slice of bread and drink a glass of milk. Trace the starch and sugars from your mouth to the liver.

steps.label: Salivary amylase
steps.text: Salivary amylase starts cutting starch into shorter chains and maltose while you chew.
steps.why: Carbohydrate digestion is the only one that starts in the mouth.

steps.label: Acid stops amylase
steps.text: In the stomach, amylase keeps working inside the bolus until acid soaks in and stops it.
steps.why: Acid needs time to penetrate a swallowed mouthful, often half an hour or more.

steps.label: Pancreatic amylase
steps.text: In the small intestine, pancreatic amylase cuts the rest of the starch into maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins.
steps.why: Pancreatic amylase does most of the work, once bicarbonate has neutralized the chyme.

steps.label: Brush border enzymes
steps.text: Brush border α-dextrinase, maltase, sucrase and lactase split the fragments and the eaten disaccharides into monosaccharides.
steps.why: Only monosaccharides can be absorbed, and the last cut happens right at the membrane that absorbs them.

steps.label: SGLT1 and GLUT5
steps.text: Glucose and galactose enter the absorptive cell with sodium through SGLT1; fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5.
steps.why: The monosaccharides are released beside their carriers, which carry them across the apical membrane.

steps.label: Out through GLUT2
steps.text: All three leave through the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion through GLUT2.
steps.why: Sugar builds up inside the cell, so it can move out down its gradient.

steps.label: Hepatic portal vein
steps.text: They enter the villus capillaries and travel in the hepatic portal vein to the liver.
steps.why: Blood from the intestine drains to the liver before the rest of the body.

distractors.text: Pancreatic amylase goes on to split the maltose, and the sucrose and lactose from the meal, into single sugars in the lumen.
distractors.why: Amylase makes maltose but cannot split it, and it does not act on sucrose or lactose. The brush border enzymes finish the job.

distractors.text: The short fragments are absorbed as they are and split inside the liver.
distractors.why: Only monosaccharides can cross the brush border, so the fragments must be split first.

error.text: Glucose, galactose and fructose all enter the absorptive cell with sodium through SGLT1.
error.why: SGLT1 carries glucose and galactose. Fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through a different carrier, GLUT5.

pathways.summary: Salivary amylase, then pancreatic amylase, make maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins; brush border enzymes finish them into monosaccharides; SGLT1 (with sodium) and GLUT5 bring them in, GLUT2 lets them out, and the hepatic portal vein carries them to the liver.

pathways.title: Protein digestion and absorption
pathways.intro: You eat a piece of grilled fish. Trace its protein from the stomach to the liver.

steps.label: Acid unfolds protein
steps.text: Stomach acid unfolds (denatures) the proteins, exposing their peptide bonds.
steps.why: Acid itself splits few bonds; it prepares proteins for enzymes, so it acts first.

steps.label: Pepsin: large polypeptides
steps.text: Pepsin cuts the proteins into large polypeptides.
steps.why: Pepsin needs acid, so it works in the stomach. It does only about 10 to 15% of protein digestion.

steps.label: Bicarbonate stops pepsin
steps.text: In the duodenum, bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes the chyme, and pepsin stops working.
steps.why: The pancreatic enzymes need a near-neutral pH, so neutralizing comes before them.

steps.label: Pancreatic proteases
steps.text: Trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase cut inside the chains, and carboxypeptidase trims amino acids from the carboxyl end.
steps.why: Once switched on by enteropeptidase and trypsin, these enzymes do most protein digestion in the lumen.

steps.label: Brush border peptidases
steps.text: Brush border aminopeptidase and dipeptidase finish the job, leaving amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides.
steps.why: The last cuts happen at the membrane, right beside the carriers.

steps.label: Into the absorptive cell
steps.text: Amino acids enter with sodium; dipeptides and tripeptides enter with hydrogen ions and are split inside the cell.
steps.why: Carriers take up the products at the brush border once they are small enough.

steps.label: To the liver in portal blood
steps.text: Amino acids leave through basolateral carriers into the villus capillaries and the hepatic portal vein.
steps.why: Almost all of it reaches the blood as single amino acids, which drain to the liver first.

distractors.text: Pepsin keeps working in the duodenum and does most of the digestion there.
distractors.why: Pepsin stops working as the pH rises toward neutral. It does only a minority of protein digestion.

distractors.text: Bile salts break the peptide bonds of the polypeptides.
distractors.why: Bile has no enzymes. Peptide bonds are cut by the pancreatic proteases and brush border peptidases.

error.text: Amino acids are packaged into chylomicrons and leave through the lacteal.
error.why: Chylomicrons carry absorbed fat. Amino acids are water-soluble and go into the villus capillaries and the hepatic portal vein.

pathways.summary: Acid unfolds; pepsin makes large polypeptides; bicarbonate neutralizes; trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase and carboxypeptidase make short peptides; brush border peptidases leave amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides; these enter with sodium or hydrogen ions and reach the liver as amino acids in portal blood.

pathways.title: Lipid digestion and absorption
pathways.intro: You eat a buttered roll. The fat does not dissolve in water, but everything between it and your blood does. Trace how a triglyceride gets from the duodenum into your blood.

steps.label: Bile salts emulsify
steps.text: In the duodenum, bile salts coat the fat, and churning breaks it into tiny droplets.
steps.why: Lipase is water-soluble and works only at a droplet’s surface, so the surface must be made large first.

steps.label: Pancreatic lipase
steps.text: Pancreatic lipase, anchored by colipase, splits each triglyceride into two fatty acids and a monoglyceride.
steps.why: Digestion follows emulsification: the enzyme works on the enlarged surface.

steps.label: Micelles form
steps.text: Fatty acids and monoglycerides gather with bile salts into micelles, which carry them through the still water layer to the brush border.
steps.why: Only the digested products fit into micelles.

steps.label: Enter the cell
steps.text: At the brush border, fatty acids and monoglycerides leave the micelle and cross the apical membrane; the bile salts stay in the lumen.
steps.why: The micelle delivers its cargo at the surface; the bile salts go on to be reclaimed in the ileum.

steps.label: Triglycerides rebuilt
steps.text: In the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, fatty acids are joined back onto monoglycerides to make triglycerides again.
steps.why: This happens inside the cell, and keeping free fatty acids low there lets more diffuse in.

steps.label: Chylomicrons packaged
steps.text: The endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus wrap the triglycerides and cholesterol in phospholipid and protein, making chylomicrons.
steps.why: Triglycerides must be rebuilt before they can be packaged.

steps.label: Into the lacteal
steps.text: Chylomicrons leave by exocytosis and enter the lacteal, because they are too large for the villus’s blood capillaries.
steps.why: Size decides the route: blood capillaries exclude chylomicrons, lymphatic capillaries take them in.

steps.label: Thoracic duct to veins
steps.text: Chyle flows to the cisterna chyli and the thoracic duct, which empties where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet.
steps.why: Lymph returns to the blood at the base of the neck, so absorbed fat reaches the blood without passing through the liver first.

distractors.text: The rebuilt triglycerides diffuse straight out into the villus capillaries.
distractors.why: Long-chain fats are packaged into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries.

distractors.text: The triglycerides are packed back into micelles inside the cell.
distractors.why: Micelles form in the lumen with bile salts, which stay outside the cell. Inside, the fats are packaged into chylomicrons.

error.text: Chylomicrons enter the blood capillaries of the villus and travel in the hepatic portal vein to the liver.
error.why: Chylomicrons are too large for the blood capillaries. They enter the lacteal and travel in lymph, reaching the blood at the left venous angle.

pathways.summary: Emulsify, digest, micelles, enter, rebuild, package, lacteal, thoracic duct. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are the exception: they enter the villus capillaries and go straight to the liver.

pathways.title: The escorted route of vitamin B12
pathways.intro: Vitamin B12 is too large to cross the brush border by any ordinary carrier. Trace the escorted route it takes from a bite of egg to your liver.

steps.label: Freed from food protein
steps.text: In the stomach, acid and pepsin free B12 from the food proteins it is bound to.
steps.why: B12 must be released from food before anything else can bind it.

steps.label: Binds haptocorrin
steps.text: Free B12 binds haptocorrin, a protein from saliva that protects it from acid.
steps.why: Haptocorrin is waiting in the stomach and grabs B12 as soon as it is freed, before intrinsic factor can.

steps.label: Switch to intrinsic factor
steps.text: In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases digest haptocorrin, and B12 binds intrinsic factor from the parietal cells.
steps.why: Intrinsic factor cannot bind B12 while haptocorrin holds it, so the swap waits for the pancreatic enzymes.

steps.label: Taken up in terminal ileum
steps.text: In the terminal ileum, receptor proteins bind the B12–intrinsic factor complex, and the cells take it in by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
steps.why: These receptor proteins are found only at the far end of the ileum, so uptake happens late.

steps.label: Into the blood
steps.text: B12 leaves the absorptive cell bound to a transport protein in the blood.
steps.why: It crosses the cell before it can be carried away.

steps.label: Stored in the liver
steps.text: The liver stores enough B12 to last three to five years.
steps.why: The store is filled from the blood, so it comes last, and it explains why deficiency appears years after the route breaks.

distractors.text: In the duodenum, B12 crosses the brush border on its own by simple diffusion.
distractors.why: B12 is large and water-soluble. Only about 1% of a dose slips across without an escort, far too little to absorb what food supplies. The normal route needs intrinsic factor and the ileum’s receptor proteins.

distractors.text: In the duodenum, bile salts carry B12 into micelles.
distractors.why: Micelles carry fats. B12 dissolves in water and is escorted by intrinsic factor.

error.text: In the jejunum, carriers take up the B12–intrinsic factor complex by facilitated diffusion.
error.why: The complex is taken up only in the terminal ileum, by receptor-mediated endocytosis. That is why removing the terminal ileum causes B12 deficiency.

pathways.summary: Freed by acid and pepsin, guarded by haptocorrin, handed to intrinsic factor in the duodenum, taken up in the terminal ileum, carried in the blood, stored in the liver. A break anywhere, from parietal cells to pancreas to ileum, causes deficiency years later.

pathways.title: The defecation reflex
pathways.intro: Half an hour after breakfast, you feel the urge to go. Trace the reflex from the stomach to the moment of defecation.

steps.label: Gastrocolic reflex
steps.text: Food stretching the stomach triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which increases colon motility.
steps.why: Mass movements are most likely in the first hour after a meal, so eating starts the chain.

steps.label: Mass movement
steps.text: A mass movement sweeps feces from the colon into the rectum.
steps.why: The rectum is usually empty; a mass movement is what fills it.

steps.label: Rectal wall stretches
steps.text: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the rectal wall fire.
steps.why: Feces must arrive in the rectum before they can stretch it.

steps.label: Signal to sacral cord
steps.text: Sensory neurons carry the signal to the sacral spinal cord (S2–S4) and up to the brain, where you feel the urge.
steps.why: The signal has to reach the cord before the cord can respond.

steps.label: Rectum contracts, IAS opens
steps.text: Parasympathetic neurons from the sacral cord contract the rectum and sigmoid colon and relax the internal anal sphincter.
steps.why: This is the reflex output, the step you do not control.

steps.label: You relax the EAS
steps.text: You decide to go: you relax the external anal sphincter and pelvic floor, often adding a Valsalva’s maneuver.
steps.why: The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control, the final gate.

steps.label: Feces pass out
steps.text: Pressure in the abdomen rises, and feces pass out through the anus.
steps.why: Defecation happens only once both sphincters are open.

distractors.text: Sympathetic neurons contract the rectum and relax the internal anal sphincter.
distractors.why: The reflex output is parasympathetic, from the sacral cord. Sympathetic activity tightens sphincters and slows the gut.

distractors.text: You relax the internal anal sphincter on purpose.
distractors.why: The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle, not under your control. It relaxes by reflex.

error.text: You decide to go: you relax the internal anal sphincter, the one under your control.
error.why: The sphincter you control is the external anal sphincter, which is skeletal muscle. The internal one is smooth muscle and relaxes by reflex.

pathways.summary: Meal, gastrocolic reflex, mass movement, rectal stretch, sacral cord, parasympathetic contraction of the rectum and relaxation of the internal anal sphincter, then your choice at the external anal sphincter. Put it off, and the rectum relaxes and the urge fades until the next mass movement.

pathways.title: Glucose to ATP: glycolysis, citric acid cycle, electron transport
pathways.intro: A liver cell with plenty of oxygen breaks down one glucose molecule completely. Trace it from the cytosol to the last ATP, step by step.

steps.label: Hexokinase traps glucose
steps.text: Hexokinase moves a phosphate from ATP onto glucose, making glucose-6-phosphate, which cannot leave the cell.
steps.why: Every later step needs glucose inside the cell and activated; this is the first ATP spent in the energy-consuming phase.

steps.label: Phosphofructokinase commits
steps.text: After a rearrangement, phosphofructokinase spends a second ATP to make fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
steps.why: This is the committed, main control step, and it needs the rearranged sugar made from glucose-6-phosphate.

steps.label: Six carbons split in two
steps.text: The six-carbon sugar is split into two three-carbon sugar phosphates, which are made identical.
steps.why: Only the doubly phosphorylated sugar is split, so it follows the second ATP investment; from here every step happens twice.

steps.label: Oxidation makes NADH
steps.text: Each three-carbon half gives two electrons to NAD+, making NADH, and picks up a free phosphate.
steps.why: This first step of the energy-yielding phase needs the three-carbon halves made by the split.

steps.label: 4 ATP made; pyruvate left
steps.text: The phosphates are passed to ADP by substrate-level phosphorylation, making 4 ATP, and two pyruvate remain.
steps.why: The phosphates can be passed on only once oxidation has put them in high-energy positions; this ends glycolysis with a net 2 ATP.

steps.label: Pyruvate to acetyl CoA
steps.text: In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO2, gives electrons to NAD+, and its acetyl group joins coenzyme A.
steps.why: Pyruvate from the cytosol must enter the mitochondrion and be trimmed to a two-carbon acetyl group before the cycle can use it. This step cannot run backward.

steps.label: Acetyl CoA joins oxaloacetate
steps.text: Acetyl CoA joins four-carbon oxaloacetate to make six-carbon citrate, and CoA is released.
steps.why: The cycle starts only when acetyl CoA is available, so it follows the step that makes it.

steps.label: Two carbons leave as CO2
steps.text: Two oxidation steps each remove a carbon as CO2 and make NADH.
steps.why: Citrate has to be formed and rearranged before its carbons can be removed; after these steps, all six carbons of glucose have left as CO2.

steps.label: FADH2, ATP; oxaloacetate back
steps.text: The cycle makes one ATP (by way of GTP), one FADH2 and a third NADH, and rebuilds oxaloacetate.
steps.why: These last steps turn the four-carbon remainder back into oxaloacetate, ready for the next acetyl CoA.

steps.label: Carriers deliver electrons
steps.text: NADH hands its electrons to complex I and FADH2 to complex II in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
steps.why: The chain runs on electrons loaded onto carriers by glycolysis, pyruvate breakdown and the cycle, so it comes after them.

steps.label: Complexes I, III, IV pump H+
steps.text: Electrons pass along the chain to carriers that hold them more tightly, and complexes I, III and IV use the energy released to pump H+ into the intermembrane space.
steps.why: Pumping needs electrons moving downhill through the complexes, so it follows their delivery.

steps.label: Oxygen takes the electrons
steps.text: At complex IV, oxygen accepts the electrons and H+ and becomes water.
steps.why: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor: it clears electrons from the end of the chain so the carriers upstream can keep passing them along.

steps.label: ATP synthase makes ATP
steps.text: H+ flows back into the matrix through ATP synthase, turning it and making most of the cell’s ATP: about 30 to 32 per glucose in all.
steps.why: ATP synthase spends the gradient the chain has built, so it can run only after pumping has stored energy in the H+ gradient.

distractors.text: In the cytosol, pyruvate is turned into lactate, which then enters the mitochondrion and joins the citric acid cycle unchanged.
distractors.why: With oxygen available, pyruvate goes into the mitochondrion. Lactate is made when oxygen is short, and it does not enter the cycle.

distractors.text: In the matrix, pyruvate joins oxaloacetate directly, keeping all three of its carbons, and no NADH or CO2 is made at this step.
distractors.why: Pyruvate first loses one carbon as CO2; it is the two-carbon acetyl group that joins oxaloacetate.

distractors.text: In the matrix, pyruvate is turned back into glucose for storage.
distractors.why: That would reverse the pathway. The liver can make glucose from pyruvate, but by gluconeogenesis, not as a step of glucose breakdown.

error.text: H+ is pumped back into the matrix by ATP synthase, which spends ATP to do it.
error.why: ATP synthase does not pump; H+ flows through it down the gradient built by the chain, and that flow makes ATP rather than spending it.

pathways.summary: Glycolysis spends 2 ATP and then makes 4 ATP and 2 NADH in the cytosol; pyruvate becomes acetyl CoA in the matrix; the citric acid cycle strips its carbons to CO2 and loads NADH and FADH2; the electron transport chain uses those electrons, with oxygen at the end, to build an H+ gradient that ATP synthase spends to make most of the ATP.

pathways.title: Liver glycogen to blood glucose
pathways.intro: It is 11 am and you skipped breakfast. Blood glucose is drifting down and glucagon is rising. Trace one glucose unit from a glycogen branch in a liver cell into the blood.

steps.label: Glucagon binds liver cells
steps.text: Glucagon binds receptor proteins on the liver cell’s plasma membrane.
steps.why: Glucagon is a water-soluble hormone, so it acts from outside the cell, and everything else follows its binding.

steps.label: cAMP and protein kinase A
steps.text: A G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase; cyclic AMP rises and switches on protein kinase A.
steps.why: The second messenger carries the signal inside only after the receptor protein has been activated.

steps.label: Phosphorylase on, synthase off
steps.text: Protein kinase A switches glycogen phosphorylase on and glycogen synthase off.
steps.why: Both enzymes are set at once, so the cell does not build and break glycogen at the same time.

steps.label: Phosphorolysis: glucose-1-P
steps.text: Glycogen phosphorylase clips glucose units off the branch ends, using phosphate, releasing glucose-1-phosphate (a debranching enzyme clears the branch points it cannot reach).
steps.why: The enzyme must be switched on before it works; it breaks each bond with phosphate, not water.

steps.label: Glucose-1-P to glucose-6-P
steps.text: Glucose-1-phosphate is converted to glucose-6-phosphate.
steps.why: Glucose-6-phosphate is the meeting point of glycogen, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; it is also the substrate of the enzyme that frees glucose.

steps.label: Glucose-6-phosphatase
steps.text: Glucose-6-phosphatase in the endoplasmic reticulum removes the phosphate, leaving free glucose.
steps.why: Only free glucose can leave the cell, and only liver and kidney cells have this enzyme.

steps.label: Glucose leaves into the blood
steps.text: Free glucose leaves the liver cell by facilitated diffusion through glucose carriers and enters the blood.
steps.why: Inside the cell free glucose is now higher than in the blood, so it moves down its gradient into the sinusoids.

distractors.text: Hexokinase adds another phosphate to the glucose, so that it can cross the plasma membrane through the glucose carriers.
distractors.why: A phosphate traps glucose inside; the carriers do not carry phosphorylated glucose. The phosphate must be removed, not added.

distractors.text: Glucose-6-phosphate enters glycolysis in the liver cell and leaves as pyruvate.
distractors.why: That happens in muscle, which lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. The liver releases glucose itself to supply other tissues.

distractors.text: Glycogen synthase adds the glucose back to a new glycogen branch.
distractors.why: Glucagon has switched glycogen synthase off, so the glucose is released rather than stored.

error.text: Glycogen phosphorylase adds water across each bond, releasing free glucose that leaves the cell at once.
error.why: Phosphorylase breaks each bond by phosphorolysis, adding phosphate rather than water, so the glucose comes off as glucose-1-phosphate and still needs its phosphate removed before it can leave.

pathways.summary: Glucagon acts through cyclic AMP and protein kinase A to switch glycogen phosphorylase on; glucose comes off glycogen as glucose-1-phosphate, becomes glucose-6-phosphate, and glucose-6-phosphatase frees it to leave the liver for the blood.

pathways.title: The Cori cycle: lactate back to glucose
pathways.intro: A sprinter’s leg muscles run short of oxygen and make lactate. Trace the carbon from muscle glucose to the liver and back.

steps.label: Muscle glycolysis
steps.text: In the working muscle, glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, making 2 ATP.
steps.why: The cycle starts where the energy is spent: muscle breaking glucose down for fast ATP.

steps.label: Pyruvate to lactate
steps.text: With oxygen short, pyruvate is turned into lactate, regenerating the NAD+ glycolysis needs.
steps.why: Pyruvate must exist before it can be reduced, and this step lets glycolysis keep running without the mitochondria.

steps.label: Lactate into the blood
steps.text: Lactate leaves the muscle and travels in the blood to the liver.
steps.why: Lactate made in the muscle has to be carried away before the liver can use it.

steps.label: Liver: lactate to pyruvate
steps.text: Liver cells take up lactate and turn it back into pyruvate, regaining NADH.
steps.why: Gluconeogenesis starts from pyruvate, so lactate must first be converted.

steps.label: Pyruvate to oxaloacetate
steps.text: Inside the mitochondrion, an enzyme that needs biotin adds CO2 to pyruvate, making oxaloacetate, which becomes phosphoenolpyruvate.
steps.why: This detour gets around the step of glycolysis that cannot be reversed, so it must come first on the way up.

steps.label: Up to fructose-6-phosphate
steps.text: Most of glycolysis’s steps run in reverse to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and a phosphatase removes one phosphate.
steps.why: Once phosphoenolpyruvate is made, the reversible steps can climb back toward six carbons; the phosphatase is the second detour.

steps.label: Phosphate off: free glucose
steps.text: Glucose-6-phosphate is made, and glucose-6-phosphatase removes its phosphate.
steps.why: The last detour releases free glucose; only the liver and kidneys have this enzyme.

steps.label: Glucose back to muscle
steps.text: The glucose enters the blood and returns to the muscle, which can break it down again.
steps.why: The new glucose must leave the liver before the muscle can take it up, closing the loop. Each turn costs the body 4 ATP.

distractors.text: Pyruvate is turned straight back into phosphoenolpyruvate by running the last enzyme of glycolysis in reverse, which costs the liver no ATP at all.
distractors.why: That step of glycolysis releases so much energy that it cannot be reversed; gluconeogenesis goes around it by way of oxaloacetate.

distractors.text: Pyruvate becomes acetyl CoA, which the liver builds into glucose.
distractors.why: Acetyl CoA can never become glucose, because the step from pyruvate to acetyl CoA cannot run backward.

distractors.text: Pyruvate is stored as glycogen in the muscle.
distractors.why: The carbon has already left the muscle as lactate; this part of the cycle happens in the liver.

error.text: The glucose is kept in the liver, which needs it more than the muscle.
error.why: The point of the cycle is to return the carbon to working muscle. The liver pays for the new glucose with its own aerobic ATP and releases it into the blood.

pathways.summary: Muscle turns glucose into lactate to keep glycolysis going; the liver turns lactate back into glucose by gluconeogenesis, spending 6 high-energy phosphates to regain the muscle’s 2, and sends the glucose back.

pathways.title: Fat to ATP
pathways.intro: An hour into a long, easy bike ride, your insulin is low and your epinephrine is up. Trace one stored fatty acid from a fat cell to ATP in a leg muscle.

steps.label: Low insulin, epinephrine up
steps.text: With insulin low, epinephrine acts through beta receptor proteins, cyclic AMP and protein kinase A to switch on the lipases in the fat cell.
steps.why: Stored fat stays locked up until the insulin brake is off and a signal switches the lipases on.

steps.label: Lipolysis
steps.text: Lipases hydrolyze the stored triglyceride into glycerol and three fatty acids.
steps.why: The lipases act only once they are switched on; this is the step that releases the fuel.

steps.label: Fatty acids ride on albumin
steps.text: The fatty acids leave the fat cell and travel in the blood bound to albumin.
steps.why: Fatty acids do not dissolve in plasma, so they need a carrier to reach the muscle.

steps.label: Activation with CoA
steps.text: The muscle cell takes up the fatty acid and joins it to coenzyme A in the cytosol, at a cost of 2 ATP.
steps.why: The fatty acid must be inside the cell and activated before it can be carried into the mitochondrion.

steps.label: Carnitine carries it in
steps.text: Carnitine carries the activated fatty acid across the inner mitochondrial membrane, and it is joined to CoA again in the matrix.
steps.why: The inner membrane does not let activated fatty acids through, so this carrier step comes before any oxidation.

steps.label: One turn of beta oxidation
steps.text: Four enzyme steps oxidize the beta carbon, making 1 FADH2 and 1 NADH and cutting off 1 acetyl CoA.
steps.why: Beta oxidation runs in the matrix, so it follows entry.

steps.label: Repeat until all acetyl CoA
steps.text: The shortened chain goes around again until all of it is acetyl CoA: 8 from a 16-carbon chain, in 7 turns.
steps.why: Each turn leaves a chain two carbons shorter, which is the substrate for the next turn.

steps.label: Citric acid cycle
steps.text: The acetyl CoA enters the citric acid cycle and is taken apart to CO2, loading more NADH and FADH2.
steps.why: The cycle takes in acetyl CoA from any fuel, so it follows the step that makes it.

steps.label: Chain, oxygen, ATP synthase
steps.text: NADH and FADH2 feed the electron transport chain, oxygen accepts the electrons, and ATP synthase makes ATP: about 106 per palmitic acid.
steps.why: The chain runs on the carriers that beta oxidation and the cycle loaded, and it regenerates the NAD+ and FAD they need. Without oxygen, fat cannot be burned.

distractors.text: The activated fatty acid diffuses freely across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
distractors.why: The inner membrane is not permeable to it; the carnitine carrier is required, which is why this step can limit fat burning.

distractors.text: The fatty acid is broken down by glycolysis in the cytosol.
distractors.why: Glycolysis breaks down sugars. Fatty acids are broken down by beta oxidation, inside the mitochondrion.

distractors.text: The fatty acid is converted to glucose, which then enters the mitochondrion.
distractors.why: Fatty acids can never become glucose; their carbon ends as acetyl CoA.

error.text: Insulin rises and switches on the lipases in the fat cell.
error.why: Insulin does the opposite: it brakes lipolysis even at low levels. Fat release rises when insulin falls and epinephrine, cortisol or growth hormone rise.

pathways.summary: With insulin low, epinephrine switches on lipolysis; fatty acids ride on albumin to muscle, are activated, carried into the mitochondrion by carnitine and cut into acetyl CoA by beta oxidation; the citric acid cycle and electron transport chain then turn them into ATP, which needs oxygen.

pathways.title: Ketone bodies: from liver to heart
pathways.intro: It is the third day of a fast. Fatty acids are flooding into the liver. Trace the carbon from surplus acetyl CoA in a liver cell to ATP in a heart muscle cell.

steps.label: Acetyl CoA piles up
steps.text: Beta oxidation makes acetyl CoA faster than the citric acid cycle can take it, and oxaloacetate is being drawn off for gluconeogenesis.
steps.why: Ketogenesis starts only when acetyl CoA is in surplus; with plenty of oxaloacetate it would simply enter the cycle.

steps.label: Two acetyl CoA join
steps.text: Two acetyl CoA join to make a four-carbon molecule.
steps.why: The ketone bodies are built from the surplus acetyl groups, so joining them is the first step.

steps.label: Acetoacetate released
steps.text: A third acetyl CoA is added and removed again, releasing acetoacetate.
steps.why: The four-carbon molecule must be built up and cut back to free acetoacetate, the first ketone body.

steps.label: Beta-hydroxybutyrate
steps.text: Much of the acetoacetate gains two hydrogens from NADH and becomes beta-hydroxybutyrate.
steps.why: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is made from acetoacetate, so it comes after it; it becomes the main ketone body in the blood.

steps.label: Exported to the blood
steps.text: The liver releases the ketone bodies into the blood, because it lacks the enzyme to use them.
steps.why: The ketone bodies must be made before they can leave; the liver cannot burn them itself.

steps.label: Heart takes them up
steps.text: Heart muscle cells take up the ketone bodies and turn them back into acetyl CoA.
steps.why: Other tissues can use them only after they arrive in the blood.

steps.label: Burned for ATP
steps.text: The acetyl CoA enters the heart cell’s citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain makes ATP.
steps.why: Once back as acetyl CoA, the carbon joins the same final pathway as any fuel.

distractors.text: The liver burns the ketone bodies in its own citric acid cycle, which is why it makes them in the first place.
distractors.why: The liver lacks the enzyme that turns acetoacetate back into acetyl CoA, so it cannot use its own ketone bodies.

distractors.text: The ketone bodies are turned into glucose and released.
distractors.why: Ketone bodies are made from acetyl CoA, and acetyl CoA carbon can never become glucose.

distractors.text: The ketone bodies are stored in liver cells as fat.
distractors.why: In a fast insulin is low and fat is being released, not stored; the ketone bodies are exported as fuel for other tissues.

error.text: Much of the acetoacetate loses CO2 and becomes beta-hydroxybutyrate.
error.why: Acetoacetate becomes beta-hydroxybutyrate by gaining two hydrogens from NADH. It is the small share that loses CO2 on its own that forms acetone, which leaves in the breath.

pathways.summary: When acetyl CoA is in surplus, the liver joins acetyl groups into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate and exports them; heart, muscle, kidney and, after a few days, brain cells turn them back into acetyl CoA and burn them.

pathways.title: Amino acid to urea
pathways.intro: After a high-protein meal, extra amino acids reach the liver. Trace the nitrogen of one amino acid until it leaves the body.

steps.label: Transamination
steps.text: A transaminase, using a coenzyme made from vitamin B6, moves the amino group onto alpha-ketoglutarate, making glutamate and leaving the carbon skeleton.
steps.why: The amino group must be collected from each kind of amino acid onto one carrier before it can be removed.

steps.label: Deamination releases ammonia
steps.text: In liver mitochondria, glutamate’s amino group is stripped off as ammonia, and alpha-ketoglutarate is freed to collect again.
steps.why: Glutamate is made first by transamination; its amino group is then released in one place, the liver.

steps.label: Carbamoyl phosphate
steps.text: Ammonia joins bicarbonate, using 2 ATP, to make carbamoyl phosphate.
steps.why: The urea cycle can take in ammonia only once it has been released; this is where the first nitrogen enters.

steps.label: Ornithine to citrulline
steps.text: Carbamoyl phosphate joins ornithine to make citrulline, which moves to the cytosol.
steps.why: Ornithine is the cycle’s carrier; it must take on carbamoyl phosphate before the second nitrogen can be added.

steps.label: Aspartate adds nitrogen 2
steps.text: Citrulline picks up a second amino group from aspartate, using another ATP, making argininosuccinate.
steps.why: The second nitrogen is added to citrulline, so it follows the first.

steps.label: Arginine and fumarate
steps.text: Argininosuccinate splits into arginine and fumarate, which links to the citric acid cycle.
steps.why: The split frees arginine, which now holds both nitrogens.

steps.label: Arginase releases urea
steps.text: Arginase splits arginine into urea and ornithine, and ornithine returns for the next turn.
steps.why: Urea can be released only once arginine carries both nitrogens.

steps.label: Urea to the kidneys
steps.text: Urea leaves the liver in the blood and travels to the kidneys.
steps.why: Urea is made in the liver but removed by the kidneys, so it must be carried between them.

steps.label: Excreted in urine
steps.text: The kidneys excrete urea in the urine.
steps.why: This is the last step: the nitrogen that started on the amino acid leaves the body.

distractors.text: Glutamate leaves the liver in the blood and is excreted unchanged by the kidneys, carrying the amino group out in the urine.
distractors.why: Glutamate is an amino acid the body reuses; its amino group is released as ammonia in the liver and turned into urea.

distractors.text: The carbon skeleton is turned directly into urea.
distractors.why: Urea is made from the nitrogen, not the carbon skeleton. The skeleton is burned or built into glucose, ketone bodies or fat.

distractors.text: The amino group is stored in muscle for later use.
distractors.why: The body has no store of amino acids or amino groups; nitrogen not used for building is excreted.

error.text: Arginase splits arginine into ammonia and ornithine, and the ammonia leaves in the urine.
error.why: Arginase releases urea, not ammonia. Turning toxic ammonia into urea is the whole point of the cycle; ammonia that builds up in the blood harms the brain.

pathways.summary: Transamination collects amino groups onto glutamate; deamination in the liver releases them as ammonia; the urea cycle adds one nitrogen from ammonia and one from aspartate to make urea, which the blood carries to the kidneys for excretion.

pathways.title: The fuel switch over a long fast
pathways.intro: A lost hiker has water but no food for several weeks. Put the body’s fuel changes in the order they cause one another.

steps.label: Liver glycogen runs out
steps.text: Within about a day, liver glycogen is used up.
steps.why: Glycogen is the first store the liver draws on between meals, and it holds only about 100 g.

steps.label: Muscle protein makes glucose
steps.text: The brain still needs about 120 g of glucose a day, so the liver makes it mostly from amino acids released by breaking down muscle protein.
steps.why: With glycogen gone, gluconeogenesis must supply all the glucose, and amino acids are its largest source.

steps.label: Ketone bodies rise
steps.text: Low insulin lets fatty acids flood into the liver, and ketone bodies rise over the first week.
steps.why: Ketogenesis speeds up as fat breakdown rises and oxaloacetate is drawn off for making glucose.

steps.label: Brain burns ketone bodies
steps.text: The brain takes up ketone bodies in proportion to their level; by a few weeks they supply about two thirds of its energy.
steps.why: The brain can use ketone bodies only once their blood level is high.

steps.label: Brain glucose need falls
steps.text: The brain’s glucose need falls to about 40 g a day.
steps.why: Each share of energy supplied by ketone bodies is a share the brain no longer takes from glucose.

steps.label: Protein is spared
steps.text: Muscle protein breakdown falls to about 20 g a day.
steps.why: Less glucose needed means fewer amino acids have to be turned into glucose.

steps.label: Fat stores run low
steps.text: After weeks, fat stores are nearly used up.
steps.why: Fat has been the main fuel all along, so it runs out last.

steps.label: Protein breakdown surges
steps.text: With no other fuel left, protein breakdown rises sharply again, and heart and breathing muscles waste.
steps.why: Once fat is gone the body has only its proteins to burn, which leads to heart failure, rhythm problems or infection.

distractors.text: Fatty acids from the fat stores are turned into glucose for the brain, so the liver no longer needs amino acids.
distractors.why: Fatty acids break down to acetyl CoA, which can never become glucose; only glycerol can.

distractors.text: The brain starts burning fatty acids directly.
distractors.why: The brain burns little fatty acid; its neurons carry out very little beta oxidation, which is why it waits for ketone bodies.

distractors.text: Insulin rises and stores the remaining fat.
distractors.why: Without food, insulin falls; that fall is what frees lipolysis.

error.text: Muscle protein breakdown rises further as the brain switches to ketone bodies.
error.why: The switch lowers the brain’s glucose need, so fewer amino acids are needed to make glucose and protein breakdown falls. That protein sparing is what lets a fast last about two months.

pathways.summary: Glycogen goes first; then muscle protein supplies glucose; rising ketone bodies let the brain cut its glucose need, which spares protein; when fat finally runs out, protein breakdown surges again.

pathways.title: Hunger to fullness: one meal
pathways.intro: You have not eaten since breakfast, and it is nearly your usual lunchtime. Trace the signals that start and end your lunch.

steps.label: Empty stomach releases ghrelin
steps.text: Your empty stomach releases ghrelin, which rises before your usual mealtime.
steps.why: Ghrelin is the short-term signal that starts the cycle; it rises while the stomach is empty.

steps.label: Hypothalamus drives hunger
steps.text: Ghrelin acts on the hypothalamus, where the neurons that drive hunger win out, and you feel hungry.
steps.why: The hormone must reach the hypothalamus before it can change how hungry you feel.

steps.label: You eat
steps.text: You eat lunch, and food stretches your stomach.
steps.why: Hunger leads to eating, which provides every signal that follows.

steps.label: Stretch signals via vagus
steps.text: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the stomach wall fire, and the vagus nerve carries the signal to the brainstem.
steps.why: The stomach must be stretched by food before these sensory receptors fire.

steps.label: CCK and GLP-1 released
steps.text: As food reaches the small intestine, cells in its lining release cholecystokinin and GLP-1, which act on the brainstem and hypothalamus.
steps.why: These hormones are released only once food has left the stomach for the small intestine.

steps.label: Satiety ends the meal
steps.text: You feel full, stop eating, and ghrelin falls.
steps.why: Satiety is the sum of the stretch and gut hormone signals, so it comes after them.

distractors.text: Leptin released by the stomach wall jumps within minutes of the first bites and, acting on the brainstem, brings the meal to an end.
distractors.why: Leptin comes from fat cells and tracks fat stores over days to months; it is not the meal-to-meal signal.

distractors.text: Ghrelin rises further as food reaches the small intestine.
distractors.why: Ghrelin falls after eating; it is the hunger signal, not the fullness signal.

distractors.text: Insulin from the stomach wall makes you hungrier.
distractors.why: Insulin comes from the pancreas, and in the hypothalamus it reduces hunger over the longer term.

error.text: Your fat cells release ghrelin, which rises before your usual mealtime.
error.why: Ghrelin is released by the empty stomach. Fat cells release leptin, the long-term signal of how much energy is stored.

pathways.summary: Ghrelin from the empty stomach makes the hypothalamus drive hunger; eating stretches the stomach and releases gut hormones such as cholecystokinin and GLP-1, which together produce satiety.

pathways.title: From carrot to rhodopsin: a fat-soluble vitamin
pathways.intro: You eat carrots cooked in a little oil. Trace their beta-carotene until it helps a rod in your retina detect light.

steps.label: Dissolves in fat droplets
steps.text: Beta-carotene dissolves in the fat of the meal.
steps.why: It is fat-soluble, so it travels with dietary fat from the start; without fat in the meal little is absorbed.

steps.label: Carried in micelles
steps.text: Bile salts gather it with the products of fat digestion into micelles, which carry it to the absorptive cells.
steps.why: Micelles form only once bile has acted on the fat droplets, and they are the route to the cell surface.

steps.label: Converted to vitamin A
steps.text: Inside the absorptive cells, much of the beta-carotene is converted to vitamin A.
steps.why: The gut does the conversion after absorption, so this comes after the micelle step.

steps.label: Chylomicrons into lymph
steps.text: Vitamin A is packed into chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals and the lymph.
steps.why: Chylomicrons are built inside the absorptive cell, and they are too large for blood capillaries.

steps.label: Stored in the liver
steps.text: Chylomicron remnants deliver vitamin A to the liver, which stores it.
steps.why: The liver takes up what the chylomicrons leave, which is why fat-soluble vitamins are stored for months.

steps.label: Released on a carrier
steps.text: The liver releases vitamin A into the blood on a carrier protein.
steps.why: Vitamin A does not dissolve in plasma, so it must be carried to the tissues that need it.

steps.label: Retinal joins opsin
steps.text: In the retina, vitamin A is converted to retinal, which joins opsin in the rods to form rhodopsin.
steps.why: The rod can build rhodopsin only once vitamin A reaches it from the blood; some retinal is lost each time light is absorbed and must be replaced.

distractors.text: Beta-carotene dissolves in the watery gut fluid and crosses the lining by carriers, passing straight into the blood capillaries of the villi.
distractors.why: That is the route of water-soluble vitamins. Beta-carotene is fat-soluble and needs bile and micelles.
