distractors.text: Intrinsic factor binds beta-carotene and carries it to the ileum.
distractors.why: Intrinsic factor escorts vitamin B12, not the fat-soluble vitamins.

distractors.text: Beta-carotene is excreted in urine within hours.
distractors.why: Excess water-soluble vitamins leave in urine. Fat-soluble ones are stored, which is why vitamin A can build up to toxic levels.

error.text: Vitamin A is released straight into the blood capillaries of the villus, dissolved in plasma.
error.why: Vitamin A travels with fat: it is packed into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the lacteals and lymph instead.

pathways.summary: A fat-soluble vitamin follows fat: it dissolves in fat, rides in micelles, is packed into chylomicrons and enters the lymph, is stored in the liver, and reaches its target tissue on a carrier protein.

pathways.title: Blood through the kidney
pathways.intro: About a fifth of your cardiac output passes through your kidneys every minute. Trace one red blood cell from the aorta, through a kidney and back to the vena cava.

steps.label: Renal artery
steps.text: Blood leaves the abdominal aorta at about L1 to L2 in a renal artery, which enters the kidney at the hilum.
steps.why: The renal arteries are the kidney’s only supply, branching straight off the aorta.

steps.label: Segmental arteries
steps.text: In the renal sinus, the renal artery divides into about five segmental arteries.
steps.why: Each segmental artery supplies one segment of the kidney, so the division comes first, in the sinus.

steps.label: Interlobar arteries
steps.text: Interlobar arteries run outward through the renal columns, between the pyramids.
steps.why: They carry blood from the sinus out toward the cortex, between the lobes, as their name says.

steps.label: Arcuate arteries
steps.text: At the base of each pyramid, arcuate arteries bend and arch along the border of cortex and medulla.
steps.why: They turn to follow the boundary before branching into the cortex above.

steps.label: Cortical radiate arteries
steps.text: Cortical radiate arteries run straight out into the cortex toward the surface.
steps.why: The cortex, where the filtering units start, is served from these last named arteries.

steps.label: Filtering units’ vessels
steps.text: Tiny arterioles lead into the capillaries of the kidney’s microscopic filtering units, where fluid is filtered and taken back.
steps.why: Here, and only here, blood exchanges fluid and solutes with the tubules; everything before was delivery.

steps.label: Cortical radiate veins
steps.text: Blood drains into cortical radiate veins.
steps.why: The veins run back along the same paths as the arteries and carry the same names.

steps.label: Arcuate veins
steps.text: Cortical radiate veins drain into arcuate veins at the base of the pyramids.
steps.why: They lie beside the arcuate arteries along the cortex–medulla boundary.

steps.label: Interlobar veins
steps.text: Arcuate veins drain into interlobar veins in the renal columns.
steps.why: Blood heads back toward the sinus, between the pyramids.

steps.label: Renal vein
steps.text: Interlobar veins join directly into the renal vein, which leaves at the hilum in front of the renal artery.
steps.why: There are no segmental veins, so the interlobar veins meet the renal vein directly.

steps.label: Inferior vena cava
steps.text: The renal vein empties into the inferior vena cava; the left one crosses in front of the aorta to get there.
steps.why: The vena cava lies right of the midline, which is why the left renal vein is the longer.

distractors.text: At the base of each pyramid, blood enters the renal pelvis and collects there before moving on toward the cortex.
distractors.why: The renal pelvis collects urine, not blood. Blood stays in vessels the whole way.

distractors.text: Interlobar arteries drain into interlobar veins at the papilla.
distractors.why: Arteries do not connect straight to veins here; blood has to pass the capillaries of the cortex first.

error.text: Interlobar veins drain into segmental veins, which join into the renal vein.
error.why: The veins mirror the arteries except at this point: there are no segmental veins. Interlobar veins join the renal vein directly.

pathways.summary: Renal artery, segmental, interlobar, arcuate and cortical radiate arteries, the filtering units’ arterioles and capillaries, then cortical radiate, arcuate and interlobar veins, the renal vein and the inferior vena cava. Segmental arteries are end arteries: block one and its segment dies.

pathways.title: Urine from the kidney to the outside
pathways.intro: Urine is finished by the time it drips from a renal papilla. Follow it through the plumbing that stores it and carries it out.

steps.label: Renal papilla
steps.text: Urine drips from tiny openings on the renal papilla, the tip of a pyramid.
steps.why: Urine is made in the pyramids and cortex and leaves them at their points.

steps.label: Minor calyx
steps.text: A minor calyx cups each papilla and catches the urine.
steps.why: Each papilla has its own minor calyx, the first cup of the collecting system.

steps.label: Major calyx
steps.text: Several minor calyces join into a major calyx.
steps.why: The cups merge step by step: two or three major calyces per kidney.

steps.label: Renal pelvis
steps.text: The major calyces join into the renal pelvis, a funnel.
steps.why: The pelvis gathers all the major calyces before narrowing into one tube.

steps.label: Ureter
steps.text: The ureter carries urine down behind the peritoneum by waves of peristalsis.
steps.why: The ureter starts where the pelvis narrows at the hilum; its smooth muscle moves urine whatever your position.

steps.label: Slanted path through the wall
steps.text: The ureter passes at a slant through the bladder wall and opens at a back corner of the trigone.
steps.why: The slanted tunnel is squeezed flat as the bladder fills, a one-way valve against backflow.

steps.label: Urinary bladder
steps.text: Urine is stored in the bladder, whose detrusor relaxes as it fills.
steps.why: Storage comes between the ureters and the urethra, so you empty at a time you choose.

steps.label: Internal sphincter
steps.text: Urine leaves at the bladder neck, through the internal urethral sphincter, when you void.
steps.why: The bladder neck is the bladder’s lowest point, at the front corner of the trigone. In females the internal sphincter is a functional zone of smooth muscle rather than a distinct ring.

steps.label: External sphincter
steps.text: It passes the external urethral sphincter, where the urethra crosses the pelvic floor.
steps.why: The voluntary sphincter lies below the involuntary one.

steps.label: Out of the body
steps.text: The urethra carries urine out of the body: about 3 to 4 cm in females, 18 to 20 cm in males.
steps.why: The urethra is the last part of the tract.

distractors.text: The major calyces join into the renal sinus, a funnel.
distractors.why: The renal sinus is the fat-filled space that holds the calyces and pelvis; urine does not flow through it.

distractors.text: The major calyces join into a renal column.
distractors.why: Renal columns are bands of cortex-like tissue between the pyramids; they carry blood vessels, not urine.

error.text: A major calyx cups each papilla and catches the urine.
error.why: The cup around each papilla is a minor calyx. Several minor calyces then join into a major calyx.

pathways.summary: Papilla, minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter, a slanted path through the bladder wall, bladder, internal urethral sphincter, external urethral sphincter, urethra. Only the kidney changes urine; everything after the papilla stores or carries it.

pathways.title: The micturition reflex
pathways.intro: Your bladder has been filling all morning. Trace what happens from the first stretch to an empty bladder, in a healthy adult.

steps.label: Bladder fills at low pressure
steps.text: While the bladder fills, sympathetic output relaxes the detrusor and keeps the internal sphincter closed, and the pudendal nerve holds the external sphincter shut.
steps.why: Storage is the starting state: the switch for emptying is off.

steps.label: Stretch signals rise
steps.text: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the bladder wall fire more as it fills; at about 150 to 250 mL you first notice it.
steps.why: The bladder has to fill before stretch can build the signal.

steps.label: You decide to go
steps.text: The signals reach the brain, and when you decide to go, the cerebral cortex releases its hold on the pontine micturition center.
steps.why: The cortex can only allow emptying once the stretch signal has reached it.

steps.label: Pons throws the switch
steps.text: The pontine micturition center switches from storing to emptying and signals the sacral micturition center (S2 to S4).
steps.why: The pons decides; the sacral center carries out the command.

steps.label: External sphincter relaxes
steps.text: Pudendal output falls, and the external urethral sphincter relaxes. Pressure in the urethra drops.
steps.why: The outlet opens first, a few seconds before the squeeze.

steps.label: Detrusor contracts
steps.text: A few seconds later, parasympathetic fibers from the sacral center fire, and the detrusor contracts.
steps.why: Once the outlet is relaxing, contraction pushes urine out instead of against a closed gate.

steps.label: Bladder neck opens
steps.text: Sympathetic output falls, and the internal urethral sphincter opens as the bladder neck is pulled open.
steps.why: The contracting detrusor pulls the bladder neck open as sympathetic tone is withdrawn.

steps.label: Flow keeps it going
steps.text: Urine flows, and flow in the urethra sends signals that strengthen the detrusor contraction until the bladder is nearly empty.
steps.why: This positive feedback needs flow to have started.

distractors.text: The sympathetic neurons at T11 to L2 switch from storing to emptying and signal the detrusor and the bladder neck to contract.
distractors.why: Sympathetic output serves storage: it relaxes the detrusor. Emptying is switched on in the pons and carried out by the sacral parasympathetic neurons.

distractors.text: The pudendal nerve fires harder, and the external urethral sphincter tightens.
distractors.why: That is how you hold on. Emptying needs pudendal output to fall.

error.text: A few seconds later, sympathetic fibers from T11 to L2 fire, and the detrusor contracts.
error.why: Sympathetic fibers relax the detrusor (beta-3) during storage. The detrusor contracts when parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptor proteins.

pathways.summary: Filling with sympathetic and pudendal tone, stretch signals, the cortex allows it, the pons throws the switch, the external sphincter relaxes, then the detrusor contracts, the bladder neck opens, and flow feeds back to keep the contraction going. For your exam: if asked where the reflex is integrated, the expected answer is the sacral spinal cord, S2 to S4.

pathways.title: Filtrate through the nephron
pathways.intro: Follow one drop of plasma fluid from the blood in a glomerulus until it drips from a renal papilla as urine.

steps.label: Glomerulus
steps.text: Blood arriving in the afferent arteriole enters the glomerulus, and pressure pushes plasma fluid out of its capillaries.
steps.why: Filtration is the first step: nothing enters the tubule any other way at its start.

steps.label: Capsular space
steps.text: The fluid passes the podocytes and collects in the capsular space of the glomerular capsule.
steps.why: The capsule surrounds the glomerulus, so the capsular space is where filtered fluid lands.

steps.label: Proximal convoluted tubule
steps.text: At the tubular pole the fluid flows into the proximal convoluted tubule, which takes back most of it.
steps.why: The proximal tubule is the first and longest part of the tubule, next to its own corpuscle in the cortex.

steps.label: Descending limb
steps.text: What remains runs down the descending limb of the nephron loop into the medulla.
steps.why: The tubule straightens and dives toward the medulla after the proximal tubule.

steps.label: Ascending limb
steps.text: It turns at the hairpin and climbs the ascending limb, ending in the thick ascending limb.
steps.why: The loop comes back up to the cortex after its bend.

steps.label: Macula densa
steps.text: At the top it passes the macula densa, where the tubule touches its own arterioles.
steps.why: The thick ascending limb returns to its own renal corpuscle before becoming the distal tubule.

steps.label: Distal convoluted tubule
steps.text: It flows through the distal convoluted tubule, where hormones fine-tune salt reabsorption.
steps.why: The DCT follows the macula densa in the cortex.

steps.label: Collecting duct
steps.text: A connecting segment carries it into a collecting duct, shared with many nephrons, which runs down through the medulla.
steps.why: Collecting ducts gather from many nephrons after the DCT; ADH acts here.

steps.label: Papilla to minor calyx
steps.text: Collecting ducts open on the tip of a renal papilla, and the fluid, now urine, drips into a minor calyx.
steps.why: The papilla is where the renal tubule system ends and the collecting cups begin.

distractors.text: The fluid enters the peritubular capillaries around the tubule.
distractors.why: The peritubular capillaries carry blood, not filtrate; they receive what the tubule takes back.

distractors.text: The fluid flows into the efferent arteriole.
distractors.why: The efferent arteriole carries away the blood that was not filtered. Filtrate goes into the capsule.

error.text: It flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, where hormones fine-tune salt reabsorption.
error.why: The proximal tubule comes right after the capsule. After the macula densa, the fluid enters the distal convoluted tubule.

pathways.summary: Glomerulus, capsular space, proximal convoluted tubule, descending limb, ascending limb, macula densa, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct, papilla and minor calyx. The blood that was not filtered leaves by the efferent arteriole and collects what the tubule returns.

pathways.title: Blood through a nephron
pathways.intro: A nephron has two capillary beds in a row, with an arteriole between them. Trace the blood that serves one juxtamedullary nephron.

steps.label: Cortical radiate artery
steps.text: Blood runs out through the cortex in a cortical radiate artery.
steps.why: These are the last named arteries of the kidney; the nephron’s own vessels branch from them.

steps.label: Afferent arteriole
steps.text: An afferent arteriole branches off and carries blood toward the glomerulus, past its renin-releasing juxtaglomerular cells.
steps.why: Af- means toward: this arteriole leads into the capillary tuft.

steps.label: Glomerular capillaries
steps.text: Blood runs through the glomerular capillaries, the first bed, where high pressure filters fluid out.
steps.why: Filtration needs high pressure, so it happens in the first bed, before any more resistance.

steps.label: Efferent arteriole
steps.text: An efferent arteriole, not a venule, carries the unfiltered blood away, now richer in protein.
steps.why: A resistance vessel downstream keeps glomerular pressure high.

steps.label: Peritubular capillaries
steps.text: Blood enters the second bed, the peritubular capillaries and, for this nephron, the vasa recta beside the long loop.
steps.why: After two resistances, pressure here is low and oncotic pull high, so fluid the tubule returns moves in.

steps.label: Venules
steps.text: The capillaries drain into venules.
steps.why: Blood leaves the second bed as it would any capillary bed.

steps.label: Cortical radiate vein
steps.text: Venules drain into a cortical radiate vein and back toward the renal vein.
steps.why: The veins then follow the arteries back out of the kidney.

distractors.text: A venule, not an arteriole, carries the unfiltered blood away from the glomerulus, now richer in protein.
distractors.why: The vessel leaving the glomerulus is an arteriole; a low-resistance venule could not hold glomerular pressure up.

distractors.text: The blood drains straight into the renal pelvis.
distractors.why: The renal pelvis carries urine. Blood leaving the glomerulus goes on to a second capillary bed.

error.text: Blood runs through the peritubular capillaries, the first bed, where high pressure filters fluid out.
error.why: The first bed is the glomerulus. The peritubular capillaries come second, after the efferent arteriole, and they take fluid in rather than filtering it out.

pathways.summary: Cortical radiate artery, afferent arteriole, glomerular capillaries, efferent arteriole, peritubular capillaries or vasa recta, venules, cortical radiate vein. An arteriole on each side of the glomerulus lets the kidney set glomerular pressure by narrowing either one.

pathways.title: Across the filtration membrane
pathways.intro: A water molecule and a sodium ion leave the blood in a glomerular capillary. Trace their path through the three layers into the tubule.

steps.label: Pushed by GBHP
steps.text: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure, about 55 mm Hg, pushes plasma against the capillary wall.
steps.why: Pressure is what drives filtration, so it comes first.

steps.label: Fenestrated endothelium
steps.text: The fluid passes through fenestrations in the endothelial cells; blood cells are too big to follow.
steps.why: The endothelium lines the capillary, so it is the first layer from the blood side.

steps.label: Basement membrane
steps.text: It crosses the thick, negatively charged glomerular basement membrane, which holds back large proteins.
steps.why: The fused basement membrane lies between the endothelium and the podocytes.

steps.label: Filtration slits
steps.text: It squeezes through a filtration slit between two pedicels, across the slit diaphragm, the finest sieve.
steps.why: The podocytes wrap the outside of the capillary, so their slits are the last layer.

steps.label: Capsular space
steps.text: It enters the capsular space as glomerular filtrate, with about the same small-solute concentrations as plasma.
steps.why: Past all three layers, the fluid is in the capsule.

steps.label: Proximal tubule
steps.text: It flows out of the capsule at the tubular pole into the proximal convoluted tubule.
steps.why: The capsular space opens into the tubule on the opposite side from the vessels.

distractors.text: It crosses a thin layer of smooth muscle around the capillary, which contracts to hold back large proteins.
distractors.why: Capillaries have no smooth muscle; the filter is endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes.

distractors.text: It passes through the macula densa, which holds back large proteins.
distractors.why: The macula densa is a patch of tubule wall at the end of the thick ascending limb, not part of the filter.

error.text: The fluid passes through fenestrations in the endothelial cells, which hold back albumin and other large proteins.
error.why: Fenestrations, 70 to 100 nm across, are far too large to hold back any dissolved molecule; they stop blood cells. Large proteins are held back mostly by the basement membrane and the slit diaphragms.

pathways.summary: Pushed by GBHP through fenestrated endothelium (stops cells), the basement membrane (stops large proteins), the filtration slits and slit diaphragms, into the capsular space and on to the proximal tubule. Size is the main sort, with charge adding to it.

pathways.title: Taking glucose back in the proximal tubule
pathways.intro: Every minute your glomeruli filter about 125 mg of glucose, and the proximal tubule returns all of it. Trace how, starting with the protein that powers it.

steps.label: Na–K pump spends ATP
steps.text: On the basolateral membrane, the sodium–potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ in.
steps.why: The pump builds the gradient everything else spends, so it comes first.

steps.label: Low Na+, negative cell
steps.text: Sodium inside the cell stays low and the inside is negative, so sodium in the lumen has a steep path into the cell.
steps.why: This gradient exists only because the pump keeps running.

steps.label: Na+ and glucose enter
steps.text: A sodium–glucose symporter in the apical membrane lets sodium flow in down its gradient and drags glucose in with it.
steps.why: Secondary active transport: the carrier spends the sodium gradient, not ATP.

steps.label: Glucose builds up in the cell
steps.text: Glucose becomes more concentrated inside the cell than in the interstitial fluid.
steps.why: The symporter keeps loading glucose in, uphill.

steps.label: Out by facilitated diffusion
steps.text: Glucose leaves across the basolateral membrane on carriers, by facilitated diffusion, down its gradient.
steps.why: Once concentrated inside, glucose can flow out passively.

steps.label: Into peritubular capillaries
steps.text: From the interstitial fluid it moves into the peritubular capillaries, where hydrostatic pressure is low and oncotic pressure high.
steps.why: Everything reabsorbed lands in the interstitial fluid first, then enters the blood.

distractors.text: Glucose is split for ATP inside the cell, and that ATP powers the carriers that bring more glucose in from the lumen.
distractors.why: Filtered glucose is returned to the blood whole; the energy comes from the pump’s sodium gradient.

distractors.text: Sodium inside the cell rises until it matches the filtrate.
distractors.why: If cell sodium matched the filtrate, there would be no gradient to drive the symporter.

error.text: A glucose pump in the apical membrane uses ATP directly to carry glucose into the cell.
error.why: No apical carrier here splits ATP. The symporter uses the sodium gradient set up by the basolateral pump: secondary active transport. Stop the pump and glucose uptake stops too.

pathways.summary: Pump builds a sodium gradient, sodium flows in through the symporter and drags glucose, glucose builds up in the cell, leaves by facilitated diffusion, and enters the peritubular capillaries. The number of symporters caps the rate: the transport maximum.

pathways.title: Salt out of the thick ascending limb
pathways.intro: The thick ascending limb removes about a quarter of the filtered sodium without letting any water follow. Trace the steps in one of its cells.

steps.label: Basolateral pump
steps.text: The basolateral sodium–potassium pump keeps sodium low inside the cell.
steps.why: The pump supplies the gradient the apical carrier runs on.

steps.label: NKCC2 loads salt
steps.text: NKCC2 in the apical membrane moves 1 Na+, 1 K+ and 2 Cl− from the lumen into the cell together.
steps.why: Sodium flowing downhill into the cell drags the other three ions with it.

steps.label: Na+ and Cl− exit
steps.text: Sodium leaves on the pump and chloride through chloride channels, into the interstitial fluid.
steps.why: Salt taken in at the apical side must leave at the basolateral side to be reabsorbed.

steps.label: K+ leaks back
steps.text: Most of the potassium leaks back into the lumen through apical potassium channels.
steps.why: Recycling keeps NKCC2 supplied with potassium, which is scarce in the lumen.

steps.label: Lumen turns positive
steps.text: The returning potassium leaves the lumen positively charged.
steps.why: The charge is a result of potassium leaking back while chloride leaves.

steps.label: Ca2+ and Mg2+ between cells
steps.text: The positive lumen pushes calcium, magnesium and more sodium out between the cells.
steps.why: The paracellular route is passive, so it needs the charge to drive it.

steps.label: No water follows
steps.text: Water cannot follow, because this segment has almost no aquaporins; the fluid falls to about 100 mOsm/L.
steps.why: Salt leaving without water is what makes this the diluting segment.

distractors.text: Potassium is pumped into the interstitial fluid by NKCC2.
distractors.why: NKCC2 sits on the apical membrane and moves ions into the cell, not out the far side.

distractors.text: Water follows the salt out through aquaporins.
distractors.why: The thick ascending limb has almost no aquaporins; that is why its fluid becomes dilute.

error.text: Water follows the salt out by osmosis, so the fluid stays at about 300 mOsm/L.
error.why: This segment is nearly waterproof. Salt leaves without water, so the fluid leaving it is dilute, about 100 mOsm/L, and the salt it pumps out builds up in the medulla.

pathways.summary: Pump, NKCC2 loads Na+, K+ and 2 Cl−, Na+ and Cl− exit the base, K+ recycles into the lumen, the lumen turns positive, Ca2+ and Mg2+ leave between cells, and no water follows. Block NKCC2 and every later step stops.

pathways.title: Building the medullary gradient
pathways.intro: Imagine a nephron loop filled with 300 mOsm/L fluid everywhere. Trace the rounds of pumping and flowing that turn a 200 mOsm/L single step into a 900 mOsm/L gradient.

steps.label: All 300 mOsm/L
steps.text: Fluid in both limbs and the interstitial fluid around them is 300 mOsm/L, the same as plasma.
steps.why: This is the starting state, before any pumping.

steps.label: Pump: 200 inside, 400 outside
steps.text: The thick ascending limb pumps NaCl out until, at each level, its fluid is 200 and the interstitial fluid beside it is 400.
steps.why: The pump can make a 200 mOsm/L difference at any single level; that is the effect to be multiplied.

steps.label: Descending limb loses water
steps.text: The descending limb loses water to the 400 mOsm/L interstitial fluid until its own fluid is 400.
steps.why: The descending limb is permeable to water, not salt, so it can only match the fluid around it by losing water.

steps.label: Flow pushes fluid round
steps.text: New 300 fluid enters the top of the descending limb and pushes the 400 fluid around the bend into the bottom of the ascending limb.
steps.why: Flow moves the more concentrated fluid to where the pump will act on it next.

steps.label: Pump again from a higher start
steps.text: At the bottom, the pump lowers the 400 fluid to 300 and raises the interstitial fluid there to 500.
steps.why: The same 200 difference now starts from a higher level at the bottom.

steps.label: Bottom climbs to 1,200
steps.text: Round after round, the bottom of the loop climbs toward 1,200 mOsm/L while the top stays near 300.
steps.why: Each round builds on the last, so a single-step difference is multiplied along the loop.

steps.label: Vasa recta keep it
steps.text: The hairpin vasa recta exchange salt and water passively and carry off reabsorbed water without washing the gradient away.
steps.why: The gradient must be built before blood flow can threaten it.

distractors.text: The descending limb pumps salt in from the 400 mOsm/L interstitial fluid until its own fluid is 400.
distractors.why: The descending limb has few salt carriers. Its fluid concentrates because water leaves it.

distractors.text: The collecting duct pumps water out until the medulla is 400.
distractors.why: No part of the tubule pumps water; water only follows solute by osmosis.

error.text: At the bottom, the descending limb pumps NaCl out, raising the interstitial fluid there to 500.
error.why: Only the thick ascending limb pumps salt, on NKCC2. The descending limb is passive: it loses water.

pathways.summary: Start at 300, pump to a 200 difference, the descending limb loses water, flow carries concentrated fluid round the bend, the pump acts again from a higher start, and the bottom climbs to 1,200. The vasa recta keep the gradient; they do not build it.

pathways.title: How ADH opens the collecting duct
pathways.intro: ADH has just been released from the posterior pituitary on a hot day. Trace how it makes the collecting duct let water out, from the blood to concentrated urine.

steps.label: ADH reaches the duct
steps.text: ADH reaches the collecting duct in the blood.
steps.why: A hormone must first be carried to its target.

steps.label: Binds on the basolateral side
steps.text: ADH binds its receptor protein on the basolateral membrane of principal cells.
steps.why: ADH is a peptide and cannot cross the membrane, so it binds on the blood side of the cell.

steps.label: G protein raises cAMP
steps.text: The receptor protein is coupled to a G protein, which raises cAMP inside the cell.
steps.why: cAMP is the second messenger that carries the signal inside.

steps.label: Protein kinase A
steps.text: cAMP activates protein kinase A.
steps.why: The kinase is what acts on the stored water channels.

steps.label: Aquaporins fuse in
steps.text: Vesicles carrying aquaporins fuse with the apical membrane within minutes.
steps.why: The water channels are already made and stored just under the apical membrane.

steps.label: Water crosses the cell
steps.text: Water enters the cell through the new apical aquaporins and leaves through basolateral aquaporins that are always present.
steps.why: The apical membrane was the only barrier; the basolateral side already lets water through.

steps.label: Medulla draws water out
steps.text: The salty medulla draws the water out, the vasa recta carry it away, and urine nears 1,200 mOsm/L.
steps.why: Water moves only by osmosis, so the medullary gradient decides how far the urine concentrates.

distractors.text: ADH moves on into the nucleus and switches on the gene for a new salt pump in the apical membrane.
distractors.why: ADH is a peptide that acts through a receptor protein on the membrane; its fast effect needs no new genes.

distractors.text: The receptor protein opens a channel that lets sodium into the cell.
distractors.why: ADH’s receptor protein is coupled to a G protein; it is aldosterone that adds sodium channels.

error.text: ADH enters the principal cell and binds a receptor protein in its cytoplasm.
error.why: ADH is a water-soluble peptide. It cannot cross the membrane, so it binds a receptor protein on the basolateral surface and works through cAMP.

pathways.summary: ADH in the blood, receptor protein on the basolateral membrane, G protein and cAMP, protein kinase A, aquaporin vesicles fuse with the apical membrane, water crosses the cell, and the medulla draws it out. When ADH falls, the aquaporins are pulled back in by endocytosis.

pathways.title: Urea recycling
pathways.intro: Urea is waste, yet the kidney uses it to build half the inner medulla’s osmolarity. Follow urea from the glomerulus to the inner medulla on a day with high ADH.

steps.label: Filtered freely
steps.text: Urea is filtered freely at the glomerulus.
steps.why: Everything small in plasma enters the tubule first.

steps.label: Half back in the PCT
steps.text: About half is reabsorbed passively in the proximal tubule, as water leaves and concentrates it.
steps.why: The proximal tubule is the first segment and its leaky walls let urea follow its gradient.

steps.label: Kept in the distal parts
steps.text: The distal tubule and the collecting duct in the cortex and outer medulla are nearly impermeable to urea.
steps.why: These segments keep urea in while they reabsorb other things.

steps.label: Urea concentrates
steps.text: As ADH lets water out of the collecting duct, the urea left inside becomes more and more concentrated.
steps.why: Concentration builds because water leaves but urea cannot.

steps.label: Out through urea carriers
steps.text: In the inner medullary collecting duct, urea carriers, increased by ADH, let concentrated urea diffuse into the interstitial fluid.
steps.why: Only the deepest part of the duct has the carriers, so urea is released where the gradient is highest.

steps.label: Half the inner medulla
steps.text: That urea supplies about half the osmolarity of the inner medulla.
steps.why: Urea released there adds directly to the gradient.

steps.label: Round again
steps.text: Some urea diffuses into the thin limbs of the loop and travels round again; some is carried off by the vasa recta.
steps.why: The loop takes urea back into the tubule, so it can reach the collecting duct again.

distractors.text: The distal tubule and the collecting duct in the cortex pump all of the remaining urea straight back into the blood.
distractors.why: No segment pumps urea; it moves only by diffusion and carriers down its gradient.

distractors.text: The distal tubule secretes extra urea into the fluid, using ATP.
distractors.why: Urea is not pumped anywhere; it becomes concentrated because water leaves while urea stays.

error.text: In the cortical collecting duct, urea carriers let concentrated urea diffuse into the interstitial fluid of the cortex.
error.why: The collecting duct in the cortex keeps urea in. Urea leaves only in the inner medullary collecting duct, so it builds the gradient deep in the medulla.

pathways.summary: Filtered, half reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, kept in the distal parts while water leaves, released in the inner medulla through ADH-increased carriers, supplies half the inner medulla’s osmolarity, and partly cycles back through the loop. A low-protein diet makes less urea and weakens concentrating.

pathways.title: The stages of meiosis
pathways.intro: One diploid cell copies its DNA once and divides twice, ending as four haploid cells. Put the stages in order.

steps.label: DNA copied (S phase)
steps.text: In S phase the cell copies its DNA: each of its 46 chromosomes now has two sister chromatids.
steps.why: Copying happens once, before meiosis starts, exactly as before mitosis.

steps.label: Prophase I
steps.text: Each chromosome pairs with its homolog along its whole length, and crossing over swaps pieces between them.
steps.why: Pairing has to come first: homologs can only swap pieces and later separate as partners once they have found each other.

steps.label: Metaphase I
steps.text: The pairs line up across the middle of the cell as pairs, one homolog facing each end.
steps.why: The pairs formed in prophase I now line up, each pair facing the ends at random: independent assortment.

steps.label: Anaphase I
steps.text: Homologs are pulled to opposite ends while each one’s sister chromatids stay joined at the centromere.
steps.why: Separation follows alignment. Only the partners separate here, so each chromosome stays double.

steps.label: Telophase I and cytokinesis
steps.text: The cell divides into two haploid cells, each with 23 chromosomes still made of two chromatids.
steps.why: Division ends meiosis I, the reduction division: the number of chromosomes per cell has halved.

steps.label: Metaphase II
steps.text: With no new DNA copying, the chromosomes in each cell line up singly across the middle.
steps.why: Meiosis II starts straight away, without an S phase, and single chromosomes line up as in mitosis.

steps.label: Anaphase II
steps.text: The centromeres are released and the sister chromatids are pulled to opposite ends.
steps.why: Sister chromatids can only separate after they have lined up singly in metaphase II.

steps.label: Telophase II and cytokinesis
steps.text: Each cell divides again, giving four haploid cells with 23 single chromosomes each.
steps.why: The second division finishes the process: four genetically different haploid cells from one diploid cell.

distractors.text: Sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite ends, so each cell briefly holds 92 chromosomes.
distractors.why: That is anaphase of mitosis. In anaphase I, sister chromatids stay joined and the homologs separate.

distractors.text: The cell copies its DNA a second time before it divides, so that each daughter cell can still get 46 chromosomes.
distractors.why: DNA is copied only once, before meiosis I. There is no copying between the two divisions.

error.text: Each chromosome lines up singly across the middle of the cell, and its sister chromatids swap pieces.
error.why: In prophase I the homologs pair and swap pieces between a chromatid of each partner. Sister chromatids are identical copies, so swapping between them would change nothing.

pathways.summary: S phase, then prophase I (pairing and crossing over), metaphase I (pairs line up), anaphase I (homologs separate), telophase I (two haploid cells with double chromosomes), metaphase II, anaphase II (sister chromatids separate), telophase II (four haploid cells). Meiosis I separates partners; meiosis II separates sisters.

pathways.title: Sperm from testis to urethra
pathways.intro: Sperm made in the walls of the seminiferous tubules travel a long route before they leave the body. Follow them.

steps.label: Seminiferous tubules
steps.text: Sperm are released into the lumen of a seminiferous tubule, where they were made.
steps.why: The tubules in each lobule of the testis are where sperm are made, so the route starts here.

steps.label: Rete testis
steps.text: The tubules straighten and drain into the rete testis, a network of channels at the back of the testis.
steps.why: The tubules of all the lobules empty into this one network before leaving the testis.

steps.label: Efferent ductules
steps.text: A dozen or so efferent ductules carry the sperm out of the testis.
steps.why: These small ducts connect the rete testis to the head of the epididymis.

steps.label: Epididymis
steps.text: Sperm travel from the head to the tail of the epididymis over several days, gaining the ability to swim, and are stored in its tail.
steps.why: The epididymis sits on the back of the testis and receives the efferent ductules at its head.

steps.label: Ductus deferens
steps.text: During emission, the ductus deferens squeezes sperm up the spermatic cord and through the inguinal canal into the pelvis.
steps.why: The ductus deferens begins at the tail of the epididymis and climbs out of the scrotum inside the spermatic cord.

steps.label: Ampulla
steps.text: Behind the bladder, the ductus deferens widens into its ampulla.
steps.why: After crossing over the ureter and running down the back of the bladder, the duct widens just before it ends.

steps.label: Ejaculatory duct
steps.text: The ductus deferens joins the duct of a seminal vesicle to form an ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate.
steps.why: The seminal vesicle adds most of the semen volume at this junction.

steps.label: Prostatic urethra
steps.text: The ejaculatory ducts open into the prostatic urethra, where the prostate adds its fluid.
steps.why: The ejaculatory ducts end inside the prostate, in the first part of the urethra.

steps.label: Membranous urethra
steps.text: Semen passes through the membranous urethra in the pelvic floor.
steps.why: The shortest part of the urethra lies between the prostate and the penis.

steps.label: Spongy urethra
steps.text: Semen runs through the spongy urethra in the corpus spongiosum and out of the external urethral opening.
steps.why: The spongy urethra is the last and longest part, running the length of the penis.

distractors.text: Sperm pass into the seminal vesicle, a coiled pouch behind the bladder, where they gain the ability to swim and are stored until ejaculation.
distractors.why: The seminal vesicle is a gland that adds fluid; it does not store sperm. Sperm gain the ability to swim, and are stored, in the epididymis.

distractors.text: Sperm pass through the bulbourethral gland, where they learn to swim.
distractors.why: The bulbourethral glands add a little mucus to the spongy urethra. Sperm gain the ability to swim in the epididymis.

error.text: The ductus deferens joins the ureter to form an ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate.
error.why: The ductus deferens crosses over the ureter but does not join it. It joins the duct of a seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct.

pathways.summary: Seminiferous tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis (head to tail, where sperm mature and are stored), ductus deferens in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal, ampulla, ejaculatory duct through the prostate, then the prostatic, membranous and spongy urethra.

pathways.title: Erection, emission and expulsion
pathways.intro: Erection is a vascular event run by parasympathetic nerves; ejaculation is run by sympathetic and then somatic nerves. Put the chain in order.

steps.label: Sexual stimulation
steps.text: Touch to the genitals starts a spinal reflex, and sights, sounds and thoughts add signals from the brain.
steps.why: Stimulation is the trigger; nothing downstream happens without it.

steps.label: Parasympathetic S2–S4
steps.text: Parasympathetic neurons in the sacral spinal cord fire along the pelvic splanchnic nerves to the penis.
steps.why: The reflex and the brain’s signals converge on these sacral neurons, which carry the command to the penis.

steps.label: Nitric oxide, then cGMP
steps.text: Their endings and the endothelium release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP in the smooth muscle.
steps.why: Nitric oxide is the messenger the nerve endings release; cGMP is made inside the smooth muscle in response.

steps.label: Smooth muscle relaxes
steps.text: The smooth muscle of the cavernosal arteries and blood spaces relaxes, and blood rushes in.
steps.why: cGMP makes the smooth muscle relax, which widens the arteries and lets the blood spaces expand.

steps.label: Veins squeezed shut
steps.text: The swelling tissue presses the draining veins against the tunica albuginea, so pressure rises: erection.
steps.why: Outflow falls only after the tissue has swelled with incoming blood.

steps.label: Emission (sympathetic)
steps.text: Sympathetic neurons (about T10–L2) make the ducts, seminal vesicles and prostate contract, moving semen into the urethra.
steps.why: Emission loads the urethra; it has to happen before semen can be expelled.

steps.label: Bladder neck closes
steps.text: At the same time the internal urethral sphincter contracts, so semen cannot flow back into the bladder.
steps.why: The same sympathetic discharge closes the bladder neck while semen enters the urethra.

steps.label: Expulsion (pudendal)
steps.text: Semen in the urethra triggers a reflex: the pudendal nerve makes the bulbospongiosus contract rhythmically, forcing semen out.
steps.why: Expulsion is triggered by semen already in the urethra, so it follows emission.

steps.label: Erection ends
steps.text: Sympathetic norepinephrine contracts the erectile smooth muscle again and PDE5 breaks down cGMP.
steps.why: Once ejaculation is over, sympathetic activity ends the erection and a refractory period follows.

distractors.text: Their endings release norepinephrine onto alpha-1 receptor proteins in the smooth muscle.
distractors.why: Norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins contracts smooth muscle. That drives emission and ends the erection; it cannot start one.

distractors.text: Their endings release acetylcholine, which makes skeletal muscle in the shaft contract.
distractors.why: Erection is a vascular event in smooth muscle. Acetylcholine plays only a small part, mainly by making the endothelium release nitric oxide.

error.text: Parasympathetic neurons (S2–S4) make the ducts, seminal vesicles and prostate contract, moving semen into the urethra.
error.why: Emission is sympathetic, from about T10–L2, through norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins. “Point and shoot”: parasympathetic for erection, sympathetic then somatic for ejaculation.

pathways.summary: Stimulation, parasympathetic S2–S4 nerves, nitric oxide and cGMP, smooth muscle relaxation and inflow, veins squeezed shut (erection); then sympathetic emission with the bladder neck closing, somatic expulsion through the pudendal nerve, and sympathetic ending of the erection.

pathways.title: Spermatogenesis: stem cell to sperm
pathways.intro: Sperm are made from the outside of the tubule wall inward, in about 64 to 74 days. Put the stages in order.

steps.label: Spermatogonium
steps.text: A spermatogonium on the basement membrane divides by mitosis; one daughter stays a stem cell.
steps.why: The stem cells sit at the outer edge, and mitosis keeps their supply from running out.

steps.label: Primary spermatocyte
steps.text: A committed daughter copies its DNA and grows into a primary spermatocyte (46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids), then crosses the blood-testis barrier.
steps.why: The DNA must be copied before meiosis can start, and the cell moves into the adluminal compartment to go through it.

steps.label: Meiosis I
steps.text: The primary spermatocyte completes meiosis I, giving two secondary spermatocytes, each haploid with 23 double chromosomes.
steps.why: Meiosis I separates the homologs, halving the chromosome number.

steps.label: Meiosis II
steps.text: Each secondary spermatocyte completes meiosis II, giving two spermatids with 23 single chromosomes.
steps.why: Meiosis II follows quickly, separating the sister chromatids; one primary spermatocyte has now made four spermatids.

steps.label: Spermiogenesis
steps.text: Each round spermatid reshapes without dividing: an acrosome forms, a tail grows, and most of the cytoplasm is shed.
steps.why: The divisions are over; what remains is turning a round cell into a swimming one.

steps.label: Released into the lumen
steps.text: The finished sperm are released into the lumen, still unable to swim forward.
steps.why: The Sertoli cells let go of the sperm only after reshaping is complete.

steps.label: Carried to the epididymis
steps.text: Sertoli cell fluid and contractions of the tubule wall carry the sperm to the epididymis.
steps.why: Because the sperm cannot yet swim, fluid and the tubule wall move them on to where they mature.

distractors.text: The primary spermatocyte divides by mitosis, giving two diploid spermatids that each hold 46 chromosomes and go straight on to reshape.
distractors.why: A primary spermatocyte divides by meiosis, not mitosis, and its products are secondary spermatocytes, not spermatids.

distractors.text: The primary spermatocyte reshapes directly into four sperm without dividing.
distractors.why: Reshaping without division is spermiogenesis, which acts on spermatids after both meiotic divisions.

error.text: Each spermatid divides once more by mitosis to make the sperm head and tail.
error.why: Spermatids do not divide again. They reshape into sperm in spermiogenesis, forming an acrosome and a tail and shedding cytoplasm.

pathways.summary: Spermatogonium (mitosis), primary spermatocyte (copied DNA), meiosis I into two secondary spermatocytes, meiosis II into four spermatids, spermiogenesis into sperm, release into the lumen, and transport to the epididymis. Cells move inward from the basement membrane to the lumen as they mature.

pathways.title: The male hormone chain
pathways.intro: GnRH, LH, FSH, testosterone and inhibin form a loop that keeps testosterone and sperm production steady. Put the chain in order, starting at the hypothalamus.

steps.label: GnRH pulses
steps.text: The hypothalamus releases GnRH into the portal vessels in pulses, roughly every 1 to 3 hours.
steps.why: The hypothalamus heads the axis; the pituitary responds to its rising and falling pulses.

steps.label: LH and FSH released
steps.text: Each pulse makes the anterior pituitary release LH and FSH into the blood.
steps.why: The pituitary’s gonadotropins are the command that reaches the testes.

steps.label: Leydig cells make testosterone
steps.text: LH binds the Leydig cells, which make testosterone from cholesterol.
steps.why: LH is the hormone that drives the Leydig cells between the tubules.

steps.label: Sertoli cells supported
steps.text: FSH and the high local testosterone act on the Sertoli cells, which support spermatogenesis and release inhibin.
steps.why: The Sertoli cells need both FSH and the testosterone the Leydig cells have just made.

steps.label: Two brakes
steps.text: Testosterone brakes GnRH and LH, and inhibin brakes FSH release by the pituitary, bringing the axis back down.
steps.why: The products feed back last, closing the loop: the brakes act on the hypothalamus and pituitary at the top of the chain.

distractors.text: FSH binds the Leydig cells, which make testosterone from cholesterol.
distractors.why: FSH acts on the Sertoli cells. LH is the hormone that drives the Leydig cells.

distractors.text: LH binds the Sertoli cells, which release testosterone into the tubules.
distractors.why: The Sertoli cells do not make testosterone; they hold it in the tubule with androgen-binding protein. LH acts on the Leydig cells.

error.text: Testosterone brakes FSH, and inhibin brakes LH, bringing the axis back down.
error.why: The brakes are the other way round: inhibin lowers FSH selectively, with little effect on LH, and testosterone is the main brake on GnRH and LH.

pathways.summary: GnRH pulses, LH and FSH, LH on the Leydig cells (testosterone), FSH and testosterone on the Sertoli cells (sperm support and inhibin), then two negative feedback brakes: testosterone on GnRH and LH, inhibin on FSH.

pathways.title: Milk from the alveoli to the nipple
pathways.intro: During nursing, milk made deep in the breast travels out through a branching tree of ducts. Follow it outward.

steps.label: Alveoli
steps.text: Cuboidal cells lining the alveoli make milk.
steps.why: The alveoli at the ends of the smallest duct branches are where milk is made.

steps.label: Myoepithelial squeeze
steps.text: Myoepithelial cells wrapped around each alveolus contract and squeeze the milk out.
steps.why: Milk has to be pushed out of the alveoli before it can move along the ducts.

steps.label: Small ducts
steps.text: Milk flows into the smallest ducts, which join into larger ones like the branches of a tree.
steps.why: The duct tree converges from the lobules toward the nipple.

steps.label: Lactiferous duct
steps.text: Each duct system drains into a lactiferous duct, which widens briefly under the areola while milk is flowing.
steps.why: The lactiferous ducts are the main trunks that reach the nipple.

steps.label: Nipple opening
steps.text: Milk leaves through one of several duct openings at the tip of the nipple.
steps.why: Each opening is the end of one lactiferous duct.

distractors.text: Smooth muscle in the uterine wall contracts and squeezes the milk out.
distractors.why: The myometrium is in the uterus. In the breast, myoepithelial cells around the alveoli do the squeezing.

distractors.text: The areolar glands pump the milk into the ducts.
distractors.why: Areolar glands on the areola release an oily, protective secretion; they do not move milk.

error.text: Each duct system drains into a lactiferous duct that widens into a large sac where milk is stored for hours.
error.why: Ultrasound shows no storage sacs; the ducts widen only briefly while milk is flowing. (For your exam, the widening is called the lactiferous sinus.)

pathways.summary: Alveoli make milk; myoepithelial cells squeeze it out; it flows through the branching ducts into a lactiferous duct, which widens briefly under the areola as milk flows, and leaves through a duct opening on the nipple.

pathways.title: From the ovary to the uterus
pathways.intro: The ovary is not attached to the uterine tube, so a released oocyte has to be caught. Follow it to the uterus.

steps.label: Ovary surface
steps.text: The oocyte leaves a follicle at the surface of the ovary, into the pelvic cavity.
steps.why: The oocyte starts in the ovary’s cortex and leaves from its surface.

steps.label: Fimbriae
steps.text: The fimbriae sweep over the ovary, and their cilia draw the oocyte into the open end of the tube.
steps.why: The fimbriae drape over the ovary, so they are the first part of the tube the oocyte meets.

steps.label: Ampulla
steps.text: The oocyte moves into the ampulla, the longest and widest part of the tube, where sperm usually meet it.
steps.why: The ampulla lies next to the funnel-shaped end.

steps.label: Isthmus
steps.text: It passes into the isthmus, the narrow, thick-walled part next to the uterus.
steps.why: The tube narrows as it nears the uterus.

steps.label: Through the uterine wall
steps.text: A short part of the tube passes through the uterine wall.
steps.why: The tube must cross the thick myometrium to reach the cavity.

steps.label: Uterine cavity
steps.text: The tube opens into the uterine cavity, about three to four days after the oocyte was caught.
steps.why: Cilia beating toward the uterus and slow waves of smooth muscle contraction carry it along the tube.

distractors.text: The ovarian ligament carries the oocyte along its surface to the uterus.
distractors.why: The ovarian ligament is a support that ties the ovary to the uterus. It is not a passage.

distractors.text: The oocyte travels straight into the tube through a short duct that joins the ovary to the fimbriae.
distractors.why: The ovary has no duct and is not attached to the tube; the oocyte must be swept into the tube’s open end.

error.text: It passes into the fundus, the narrow, thick-walled part of the tube next to the uterus.
error.why: The fundus is the rounded top of the uterus. The narrow, thick-walled part of the tube next to the uterus is the isthmus.

pathways.summary: Ovary surface, fimbriae, ampulla (the usual meeting place with sperm), isthmus, the short part in the uterine wall, then the uterine cavity: about three to four days, moved by cilia and smooth muscle.

pathways.title: Oogenesis: two long pauses
pathways.intro: An oocyte released at 40 began meiosis before its owner was born. Put the steps of oogenesis in order.

steps.label: Oogonia multiply
steps.text: In the fetal ovary, oogonia divide by mitosis, reaching about 6 to 7 million by mid-gestation.
steps.why: The diploid stem cells multiply first; no oogonia survive past birth.

steps.label: Arrest in prophase I
steps.text: Oogonia become primary oocytes, copy their DNA, pair and cross over, then arrest in prophase I inside primordial follicles.
steps.why: Meiosis I starts before birth and stops partway: the first long pause, lasting until shortly before that oocyte is released.

steps.label: Sudden rise in LH
steps.text: Years later, a sudden rise in LH restarts meiosis in the oocyte of the one follicle about to release it.
steps.why: From puberty on, the rise in LH each month is the signal that ends the first pause.

steps.label: Meiosis I finishes
steps.text: Meiosis I finishes unequally: a secondary oocyte keeps almost all the cytoplasm, and the first polar body gets very little.
steps.why: The restarted division completes before ovulation, and the spindle at the cell’s edge makes it lopsided.

steps.label: Arrest in metaphase II
steps.text: The secondary oocyte starts meiosis II and arrests again at metaphase II.
steps.why: The second pause begins at once; this is the cell that is released.

steps.label: Ovulation
steps.text: The secondary oocyte leaves the ovary about 34 to 36 hours after LH began to rise.
steps.why: Release comes after meiosis I has finished and the second pause has begun.

steps.label: Meiosis II on sperm entry
steps.text: Only if a sperm enters does meiosis II finish, giving an ovum and a second polar body.
steps.why: Sperm entry is the trigger for the last division; without it the secondary oocyte dies within a day.

distractors.text: The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II at once, before it is released.
distractors.why: The secondary oocyte arrests at metaphase II and finishes meiosis II only if a sperm enters it.

distractors.text: The secondary oocyte divides by mitosis to replace the oogonia that were lost before birth.
distractors.why: No new oocytes are made after birth. The secondary oocyte goes on into meiosis II, not mitosis.

error.text: Meiosis I finishes equally, giving two secondary oocytes of the same size.
error.why: Both divisions of oogenesis are unequal: one large secondary oocyte keeps nearly all the cytoplasm, and the first polar body is a tiny cell that breaks down.

pathways.summary: Oogonia multiply by mitosis before birth; primary oocytes arrest in prophase I; from puberty a rise in LH restarts one each month; meiosis I finishes unequally into a secondary oocyte and first polar body; it arrests at metaphase II, is ovulated, and completes meiosis II only if a sperm enters.

pathways.title: Follicle development to corpus luteum
pathways.intro: A follicle grows over several months from a single layer of flat cells into a fluid-filled blister about 2 cm across, then becomes a temporary gland. Put its stages in order.

steps.label: Primordial follicle
steps.text: A primary oocyte is surrounded by a single layer of flat cells: the resting stage.
steps.why: Almost all follicles in an ovary sit at this first stage.

steps.label: Primary follicle
steps.text: The flat cells become cube-shaped granulosa cells, and a clear glycoprotein coat forms around the growing oocyte.
steps.why: The first change is in the shape of the single layer.

steps.label: Secondary follicle
steps.text: The granulosa cells multiply into several layers, and a theca forms around the follicle.
steps.why: Layers are added after the single layer has become granulosa cells.

steps.label: Tertiary follicle
steps.text: Fluid gaps between the granulosa cells merge into an antrum; from now on the follicle needs FSH to keep growing.
steps.why: The antrum forms once there are many granulosa layers to hold the fluid.

steps.label: Mature vesicular follicle
steps.text: The dominant follicle grows to about 2 cm and bulges from the ovary’s surface; the others undergo atresia.
steps.why: Selection of one dominant follicle happens among the tertiary follicles as FSH falls.

steps.label: Ovulation
steps.text: A sudden rise in LH makes the follicle wall give way, and the secondary oocyte oozes out.
steps.why: Only a mature follicle responds to the rise in LH by releasing its oocyte.

steps.label: Corpus luteum
steps.text: Under LH, the emptied follicle’s cells enlarge and fill with lipid and yellow pigment, making progesterone for about two weeks.
steps.why: The corpus luteum forms from the cells left behind after ovulation.

steps.label: Corpus albicans
steps.text: Without a pregnancy, the corpus luteum dies and shrinks into a pale scar.
steps.why: The last stage is the scar left when the corpus luteum’s cells die.

distractors.text: The granulosa cells shrink back into a single layer of flat cells.
distractors.why: Follicles do not go backward. A follicle that stops growing undergoes atresia instead.

distractors.text: The follicle releases its oocyte while it is still only a few granulosa layers thick, before any fluid has collected.
distractors.why: Ovulation happens only from a mature vesicular follicle, after an antrum has formed and grown.

error.text: The emptied follicle becomes the corpus albicans, which makes progesterone for about two weeks.
error.why: The progesterone-making gland is the corpus luteum, the yellow body. The corpus albicans is the pale scar left after the corpus luteum dies, and it makes no hormones.

pathways.summary: Primordial, primary (cube-shaped granulosa cells), secondary (layers and a theca), tertiary (antrum; FSH-dependent), mature vesicular (dominant), ovulation, corpus luteum (progesterone), corpus albicans (scar).

pathways.title: One ovarian cycle, hormone by hormone
pathways.intro: The cycle runs on negative feedback, a brief burst of positive feedback, and the lifespan of the corpus luteum. Put the chain in order, starting as the old corpus luteum dies.

steps.label: Corpus luteum dies
steps.text: The old corpus luteum dies, so progesterone, estradiol and inhibin fall.
steps.why: The corpus luteum lasts 12 to 14 days; its death is where each new cycle starts.

steps.label: FSH rises
steps.text: With the brake lifted, FSH rises and rescues a group of tertiary follicles from atresia.
steps.why: FSH can rise only once the corpus luteum’s hormones have fallen.

steps.label: One follicle selected
steps.text: The growing follicles’ estradiol and inhibin lower FSH, and only the most FSH-sensitive follicle keeps growing.
steps.why: Negative feedback from the rescued follicles themselves is what narrows them to one.

steps.label: Estradiol high, sustained
steps.text: The dominant follicle’s estradiol climbs and stays high for about two days.
steps.why: In a natural cycle only one follicle is left after selection, and its growing mass of granulosa cells makes most of the ovary’s estradiol.

steps.label: LH surge
steps.text: Estradiol switches to positive feedback, and LH surges; estradiol peaks as the surge begins and then falls.
steps.why: Sustained high estradiol is the stimulus for the surge.

steps.label: Ovulation
steps.text: About 34 to 36 hours after the surge begins, the follicle releases its secondary oocyte.
steps.why: The surge is the trigger for ovulation.

steps.label: Corpus luteum forms
steps.text: The same LH turns the follicle’s cells into a corpus luteum that makes mostly progesterone.
steps.why: The emptied follicle is converted after ovulation, which also ends the positive feedback.

steps.label: Luteal brake
steps.text: Progesterone, estradiol and inhibin hold GnRH, FSH and LH at their lowest, and progesterone makes the lining secretory.
steps.why: The corpus luteum’s hormones give the strongest negative feedback of the cycle, until it dies again.

distractors.text: The growing follicles’ estradiol drives a second rise of FSH, so all of them go on to ovulate.
distractors.why: Through most of the follicular phase estradiol is a brake. FSH falls, and all but one follicle undergo atresia.

distractors.text: Progesterone from the growing follicles lowers FSH.
distractors.why: Growing follicles make estradiol and inhibin. Large amounts of progesterone come only from the corpus luteum after ovulation.

error.text: Estradiol switches to positive feedback, and LH surges; estradiol keeps rising until ovulation.
error.why: Estradiol peaks as the surge begins and then falls, because the LH is already turning the follicle’s cells toward making progesterone. That fall removes the stimulus and helps end the loop.

pathways.summary: The corpus luteum dies; FSH rises and rescues follicles; their estradiol and inhibin lower FSH and one follicle is selected; its high, sustained estradiol triggers the LH surge; ovulation follows; the corpus luteum forms and its progesterone holds everything down until it dies and the cycle repeats.

pathways.title: Why the functional layer is shed
pathways.intro: Without a pregnancy, the endometrium’s functional layer breaks down and is shed at the end of each cycle. Put the chain in order.

steps.label: Corpus luteum dies
steps.text: Without a pregnancy, the corpus luteum dies after 12 to 14 days.
steps.why: The corpus luteum’s lifespan sets the length of the luteal phase.

steps.label: Progesterone falls
steps.text: Progesterone falls, and the functional layer loses its support.
steps.why: The corpus luteum was the main source of progesterone.

steps.label: Prostaglandins, white cells
steps.text: Endometrial cells release prostaglandins and signals that draw in white blood cells.
steps.why: Progesterone withdrawal sets off this inflammatory response first.

steps.label: Enzymes digest the layer
steps.text: Enzymes from the white blood cells and the endometrium digest the tissue holding the functional layer together.
steps.why: The recruited white blood cells bring the enzymes that break the tissue down.

steps.label: Coiled arteries spasm
steps.text: The coiled arteries of the functional layer constrict in spasms, starving it of blood.
steps.why: Artery spasm adds to the breakdown already under way; it is not the main cause.

steps.label: Functional layer shed
steps.text: The functional layer breaks away and is shed with blood, and prostaglandins make the myometrium contract.
steps.why: The loosened, starved layer comes away, and the contractions squeeze it out, which is felt as cramps.

steps.label: Basal layer rebuilds
steps.text: The basal layer survives, and rising estradiol from new follicles makes its cells rebuild the functional layer.
steps.why: The basal layer has its own short arteries, so it is spared and supplies the cells for the next proliferative phase.

distractors.text: Estradiol rises sharply, and the functional layer is overstimulated.
distractors.why: Estradiol builds the lining; it does not shed it. Menstruation follows the fall of progesterone when the corpus luteum dies.

distractors.text: FSH falls, and the functional layer loses its support.
distractors.why: FSH does not act on the endometrium, and at this point FSH is rising. The endometrium depends on progesterone.

error.text: The basal layer is shed too, and the endometrium regrows from the myometrium.
error.why: Only the functional layer is shed. The basal layer stays, kept alive by its own short straight arteries, and regrows the functional layer.

pathways.summary: The corpus luteum dies, progesterone falls, prostaglandins and white blood cells arrive, enzymes digest the functional layer, the coiled arteries spasm, the layer is shed with cramps, and the surviving basal layer rebuilds it under rising estradiol.

pathways.title: Renal hydrogen ion secretion and new bicarbonate
pathways.intro: Your diet leaves about 70 mmol of sulfuric and phosphoric acid in your blood each day, and only the kidneys can remove it. Trace one hydrogen ion through a type A intercalated cell of the collecting duct, and see where the new bicarbonate comes from.

steps.label: CO2 enters the cell
steps.text: Carbon dioxide diffuses into a type A intercalated cell, from the blood and from the cell’s own metabolism.
steps.why: The H+ the cell secretes must be made first, and carbon dioxide and water are its raw materials.

steps.label: Carbonic anhydrase: H+ + HCO3−
steps.text: Carbonic anhydrase combines the carbon dioxide with water; the carbonic acid splits into H+ and HCO3−.
steps.why: This makes an acid and a base together inside the cell, so every H+ to be secreted comes with a partner bicarbonate.

steps.label: Proton pumps push H+ out
steps.text: An H+-ATPase, helped by an H+/K+ pump, spends ATP to push the H+ into the tubular fluid.
steps.why: The tubular fluid here is already more acidic than the cell, so moving H+ into it is uphill and needs primary active transport.

steps.label: H+ binds a urinary buffer
steps.text: In the lumen, the H+ binds filtered hydrogen phosphate (HPO4 2−) or ammonia (NH3).
steps.why: Almost no filtered bicarbonate is left this far along, so the H+ meets a urinary buffer instead. Free H+ alone could carry only a trace, because the pumps cannot drive urine pH below about 4.5.

steps.label: H+ leaves in the urine
steps.text: The H+ leaves in the urine as dihydrogen phosphate (titratable acid) or as trapped ammonium (NH4+).
steps.why: Charged NH4+ cannot diffuse back across the membrane, so the acid is excreted instead of recycled.

steps.label: New HCO3− enters the plasma
steps.text: The bicarbonate partner of each excreted H+ crosses the basolateral side on a band 3 exchanger, swapped for Cl−, and enters the plasma as new bicarbonate, replacing bicarbonate that a fixed acid used up.
steps.why: It is new because it was made in the cell, not reclaimed from the filtrate, and it adds to the blood only because its H+ partner left in the urine. Band 3 is the same kind of exchanger that runs the chloride shift in red blood cells. This is how plasma bicarbonate stays near 24 mmol/L despite the daily acid load.

distractors.text: H+ diffuses out of the cell through open channels, down its concentration gradient.
distractors.why: The tubular fluid is more acidic than the cell, so H+ must be pumped uphill with ATP; it cannot simply diffuse out.

distractors.text: The basolateral sodium–potassium pump moves H+ into the tubular fluid.
distractors.why: The sodium–potassium pump moves sodium and potassium across the basolateral membrane. H+ leaves type A cells through apical proton pumps.

distractors.text: Vesicles of ready-made sulfuric acid are released into the lumen by exocytosis.
distractors.why: The cell does not store acid. It makes H+ from carbon dioxide and water and pumps it out one ion at a time.

error.text: In the lumen, the H+ meets filtered bicarbonate and forms carbon dioxide and water, which is how the acid is excreted.
error.why: That is bicarbonate reclaim, mostly in the proximal tubule, and it excretes no acid: the H+ ends up in a water molecule. In the collecting duct, H+ binds phosphate or ammonia and leaves in the urine.

pathways.summary: Carbon dioxide enters; carbonic anhydrase makes H+ and HCO3−; proton pumps spend ATP pushing the H+ into the tubular fluid; it binds phosphate or ammonia and leaves in the urine; the bicarbonate goes to the blood on band 3 as new bicarbonate, one for every H+ excreted.

pathways.title: Reclaiming filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule
pathways.intro: Your kidneys filter about 4,300 mmol of bicarbonate a day, many times the day’s fixed acid. Losing even a tenth would acidify your blood. Follow one filtered bicarbonate as the proximal tubule reclaims it.

steps.label: HCO3− is filtered
steps.text: Bicarbonate, small and freely filtered, enters the tubular fluid at the glomerulus.
steps.why: Nothing can be reclaimed until it has been filtered; the filtered load is GFR times plasma bicarbonate.

steps.label: H+ secreted on the exchanger
steps.text: The proximal tubule cell secretes H+ into the lumen on the sodium–hydrogen exchanger, in exchange for Na+.
steps.why: The exchanger is powered by the sodium gradient that the basolateral sodium–potassium pump keeps up, so it needs no ATP of its own.

steps.label: H+ + HCO3− → carbonic acid
steps.text: In the lumen, the secreted H+ combines with the filtered bicarbonate to form carbonic acid.
steps.why: The H+ is there to meet the filtered bicarbonate; this is what removes it from the tubular fluid.

steps.label: Brush border: CO2 + water
steps.text: Carbonic anhydrase on the brush border quickly turns the carbonic acid into carbon dioxide and water.
steps.why: Carbonic acid would break down only slowly by itself; the enzyme keeps the reaction moving so bicarbonate does not pile up in the lumen.

steps.label: CO2 diffuses into the cell
steps.text: The carbon dioxide diffuses across the apical membrane into the cell.
steps.why: Carbon dioxide is a small, uncharged gas, so it crosses the membrane freely, unlike bicarbonate.

steps.label: Cell enzyme remakes HCO3−
steps.text: Carbonic anhydrase inside the cell turns the carbon dioxide and water back into H+ and HCO3−.
steps.why: The same reaction runs the other way inside the cell, rebuilding a bicarbonate and a fresh H+ to secrete.

steps.label: HCO3− and Na+ enter the blood
steps.text: The bicarbonate leaves across the basolateral membrane on a carrier that moves it with Na+, and enters the blood.
steps.why: The bicarbonate that reaches the blood is a new ion made in the cell; the filtered one became carbon dioxide. The effect is the same as moving it across, and no acid has been excreted.

distractors.text: The carbonic acid is carried into the cell by the sodium–potassium pump.
distractors.why: The sodium–potassium pump moves sodium and potassium on the basolateral side. Carbonic acid is broken into carbon dioxide and water, and only the carbon dioxide enters.

distractors.text: The carbonic acid stays in the lumen and leaves in the urine, excreting the acid.
distractors.why: Reclaiming bicarbonate excretes no acid. The carbonic acid is turned into carbon dioxide and water, and the carbon dioxide goes back into the cell.

error.text: The filtered bicarbonate ion itself crosses the cell unchanged and enters the blood.
error.why: Bicarbonate is charged and crosses the apical membrane poorly. The filtered ion is destroyed in the lumen; the one that enters the blood is made inside the cell from the carbon dioxide.

pathways.summary: Bicarbonate is filtered; H+ secreted on the sodium–hydrogen exchanger meets it; brush-border carbonic anhydrase turns the carbonic acid into carbon dioxide and water; the carbon dioxide enters the cell and is remade into HCO3−, which leaves with Na+ for the blood. About 80% of filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed this way.

pathways.title: Ammonium: the adjustable route for acid
pathways.intro: When acid keeps being added for days, the kidneys can raise ammonium excretion five- to tenfold. Trace how glutamine becomes ammonium in the urine and new bicarbonate in the blood.

steps.label: PT cells take up glutamine
steps.text: Proximal tubule cells take up the amino acid glutamine from the blood and the filtrate.
steps.why: Glutamine carries two nitrogen groups, the raw material for ammonia; an acid load speeds its uptake and breakdown.

steps.label: Glutamine → 2 NH4+ + 2 HCO3−
steps.text: Each glutamine is broken down into two NH4+, and as its carbon skeleton is used, two new HCO3− are made.
steps.why: Breaking down glutamine produces the ammonium and the bicarbonate together; this is where the new bicarbonate comes from.

steps.label: NH4+ to lumen, HCO3− to blood
steps.text: The NH4+ is secreted into the lumen, and the new HCO3− goes into the blood.
steps.why: The two products go opposite ways: the acid-carrying ammonium toward the urine, the base toward the plasma.

steps.label: Thick limb takes NH4+ back
steps.text: In the thick ascending limb, some NH4+ is taken back up and builds up in the medulla as ammonia.
steps.why: This loads the medulla with ammonia, near the collecting ducts where it will be needed.

steps.label: NH3 diffuses into the duct
steps.text: Uncharged ammonia (NH3) diffuses from the medulla into the lumen of the collecting duct.
steps.why: Being uncharged, ammonia crosses membranes easily and moves toward the acidic tubular fluid.

steps.label: NH3 + H+ → NH4+
steps.text: In the lumen, the ammonia takes up an H+ secreted by a type A intercalated cell and becomes NH4+.
steps.why: The secreted H+ needs a buffer to carry it; ammonia is one that the kidneys can make more of.

steps.label: NH4+ trapped and excreted
steps.text: The charged NH4+ cannot diffuse back across the membrane, so it is trapped and leaves in the urine.
steps.why: Only ammonium that leaves in the urine counts; each one excreted means one new bicarbonate kept in the blood.

distractors.text: In the lumen, ammonia binds filtered bicarbonate and leaves in the urine.
distractors.why: Ammonia is a base that takes up H+, not bicarbonate. It carries secreted acid out, while the bicarbonate stays in the blood.

distractors.text: In the lumen, ammonia is turned into urea, which leaves in the urine.
distractors.why: Urea is made in the liver, not the collecting duct. In the lumen, ammonia takes up a secreted H+ and becomes ammonium.

error.text: The NH4+ diffuses back into the blood, where it adds a new bicarbonate.
error.why: Charged NH4+ is trapped in the lumen. Ammonium that does return to the blood goes to the liver and is made into urea, which uses up bicarbonate and cancels the gain.

pathways.summary: Glutamine taken up by the proximal tubule becomes two NH4+ and two new HCO3−; the ammonium is secreted and the bicarbonate goes to the blood; the thick ascending limb loads the medulla with ammonia; ammonia diffuses into the collecting duct, takes up secreted H+, and the trapped NH4+ leaves in the urine.

pathways.title: From missing insulin to Kussmaul breathing
pathways.intro: Diabetic ketoacidosis links hormones, metabolism, the blood’s buffers and the lungs. Trace how a lack of insulin ends in deep, sighing breathing.

steps.label: Insulin absent, glucagon high
steps.text: Insulin is nearly absent, as in untreated type 1 diabetes, and glucagon stays high.
steps.why: Everything that follows is set off by this hormone imbalance, often after missed doses or an infection.

steps.label: Lipolysis floods the liver
steps.text: Lipolysis runs unchecked, and fatty acids flood into the liver.
steps.why: Insulin normally holds lipolysis back; without it, adipose tissue releases far more fatty acids.

steps.label: Ketone bodies made fast
steps.text: The liver turns the fatty acids into ketone bodies far faster than other tissues can burn them.
steps.why: Ketone bodies are normally burned about as fast as they are made; here production outruns use.

steps.label: Ketone acids release H+
steps.text: Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate release hydrogen ions into the blood.
steps.why: They are acids; building up faster than they are burned, they add H+ to the ECF.

steps.label: HCO3− used up; gap rises
steps.text: Bicarbonate is used up buffering the H+, and the ketone anions take its place, raising the anion gap.
steps.why: The buffer takes the first hit; the unmeasured ketone anions are why the gap rises.

steps.label: Arterial pH falls
steps.text: With bicarbonate falling, the ratio drops below 20 and arterial pH falls.
steps.why: Once buffering has used up much of the bicarbonate, the ratio and the pH fall.

steps.label: Carotid bodies drive breathing
steps.text: The carotid bodies sense the low pH and drive deep, fast Kussmaul breathing.
steps.why: The peripheral chemoreceptors respond within seconds to a fall in arterial pH from any acid.

steps.label: PaCO2 falls: compensation
steps.text: PaCO2 falls, moving the ratio back toward 20 and raising pH part of the way.
steps.why: Respiratory compensation lowers the bottom of the ratio; it cannot replace the lost bicarbonate.

distractors.text: The ketone bodies bind to bicarbonate and carry it out in the urine.
distractors.why: Ketone bodies use up bicarbonate by releasing H+ that bicarbonate buffers, not by binding it.

distractors.text: High glucose itself releases hydrogen ions into the blood.
distractors.why: Glucose is not an acid. The H+ comes from the ketone acids.

error.text: The central chemoreceptors sense the low pH and slow breathing to keep carbon dioxide in.
error.why: A falling pH speeds breathing, not slows it, and the fast sensor of a fixed acid is the carotid bodies, because hydrogen ions cross the blood–brain barrier poorly.

pathways.summary: No insulin; lipolysis floods the liver with fatty acids; ketone bodies are made faster than they are burned; their H+ uses up bicarbonate and their anions raise the anion gap; pH falls; the carotid bodies drive Kussmaul breathing; PaCO2 falls and partly restores the ratio.

pathways.title: How vomiting makes and keeps a metabolic alkalosis
pathways.intro: Healthy kidneys can excrete extra bicarbonate fast, so a lasting alkalosis needs two things: something that makes it and something that keeps it. Trace both in a person who vomits for days.

steps.label: Acid secreted: alkaline tide
steps.text: Parietal cells secrete H+ into the stomach, and for each one a bicarbonate enters the blood (the alkaline tide).
steps.why: This is where the extra bicarbonate comes from: every H+ made for the stomach leaves a base partner in the blood.

steps.label: Acid is vomited
steps.text: The acid is vomited instead of passing into the duodenum.
steps.why: The H+ leaves the body, so it is no longer there to cancel its partner bicarbonate.

steps.label: Tide is never used up
steps.text: The pancreas is not triggered to secrete bicarbonate into the duodenum, so the extra bicarbonate stays in the blood.
steps.why: Normally the acid reaching the duodenum triggers bicarbonate secretion that draws the tide back out of the blood; vomiting skips that step.

steps.label: Water, Cl−, K+ lost
steps.text: Vomiting also removes water, chloride and potassium, lowering blood volume.
steps.why: Vomit is hydrochloric acid and fluid, so each episode lowers volume and chloride as well.

steps.label: Kidneys keep bicarbonate
steps.text: Low volume (through angiotensin II and aldosterone), low chloride and low potassium make the kidneys keep bicarbonate instead of excreting it.
